comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text: Added child task opencode-coder-al7.10 to capture this session's OpenCode command-authoring guidance in docs/design/how-to-write-commands.md.

comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text:
## Command-vs-guide audit: init.md is a 265-line workflow spec, not a command

**What**: init.md is 265 lines with 5 multi-step workflow phases, detailed decision trees, mode detection logic, docs lifecycle inspection procedures, report templates, and interaction rules. It is a full design document embedded in a command file. By the guide's own standard, this is the single biggest offender — roughly 10x the recommended command shape.

**Why**: This command carries the entire init workflow inline. The guide says "If a command starts looking like a policy document, design doc, or multi-page workflow spec, move that content into a skill or reference." init.md is all three simultaneously. Every token in this file is consumed on every /init invocation.

**Suggested action**: When opencode-coder-al7.2 is executed, init.md should be cut to ~20-30 lines: load the skill, pass any arguments, say "follow the init workflow," done. The 240+ lines of procedure, detection logic, mode rules, and interaction checkpoints must move to the skill/reference layer (which is already planned in the existing task).

comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text:
## Command-vs-guide audit: docs.md, doctor.md, improve-doc.md carry workflow logic that belongs in the skill

**What**: These three commands (57, 59, and 59 lines respectively) each include numbered workflow steps, decision logic, and reporting templates that the guide says should live in skills/references. Specific violations:

- docs.md lines 18-41: full 5-step lifecycle procedure with mode resolution, inspection rules, and phase selection logic
- doctor.md lines 30-50: complete aimgr verify/repair decision tree with JSON field parsing instructions
- improve-doc.md lines 16-26: full input contract specification with argument patterns and fallback behavior

**Why**: The guide says "The command should route. The skill should explain. The references should detail." All three of these commands explain AND detail. They are mid-sized workflow documents, not thin wrappers. Each wastes ~40 lines of tokens on logic that would be loaded once via the skill.

**Suggested action**: When the corresponding tasks (al7.3, al7.5, al7.4) are executed, each should be reduced to the recommended ~15-line shape. The lifecycle procedures, decision trees, and input contracts move to the skill/reference layer. The commands just load the skill, pass arguments where relevant, and name the workflow.

comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text:
## Command-vs-guide audit: status.md bypasses the skill entirely — no skill loading at all

**What**: status.md (48 lines) never loads the opencode-coder skill. It says "Use direct bash commands to gather the following information" and then lists 4 groups of bash-based checks. The only skill reference is a conditional escalation at line 33: "If the user wants full troubleshooting guidance, load the opencode-coder skill." The default path is entirely self-contained.

**Why**: The guide says commands should "usually be a shortcut into a skill-backed workflow." status.md is the opposite — it is a self-contained procedure that only loads the skill as an optional escalation. This means the status-collection logic lives exclusively in the command file, with no reusable skill ownership. If a future agent or command needs the same status checks, it must duplicate them.

**Suggested action**: When al7.6 is executed, status.md should load the skill by default and delegate to the status/health reference. The self-contained bash procedure moves to the skill layer. The escalation-only pattern should be eliminated.

comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text:
## Command-vs-guide audit: dump-session.md is already close to the target shape

**What**: dump-session.md is 21 lines, loads no skill, has no arguments, and carries a simple 3-step procedure. It is the closest current command to being "thin." However, it still does not load a skill — it is entirely self-contained.

**Why**: The guide allows self-contained commands if they are "very small, utility-like, not reused elsewhere." dump-session arguably fits this exception. The question is whether the existing task (al7.8) to force it through a skill is worth the overhead.

**Suggested action**: This is a judgment call for the task implementer. dump-session.md could stay self-contained and still comply with the guide's escape hatch — but only if the guide's escape hatch is made explicit enough to justify it. If the decision is to keep it self-contained, the task should be closed as "compliant via escape hatch" rather than force-fitting a skill wrapper around a 3-step utility.

comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text:
## Command-vs-guide audit: every command uses the "Use /foo when..." anti-pattern the guide prohibits

**What**: All 7 commands open their body with a line matching the pattern "Use /opencode-coder/X when..." or "Use /opencode-coder/X to...":
- docs.md:7 — "Use /opencode-coder/docs when you want help..."
- doctor.md:7 — "Use /opencode-coder/doctor when the plugin setup may be broken..."
- dump-session.md:7 — "Use /opencode-coder/dump-session to export..."
- improve-doc.md:7 — "Use /opencode-coder/improve-doc when something went wrong..."
- init.md:7 — "Use /opencode-coder/init as the single entry point..."
- report-bug.md:7 — blockquote with Purpose line (variant of the pattern)
- status.md:7 — "Use /opencode-coder/status to inspect..."

**Why**: The guide (line 205) explicitly calls this out as an anti-pattern: "Do not fill command bodies with prose that exists only to explain the command to a human who has already invoked it." A 100% violation rate means either the rule is not being followed or it was written after these commands and has not been applied retroactively.

**Suggested action**: All command refactoring tasks should strip these opening lines. The description frontmatter already tells the user what the command does. The body should start with the action instruction.

comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text:
## Command-vs-guide audit: no command uses $ARGUMENTS despite some accepting user input

**What**: improve-doc.md explicitly documents an input contract (free-text + optional issue ID) but never uses $ARGUMENTS to wire it. report-bug.md implicitly expects bug context from the user but also never references $ARGUMENTS. The guide says "Do not rely on accidental or implicit argument behavior" and "If user input matters, reference it explicitly in the command template." Both commands violate this.

**Why**: Without explicit $ARGUMENTS wiring, these commands rely on the agent picking up trailing user text from the conversation context, which is the exact "accidental" behavior the guide warns against. It works by coincidence, not by design.

**Suggested action**: When al7.4 and al7.7 are executed, both commands should include $ARGUMENTS in their body to explicitly pass user-supplied context to the skill workflow. Commands that do not accept arguments (dump-session, status, possibly doctor) should stay argument-free as the guide recommends.

comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text:
## Command-vs-guide audit: inconsistent skill-loading conventions across commands

**What**: Commands use three different patterns for loading skills:
1. Code block with tool call: doctor.md and init.md use "skill({ name: 'opencode-coder' })" in a code block
2. Prose instruction: docs.md, improve-doc.md, report-bug.md use "Load the opencode-coder skill" as prose
3. No skill loading at all: dump-session.md and status.md

The guide says "load the skill" in its recommended shape but does not specify the calling convention.

**Why**: Inconsistency in how skills are loaded makes it unclear which pattern the agent actually interprets correctly. If one pattern is more reliable than another, using the wrong one could cause silent failures where the skill is not actually loaded.

**Suggested action**: The guide (al7.10) should specify the canonical skill-loading pattern. Then all refactoring tasks should use it consistently. If the code-block tool-call pattern is what OpenCode actually resolves, use that everywhere. If prose works identically, document that and pick one.

comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text:
## Command-vs-guide audit: commands enumerate specific references, undermining the skill layer

**What**: docs.md (lines 13-14) tells the agent to use "references/project-structure.md" and "references/project-docs-lifecycle.md". init.md (lines 19-24) lists 6 specific references. improve-doc.md (lines 13-14) lists 2 references. The guide says the skill should own routing to references, but these commands hardcode the routing in the command body.

**Why**: When a command hardcodes which references to use, it duplicates routing logic that should live in the skill. If a reference is renamed, moved, or replaced, both the skill and the command need updating. This is exactly the duplication the guide warns against: "Do not restate logic in both the command and the skill."

**Suggested action**: When these commands are refactored, they should say "Load the skill and follow the X workflow" — the skill decides which references are needed. Commands should not name references unless they are intentionally overriding the skill's default routing for a specific reason.

title: Smoke test the ported skill-creator in OpenCode
description:
## Description
Run the ported `opencode-coder-skill-creator` skill in OpenCode on representative workflows to prove the documented OpenCode path actually works, using the project's documented testing infrastructure and confirming that preserved upstream guidance is still usable in practice.

## Instructions
1. Use the testing guidance in `docs/TESTING.md` to choose the appropriate project-supported test method for skill behavior verification.
2. Use the OpenCode command-line tool only for execution/testing. Do not start the OpenCode application/GUI.
3. Define a representative smoke-test set that covers at least:
   - creating a new skill from scratch
   - improving an existing skill
   - running the review/iteration loop in the OpenCode-compatible way
   - exercising at least one preserved upstream guidance section such as `Skill Writing Guide` or `How to think about improvements`
4. Execute the ported skill in OpenCode using the project's documented testing/manual-testing infrastructure and record the exact commands or scenarios used.
5. Record what worked, what failed, and any degraded/manual steps that were required.
6. If any workflow fails, create follow-up issues or update the relevant task descriptions before closing this task.
7. Summarize the smoke-test results in a durable location the acceptance review can inspect.

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] The smoke test uses the project's documented testing infrastructure from `docs/TESTING.md`
- [ ] The smoke test uses the OpenCode command-line tool only and does not rely on starting the OpenCode application/GUI
- [ ] A representative OpenCode smoke-test set is defined and executed
- [ ] Results are recorded for creating a new skill, improving an existing skill, the rewritten review loop, and at least one preserved upstream guidance section
- [ ] Any failures or degraded/manual steps are explicitly documented
- [ ] Follow-up issues are created for any discovered gaps that are out of scope for the epic
close_reason: Completed CLI-only manual smoke coverage via bun run test:manual command mode with fixture isolation; validated create/improve/review-loop/preserved-guidance behavior and recorded durable results in docs/testing/opencode-coder-a1p.6-skill-creator-smoke-2026-03-24.md; filed follow-up bug opencode-coder-aeq for non-blocking isolated dynatrace plugin install 404 noise.

comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text:
## Smoke test should verify BOTH OpenCode compatibility AND upstream content preservation

**What**: The current smoke test criteria focus on "does the skill work in OpenCode" (create a skill, improve a skill, run the review loop). Under the new direction, the smoke test should also verify that preserved upstream content actually functions. Specifically:

Additional smoke test scenarios:
1. **Skill Writing Guide usage**: Ask the skill to help write a SKILL.md for a new skill. Verify the output follows the Anatomy of a Skill structure, uses progressive disclosure, and references the patterns from the Writing Guide section. If the upstream content was preserved but the agent ignores it, that's a different problem worth catching.
2. **Improvement reasoning**: Ask the skill to improve an existing skill after a mock review cycle. Verify the agent's reasoning references the "How to think about improvements" guidance (generalization, keeping prompt lean, explaining the why).
3. **Eval query quality**: Ask the skill to generate trigger eval queries. Verify the agent produces queries matching the upstream's quality bar (realistic, detailed, with good/bad examples comparable to the upstream's examples).

**Why**: Preserving upstream content is only valuable if the agent actually uses it. The upstream content is pedagogical — it teaches the agent to do things well. If we preserve it but it sits inert in the document while the agent follows only the mechanical workflow steps, the preservation is cosmetic.

**Suggested action**: Add these scenarios to a1p.6's acceptance criteria alongside the existing functional tests.

title: Compare the OpenCode skill against the Anthropic skill on representative workflows
description:
## Description
Compare the OpenCode port against the upstream Anthropic skill with content preservation as the primary deliverable and feature-parity judgment as the secondary deliverable.

## Instructions
1. Produce a structured, section-by-section diff between the upstream Anthropic `SKILL.md` and the OpenCode port.
2. For each section, classify the port's treatment as one of:
   - preserved verbatim
   - preserved with Claude-specific/OpenCode compatibility patches
   - OpenCode-specific addition
   - removed with rationale
   - rewritten with rationale
3. Identify any generic upstream content that appears to have been unnecessarily changed, removed, or weakened.
4. Evaluate representative workflows where parity is realistically comparable, such as:
   - helping a user create a new skill
   - improving an existing skill
   - deciding whether and how to create eval prompts
   - guiding the review/iteration loop
   - handling description-optimization / trigger-eval work in whatever OpenCode replacement path now exists
5. Use a concrete comparison rubric that considers clarity, completeness, actionability, preservation of useful upstream guidance, honesty about limitations, and whether the OpenCode replacement preserves the original skill's capability.
6. Record the comparison results and identify any gaps that must be fixed before the epic can close.

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] A section-by-section upstream-vs-port diff exists
- [ ] Every material difference is classified as preserved, patched, OpenCode-specific addition, removed with rationale, or rewritten with rationale
- [ ] Generic upstream regressions are explicitly identified
- [ ] Representative workflow comparison exists for realistically comparable workflows, including the replacement path for description optimization / trigger-eval work
- [ ] Any regressions that matter for the epic are either fixed or explicitly documented before closure
- [ ] The comparison supports a credible claim that the OpenCode port reaches feature parity for the original skill's core workflows
close_reason: Completed structured upstream-vs-port parity comparison evidence with section classifications, workflow rubric evaluation, and blocker/gap assessment in tracked references artifact.

comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text:
## The parity comparison (a1p.7) should be restructured as a content-parity diff, not just a workflow comparison

**What**: The current a1p.7 description defines comparison as running both skills through representative workflows and judging output quality. With the new "minimal port" direction, the most important comparison is textual: a section-by-section diff showing what changed and why. Workflow comparison remains valuable but is secondary.

Proposed restructure for a1p.7:

**Primary deliverable**: A structured diff document that lists every section of the upstream SKILL.md and classifies the port's treatment:
- Preserved verbatim
- Preserved with Claude-specific line patches (list each patch)
- New OpenCode addition (not in upstream)
- Removed with rationale
- Rewritten with rationale

**Secondary deliverable**: The existing workflow comparison (run representative prompts against both, classify as better/equivalent/worse/intentionally different).

**Why**: The textual diff is more actionable and faster to produce than the workflow comparison. It directly answers the user's question: "did we lose upstream content?" The workflow comparison answers a different question: "does the port produce comparable outputs?" Both matter, but the content-preservation check should be primary.

**Suggested action**: Update a1p.7 instructions to lead with the structured diff, then follow with representative workflow comparison.

title: Rewrite the general skill-creator workflow and user guidance for OpenCode
description:
## Description
Rewrite the user-facing `opencode-coder-skill-creator` workflow for OpenCode beyond evaluation/validation. This task owns the main SKILL.md rewrite inside `ai-resources/skills/opencode-coder-skill-creator`, including the bundled `agents/*.md` mapping, the top-level guidance for creating new skills and improving existing ones, packaging/presentation guidance, environment assumptions, and non-Claude-CLI workflow steps that must be adapted to OpenCode.

## Instructions
1. Audit only the vendored skill content under `ai-resources/skills/opencode-coder-skill-creator/` for Claude Code-, Claude.ai-, and Cowork-specific guidance outside the description-optimization pipeline.
2. Fold the bundled `agents/*.md` mapping into the rewritten workflow and document how each instruction file should be used with the standard OpenCode agents available in this project (`orchestrator`, `tasker`, `reviewer`, `verifier`).
3. Document model-selection guidance for the ported workflow, including when to prefer stronger reasoning models for skill-writing/review work and how that differs from Anthropic's original assumptions.
4. Rewrite the user-facing workflow sections so they describe how OpenCode should help users:
   - create a new skill from scratch
   - improve an existing skill
   - choose whether to create test cases
   - run qualitative review loops
   - explain results and next steps in OpenCode terms
5. Replace Claude-specific runtime assumptions in the general workflow, including terminology, tool references, browser assumptions, session/task expectations, and packaging/presentation wording.
6. Explicitly resolve non-CLI workflow gaps that live in SKILL.md, including:
   - subagent timing/token capture guidance in the run/eval loop
   - the `eval_review.html` browser flow and cross-platform/headless fallback expectations
   - the `package_skill.py` / "Package and Present" section and any `present_files` assumptions
7. Preserve the original skill's useful intent-capture and iteration guidance, but adapt the execution layer to actual OpenCode capabilities.
8. Make sure the rewritten guidance is coherent with the separate task for the description-optimization/eval pipeline.

## Files to Modify
- ai-resources/skills/opencode-coder-skill-creator/SKILL.md — rewrite general workflow, agent mapping, model guidance, and user guidance for OpenCode
- ai-resources/skills/opencode-coder-skill-creator/agents/grader.md — clarify OpenCode usage if needed
- ai-resources/skills/opencode-coder-skill-creator/agents/comparator.md — clarify OpenCode usage if needed
- ai-resources/skills/opencode-coder-skill-creator/agents/analyzer.md — clarify OpenCode usage if needed
- ai-resources/skills/opencode-coder-skill-creator/references/* — update supporting docs if needed
- ai-resources/skills/opencode-coder-skill-creator/eval-viewer/* — update wording if the general guidance references it

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] SKILL.md contains a step-by-step OpenCode workflow for creating a new skill using only agents/tools available in this project
- [ ] SKILL.md contains a step-by-step OpenCode workflow for improving an existing skill, including at least one iteration of modify → review → improve
- [ ] The bundled `agents/*.md` instruction files have explicit OpenCode agent mappings based on the standard project agents
- [ ] SKILL.md includes explicit model-selection guidance for key skill-creation/review workflows
- [ ] Every reference to Claude Code, Claude.ai, Cowork, TodoList, `present_files`, or unavailable tooling is removed or replaced in the general workflow sections owned by this task
- [ ] The timing-capture guidance, browser-based eval-review flow, and packaging/presentation section are rewritten or documented with OpenCode-appropriate fallbacks
- [ ] All implementation edits for this task stay inside `ai-resources/skills/opencode-coder-skill-creator` and related project docs, not `.opencode/skills/*`
- [ ] The rewritten guidance is coherent with the separate description-optimization/eval task
close_reason: Rewrote skill-creator workflow for OpenCode, added agent mappings, replaced unavailable-runtime assumptions, and documented OpenCode fallbacks for timing, browser review, and packaging.

comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text:
## package_skill.py references present_files tool — not audited in any task

**What**: SKILL.md lines 408-416 say "Package and Present (only if present_files tool is available)" and reference package_skill.py. The present_files tool is a Claude Code concept that does not exist in OpenCode. The package_skill.py script itself is pure Python (zipfile, pathlib) with no Claude dependency — it works anywhere. But the SKILL.md prose around it assumes Claude Code packaging/presentation semantics. No task explicitly covers this section. Task a1p.2 lists scripts to audit but does not include package_skill.py. Task a1p.5 covers general workflow but the "Package and Present" section sits between the eval pipeline and environment-specific sections, so its ownership is ambiguous.

**Why**: After all tasks close, the SKILL.md will still contain "only if present_files tool is available" guidance that OpenCode users cannot follow. This is a minor gap but exactly the kind of thing that makes the ported skill feel unfinished.

**Suggested action**: Add package_skill.py audit and the "Package and Present" SKILL.md section to task a1p.5's scope (it fits naturally as part of general workflow rewrite). The fix is simple: rewrite the section to say "use package_skill.py to create a .skill zip" without the present_files gate, or document what the OpenCode equivalent packaging workflow is (likely aimgr-based per a1p.4).

comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text:
## Task .5 acceptance criteria are vague — "explains how" is not testable

**What**: All four acceptance criteria use the pattern "The skill explains how OpenCode should help users [do X]." This is subjective — who judges whether the explanation is sufficient? A verifier reading criterion 1 ("explains how OpenCode should help users create a new skill from scratch") could pass it if SKILL.md contains a single sentence about creating skills, or fail it if they expect a 50-line walkthrough. There is no objective bar.

**Why**: Task .5 is the largest prose-rewriting task. Its output — the rewritten SKILL.md general workflow — is the primary user-facing deliverable of the entire epic. Vague acceptance criteria for the most important task means the most important output has the least quality control.

**Suggested action**: Replace with specific, verifiable criteria:
- "SKILL.md contains a step-by-step workflow for creating a new skill that references only OpenCode agents (orchestrator, tasker, reviewer, verifier) and OpenCode-available tools"
- "SKILL.md contains a step-by-step workflow for improving an existing skill including at least one iteration of: modify → test → review feedback → modify again"
- "Every reference to Claude Code, Claude.ai, Cowork, TodoList, present_files, or claude -p has been removed or replaced with an OpenCode equivalent"
- "SKILL.md lines 420-483 (Claude.ai-specific, Cowork-specific, and closing sections) are rewritten or removed for OpenCode"

comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text:
## Task .5 has no dependency on .1 or .2 but rewrites the same file — needs sequencing

**What**: Task .5 modifies SKILL.md for general workflow rewrite. Tasks .1 and .2 also modify SKILL.md for agent mapping and eval pipeline respectively. But .5 has no blocking dependency on either .1 or .2 — it only depends on the parent epic. If a tasker starts .5 before .1 completes, they will be rewriting SKILL.md prose that .1 is simultaneously modifying for agent mappings. Similarly, .5 and .2 have overlapping scope on the Claude.ai/Cowork sections.

**Why**: Without explicit ordering, these tasks will produce conflicting edits to the same 485-line file. The existing comment about .1 blocking .2 is correct but incomplete — .5 is now a third editor that needs to be sequenced.

**Suggested action**: Make .5 depend on .1 (so agent mapping edits land first, then .5 can rewrite around them). Then make .2 depend on .5 (so the eval pipeline task works against the fully rewritten SKILL.md). Final chain: .1 → .5 → .2 → .3 (acceptance). Task .4 (packaging) is independent and can run in parallel with any of them.

comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text:
## The subagent timing/token capture (SKILL.md Step 3) needs explicit resolution — currently in a gap between tasks

**What**: SKILL.md lines 207-219 (Step 3: "As runs complete, capture timing data") assume that when a subagent completes, you "receive a notification containing total_tokens and duration_ms." This is a Claude Code-specific subagent completion metadata feature. The prior epic comment (019d1c3a-63ff) identified this as one of three hard portability problems. But looking at the task descriptions:

- a1p.1 covers agent mapping (which agent type to use), not subagent metadata
- a1p.2 covers Claude CLI scripts, not SKILL.md subagent workflow steps
- a1p.5 covers general workflow rewrite but does not specifically mention timing capture

Step 3 is a workflow step in the "Running and evaluating test cases" section. It falls in the gap between .5 (general workflow) and .2 (eval pipeline scripts). Whoever works on .5 might assume .2 handles it (because it is about evaluation). Whoever works on .2 might assume .5 handles it (because it is a SKILL.md workflow step).

**Why**: If neither task claims ownership, this Claude Code-specific assumption survives in the ported skill. A user following the workflow will hit Step 3 and have no way to capture timing data in OpenCode (unless OpenCode agents provide equivalent metadata, which is unverified).

**Suggested action**: Explicitly assign Step 3 (subagent timing capture) to task a1p.5 as part of the general workflow rewrite. Add an instruction to a1p.5: "For Step 3 (timing data capture), verify whether OpenCode agents provide total_tokens and duration_ms on subagent completion. If yes, document how to access it. If no, rewrite Step 3 to either skip timing capture or use an alternative measurement approach."

comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text:
## The eval_review.html browser flow (SKILL.md lines 362-373) needs resolution — not covered by any task

**What**: SKILL.md "Description Optimization" Step 2 (lines 362-373) describes a flow where the skill creates an HTML file from a template, opens it in the browser, the user edits eval queries in the browser UI, clicks "Export Eval Set," and the file downloads to ~/Downloads/. This flow has these issues for OpenCode:

1. `open /tmp/eval_review_<name>.html` is macOS-specific (should be xdg-open on Linux, or platform-agnostic)
2. The flow assumes browser access, which may not exist in headless/remote environments
3. The "downloads to ~/Downloads/" assumption is browser/OS-specific

This is not a Claude CLI dependency — it is a browser/OS dependency. Task .2 covers Claude CLI. Task .5 covers general workflow. Neither explicitly mentions the eval_review.html flow.

**Why**: This is a usability issue, not a blocking issue. The flow will work on most developer workstations. But it should be documented with the same honesty as other environment assumptions. Also, the eval-viewer already has a --static fallback for headless environments; a similar note should exist for the eval review HTML.

**Suggested action**: Add to a1p.5's scope: "Review the eval_review.html browser flow in the Description Optimization section and ensure it works cross-platform or has documented fallbacks for headless/remote environments."

title: Resolve Claude CLI-based description optimization and eval flow for OpenCode
description:
## Description
Resolve the Claude CLI-based description-optimization and trigger-evaluation pipeline for the OpenCode port without driving unnecessary rewrites of generic upstream skill content. This task should work against the upstream-preserving SKILL.md produced by `opencode-coder-a1p.8`.

## Instructions
1. Audit the copied scripts and supporting files for Claude Code-specific execution assumptions, with special focus on:
   - `scripts/run_eval.py`
   - `scripts/improve_description.py`
   - `scripts/run_loop.py`
   - `scripts/package_skill.py` where it interacts with workflow assumptions
2. Document exactly what each Claude-specific script currently does, including nested `claude -p`, temporary `.claude/commands` injection, and Claude stream-json/tool-event assumptions.
3. For the description-optimization/eval pipeline, evaluate whether each flow should be replaced, simplified, or explicitly deferred for OpenCode.
4. Update scripts and supporting docs as needed, but treat the main SKILL.md as owned by `opencode-coder-a1p.8`; only make SKILL.md edits here if they are strictly required to reflect the script audit outcome.
5. For every deferred capability, document the missing OpenCode primitive, the manual fallback (if any), and any needed follow-up issue.

## Files to Modify
- ai-resources/skills/opencode-coder-skill-creator/scripts/run_eval.py — replace or defer Claude CLI trigger-eval behavior
- ai-resources/skills/opencode-coder-skill-creator/scripts/improve_description.py — replace or defer Claude CLI description rewrite behavior
- ai-resources/skills/opencode-coder-skill-creator/scripts/run_loop.py — adjust orchestration/report behavior for OpenCode
- ai-resources/skills/opencode-coder-skill-creator/scripts/package_skill.py — verify packaging assumptions align with the OpenCode workflow if needed
- ai-resources/skills/opencode-coder-skill-creator/SKILL.md — only for minimal compatibility notes required by the audit outcome after `opencode-coder-a1p.8`

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] The current Claude CLI dependencies are explicitly identified and documented
- [ ] Each description-optimization/eval flow is classified as replaced, redesigned, simplified, or deferred
- [ ] No required documented workflow step still depends on `claude -p`
- [ ] Every deferred capability includes rationale, the missing OpenCode primitive or blocker, and any needed follow-up issue or manual fallback guidance
- [ ] The final documentation makes the description-optimization limitations and chosen replacement strategy explicit rather than implied
close_reason: Audited Claude CLI dependencies, deferred unsupported automation scripts with explicit machine-readable blockers/fallbacks, documented pipeline decisions in a tracked audit doc, updated SKILL.md required workflow to manual non-claude path, and verified package_skill OpenCode workflow assumptions.

comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text:
## Task 2 is massive — it contains at least 3 distinct problems conflated as one

**What**: Task opencode-coder-a1p.2 bundles three fundamentally different problems into a single task:

**Problem A — Description optimization loop (run_eval.py + improve_description.py + run_loop.py)**: This is the automated trigger-testing and description-rewriting pipeline. It requires a headless CLI that can spawn isolated sessions and parse tool-use events. This isn't a "remove dependency" fix — it requires either (a) building a new OpenCode primitive, (b) designing a completely different manual workflow, or (c) deferring the feature. This is a design problem.

**Problem B — Subagent eval execution and timing capture (SKILL.md Steps 1-3)**: The skill assumes you can spawn parallel subagents, receive structured completion notifications with total_tokens/duration_ms, and capture timing.json. This needs verification of whether OpenCode subagent spawning provides equivalent metadata, and if not, what the degraded workflow looks like.

**Problem C — Browser/viewer/report flow (generate_review.py, generate_report.py, eval-viewer)**: These are Python stdlib HTTP server + webbrowser.open(). They actually work in any environment with Python — this is NOT a Claude Code dependency. The skill already has --static fallback for headless environments. This is a non-problem being grouped with real problems.

**Why**: A tasker receiving this task has no way to estimate effort, can't make incremental progress, and will inevitably discover mid-task that Problem A requires a design decision that blocks everything. Conflating the trivial (Problem C) with the impossible (Problem A) in one task guarantees scope creep.

**Suggested action**: Split into separate tasks:
- Task for Problem A: "Design OpenCode-native approach for description optimization (or explicitly defer it)"  
- Task for Problem B: "Verify OpenCode subagent metadata and adapt eval execution flow"
- Problem C doesn't need a task — remove it from scope since the viewer already works on any Python environment. Just document this fact.

comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text:
## Task 2 acceptance criteria #2 is not testable — "there is an OpenCode-native execution design for each required flow"

**What**: Criteria #2 says "There is an OpenCode-native execution design for each required flow." This is unverifiable. Who decides whether a "design" exists? What constitutes a "design"? A paragraph? A working script? A diagram? And "each required flow" — which flows are required? The task doesn't define which flows are core vs. optional.

**Why**: A verifier checking this criterion has no objective basis to pass or fail it. This will cause disagreement at acceptance review time and likely rework. Compare with criteria #3 ("No required core workflow still depends on claude -p") which is at least binary.

**Suggested action**: Replace with specific, verifiable criteria. For example:
- "Each flow that currently depends on claude -p has one of: (a) a working OpenCode-native replacement, (b) a documented deferral with rationale for why it cannot be replaced, or (c) a documented simplification that achieves the same goal differently."
- "The SKILL.md contains an 'OpenCode Limitations' section listing every deferred or unavailable capability."

comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text:
## Task 2 misidentifies eval-viewer and schemas.md as Claude CLI dependencies — they are not

**What**: The files-to-modify list includes:
- "ai-resources/skills/opencode-coder-skill-creator/eval-viewer/* — update wording or flow if needed"
- "ai-resources/skills/opencode-coder-skill-creator/references/schemas.md — update runtime assumptions if needed"

After reading eval-viewer/generate_review.py and eval-viewer/viewer.html: these are pure Python stdlib (http.server, json, base64, pathlib) with --static fallback. They have zero Claude Code dependency. Similarly, references/schemas.md defines JSON structures — it has no runtime assumptions beyond the data formats.

**Why**: Including these files signals to a tasker that they need modification, which wastes time auditing files that don't need changes. It also inflates the apparent scope of the task.

**Suggested action**: Remove eval-viewer/* and references/schemas.md from the files-to-modify list. If schemas.md needs a note about timing.json capture differences in OpenCode, that belongs in the subagent-metadata task, not here.

comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text:
## Missing task: quick_validate.py, package_skill.py, aggregate_benchmark.py, generate_report.py not audited

**What**: Task 2's instructions list only three scripts to audit: run_eval.py, improve_description.py, run_loop.py. But the scripts/ directory also contains:
- quick_validate.py — uses yaml.safe_load, pure Python, no Claude dependency (fine as-is)
- package_skill.py — not audited in any task  
- aggregate_benchmark.py — not audited in any task
- generate_report.py — imported by run_loop.py, generates HTML reports (pure Python, fine as-is)

package_skill.py is referenced in SKILL.md line 412 in the context of "Package and Present (only if present_files tool is available)" — present_files is a Claude Code tool concept.

**Why**: If package_skill.py has Claude Code-specific assumptions (like expecting `present_files` tool), and it's not in any task's audit scope, it will slip through.

**Suggested action**: Add package_skill.py to task 2's audit list. The others (quick_validate.py, aggregate_benchmark.py, generate_report.py) are pure Python and can be noted as "no changes needed" in the audit, but should still be mentioned for completeness.

comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text:
## Task .2 acceptance criteria improved since first review but still missing the key decision output

**What**: The current acceptance criteria require: (1) Claude CLI deps identified, (2) each flow classified as replaced/redesigned/simplified/deferred, (3) no required workflow depends on claude -p, (4) unsupported behavior documented. These are better than before. But the most important deliverable of this task is missing from the criteria: a design document or decision record for the description optimization pipeline. The classification (criterion 2) will almost certainly be "defer" for run_eval.py and improve_description.py since OpenCode has no headless CLI equivalent. But "defer" without a plan for what comes next is a dead end.

**Why**: The description optimization pipeline is the most sophisticated and differentiating feature of the original Anthropic skill. If we defer it with just "OpenCode can't do this," we are explicitly accepting that our skill will be strictly worse than the Anthropic version in its most valuable capability. A "defer" classification should come with: (a) what OpenCode primitive would be needed to support this, (b) whether a manual/simplified alternative is feasible, (c) a follow-up issue for when the primitive becomes available.

**Suggested action**: Add an acceptance criterion: "Each deferred capability includes: (a) a description of what OpenCode would need to support it, (b) whether a manual alternative was considered and why it was accepted or rejected, (c) a follow-up beads issue for future implementation if applicable."

comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text:
## Task .2 needs a decision: is the description optimization pipeline worth porting manually, or is deferral the right call?

**What**: Task .2 will encounter this fork and the task does not pre-decide which path to take. The three options are:

**Option A — Defer entirely**: Document that automated trigger evaluation and description optimization require a headless CLI (opencode -p equivalent) that does not exist. File a follow-up issue. The ported skill has no eval automation. This is honest but means our skill is strictly worse than the Anthropic version for its most differentiated feature.

**Option B — Manual alternative**: Replace the automated pipeline with a manual workflow. Instead of run_eval.py spawning 20 parallel claude -p sessions, the SKILL.md could instruct: "Ask the user to manually test 5 trigger prompts and report which ones activated the skill. Use the results to manually rewrite the description." This is slower and less rigorous but preserves the capability at human speed.

**Option C — OpenCode scripting alternative**: Investigate whether OpenCode's Bash tool + LLM API calls could replicate the pipeline. Instead of claude -p, the scripts could call the OpenCode-configured LLM API directly with the eval prompts. This is more work but could produce a genuinely better result than the original.

**Why**: The task says "decide for each flow" but does not guide the tasker toward which decision framework to use. A tasker encountering this will either pick the easiest option (defer everything) or get stuck trying to evaluate options without clear criteria for choosing.

**Suggested action**: Add to .2's instructions: "For the description optimization pipeline specifically, evaluate Options A/B/C (defer, manual alternative, API-based alternative) and document your recommendation with rationale. If choosing Option A (defer), file a follow-up beads issue for future implementation. If choosing Option B or C, implement the alternative and test it once."

comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text:
## a1p.2 scope should shrink under the new "minimal port" direction — most of its SKILL.md work moves to a1p.8

**What**: Task a1p.2 currently owns resolving the Claude CLI eval pipeline AND rewriting the SKILL.md sections that reference it. Under the new direction, the SKILL.md rewrite is handled by a1p.8 (start from upstream, apply minimal patches). What remains for a1p.2 is narrower:

1. **Audit and document** the Claude-specific dependencies in scripts (run_eval.py, improve_description.py, run_loop.py) — this is still needed
2. **Classify each script** as: works in OpenCode, needs modification, or deferred — still needed
3. **For deferred scripts**: ensure the SKILL.md (as produced by a1p.8) accurately marks them as deferred with rationale — this becomes a review/verification step, not an implementation step
4. **Do NOT rewrite SKILL.md sections** — a1p.8 owns all SKILL.md changes

The key change: a1p.2 should depend on a1p.8 (not the reverse), because a1p.8 produces the SKILL.md and a1p.2 verifies that the script-related sections are correctly documented.

**Why**: Under the old plan, a1p.2 and a1p.5 both edited SKILL.md (a known collision risk flagged in prior review comments). The new direction resolves this by making a1p.8 the single owner of SKILL.md. But a1p.2's current description still claims SKILL.md ownership. If not updated, a1p.2 will re-introduce rewrites that a1p.8 was designed to prevent.

**Suggested action**: 
1. Remove "SKILL.md — replace Claude CLI workflow instructions and parity claims" from a1p.2's files-to-modify
2. Add a1p.8 as a blocking dependency for a1p.2
3. Narrow a1p.2 scope to: audit scripts, classify as working/modified/deferred, verify a1p.8's SKILL.md accurately reflects the classification, file follow-up issues for any scripts that need non-trivial modification

title: Acceptance Review: Support skill creator fully in OpenCode
description:
## Description
Verify that the `opencode-coder-skill-creator` port works in OpenCode without Claude-specific incompatibilities, without unnecessary regressions against the generic upstream Anthropic skill content, and with feature parity for the original skill's core workflows.

## Instructions
1. Verify that all child tasks for this epic are closed.
2. Read the final port and confirm that every referenced agent, tool, script, and workflow step exists and is usable in OpenCode.
3. Verify that no generic upstream guidance was unnecessarily removed or materially rewritten without rationale.
4. Verify that the OpenCode-packaged skill can be installed and reached through the documented `aimgr` workflow.
5. Review the smoke-test results for representative workflows and confirm the skill was actually exercised in OpenCode.
6. Review the upstream-vs-port diff and parity comparison results and confirm the final documentation accurately reflects where the OpenCode skill matches, extends, or intentionally differs from upstream.
7. Specifically verify that the original skill's description-optimization / trigger-eval capability now has a real OpenCode replacement path rather than a permanent deferral.

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] All epic child tasks are closed
- [ ] The documented `aimgr` workflow makes the project-packaged skill available in OpenCode
- [ ] The final SKILL.md contains no Claude-specific incompatibilities that would break or mislead OpenCode users
- [ ] The final SKILL.md preserves generic upstream content unless a specific rationale documents why a change was required
- [ ] A section-by-section upstream diff exists and every material change is classified and justified
- [ ] Representative OpenCode smoke tests were executed and their results are recorded
- [ ] A real OpenCode-capable replacement exists for description-optimization / trigger-eval workflow; permanent deferral is not accepted for epic closure
- [ ] The skill's documented workflow is internally consistent for OpenCode users and accurately states remaining limitations without overstating parity

## Owner
verifier
close_reason: Verified all child tasks closed, reconciled repo-root aimgr install state, added durable smoke load-proof logs showing opencode-coder-skill-creator tool_use in representative create/improve runs, confirmed upstream diff/parity artifacts, and confirmed the OpenCode-native trigger-eval/description-optimization replacement is implemented and documented.

comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text:
## Acceptance review task has no dependency on task 2 — only on task 1

**What**: Looking at the dependency graph, opencode-coder-a1p.3 shows "blocks" dependencies from both a1p.1 and a1p.2. Good — this is correct. However, the acceptance criteria for a1p.3 don't specifically verify the hardest deliverable: what happened to the description optimization loop. The criteria say "Claude CLI-dependent paths have been replaced, rewritten, or explicitly deferred" — but this is so vague it could pass with a one-line deferral note.

**Why**: The description optimization pipeline (run_eval + improve_description + run_loop) is the most complex and valuable part of the skill. If it gets hand-waved as "deferred" with no design for what comes next, the epic has failed in spirit while passing on paper.

**Suggested action**: Add a specific acceptance criterion to a1p.3: "The description optimization workflow either (a) has a working OpenCode-native alternative, or (b) has a documented gap analysis explaining what OpenCode primitive would be needed and what interim manual workflow users should follow."

comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text:
## Acceptance review criterion "validate the final workflow by checking that the skill can be followed entirely" is not operationally defined

**What**: Criterion #4 of a1p.3 says "The skill's documented workflow is internally consistent for OpenCode users." Instruction #4 says "Validate the final workflow by checking that the skill can be followed entirely within OpenCode's available agent and tool model." Neither defines what "followed entirely" means. Does the verifier need to actually run the skill end-to-end? Read the SKILL.md and verify each step is possible? Check that no step references unavailable tools?

**Why**: Without an operational definition, the verifier will either rubber-stamp it (reading SKILL.md and saying "looks consistent") or over-scope it (trying to actually run the full workflow, which would take hours). The effort level is undefined.

**Suggested action**: Specify that the verifier should: (1) read the final SKILL.md and for each workflow step, confirm the referenced agent/tool/script exists and is available in OpenCode, (2) verify no step references `claude -p`, Claude Code commands, or unavailable tools, (3) verify any deferred capabilities have explicit documentation. This is a document review, not a live execution test.

comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text:
## Acceptance review (a1p.3) needs teeth — currently a rubber-stamp risk

**What**: The acceptance review has 4 criteria: (1) all child tasks closed, (2) agent mapping documented, (3) CLI paths replaced/deferred, (4) workflow internally consistent. Criteria 1 is mechanical. Criteria 2-3 repeat what the implementation tasks already verify. Criterion 4 is subjective ("internally consistent") with no operational definition — prior comments flagged this and suggested the verifier should do a step-by-step document review, but the instructions were not updated.

The acceptance review also does not cover: (a) the aimgr packaging actually works (someone needs to run aimgr install and verify the skill loads), (b) the skill triggers correctly in OpenCode (someone needs to type a skill-creation prompt and verify the skill activates), (c) the deferred capabilities are honestly documented (not buried in a comment or footnote).

**Why**: Without functional checks, the acceptance review will pass as long as the implementation tasks closed and the documents look reasonable. This is a consistency check, not a quality gate. The original prior comment (019d1c3c-0056) made this same point — the description optimization pipeline could be hand-waved as "deferred" with a one-liner and pass all criteria.

**Suggested action**: Add functional acceptance criteria:
- "Running aimgr install in a clean state results in the skill being available at .opencode/skills/"
- "Typing a skill-creation prompt in OpenCode triggers the ported skill (verified by checking skill loaded message or skill-guided response)"
- "The SKILL.md contains an explicit 'Deferred Capabilities' or 'OpenCode Limitations' section listing every capability that does not work in OpenCode, with rationale for each"
- "No section of SKILL.md references Claude Code, claude -p, TodoList, present_files, Cowork, or Claude.ai without an explicit OpenCode alternative or deferral note"

comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text:
## Acceptance review must enforce upstream content preservation — add regression check criteria

**What**: The current acceptance review criteria check that the skill works in OpenCode, but do not check that upstream content was preserved. After a1p.8 executes, the reviewer must verify BOTH directions:
1. Forward: the skill works in OpenCode with no Claude-specific incompatibilities
2. Backward: no generic upstream content was unnecessarily removed or degraded

Proposed additional acceptance criteria for this task:

- [ ] A section-by-section comparison between the upstream `.opencode/skills/skill-creator/SKILL.md` and the ported version exists
- [ ] Every change from upstream is classified as: (a) Claude-specific incompatibility fix, (b) new OpenCode addition, or (c) intentional change with documented rationale
- [ ] No changes exist in category (c) without explicit rationale
- [ ] The "Skill Writing Guide" section (Anatomy, Progressive Disclosure, Principle of Lack of Surprise, Writing Patterns, Writing Style) is present and substantially matches upstream
- [ ] The "How to think about improvements" section (generalize from feedback, keep prompt lean, explain the why, look for repeated work) is present and substantially matches upstream
- [ ] The "Description Optimization" section preserves the eval query writing guidance and good/bad examples, even if the automation loop is marked as deferred
- [ ] The port's line count is within 80-120% of upstream (385-580 lines, given upstream is 485)

**Why**: Without these checks, the acceptance review will pass a port that works in OpenCode but lost 40% of the upstream's educational content. The user explicitly stated they want "no regressions against the original in generic functionality/content."

**Suggested action**: Add these criteria to the acceptance review task (a1p.3) description.
