title: Map bundled agent instruction files to existing OpenCode agents
description:
## Description
Make the copied `opencode-coder-skill-creator` skill executable in OpenCode by mapping the bundled `agents/*.md` instruction files onto existing OpenCode agents instead of treating them as Claude Code-native agents.

## Instructions
1. Audit `ai-resources/skills/opencode-coder-skill-creator/SKILL.md` and the bundled `agents/*.md` files to identify every place where the skill assumes Claude Code-native agent behavior.
2. Define and document the OpenCode mapping for each bundled agent instruction file:
   - `agents/grader.md`
   - `agents/comparator.md`
   - `agents/analyzer.md`
3. Use only existing OpenCode agent types for the mapping (for example `reviewer`, `verifier`, `general`, `explore`, `tasker`) rather than inventing new runtime agent types.
4. Update the skill documentation so it clearly explains that the bundled `agents/*.md` files are instruction resources and specifies which OpenCode agent to use for each workflow.
5. Preserve the intent of the original skill workflow while removing ambiguity about how agent execution works in OpenCode.

## Files to Modify
- ai-resources/skills/opencode-coder-skill-creator/SKILL.md — rewrite agent usage instructions for OpenCode
- ai-resources/skills/opencode-coder-skill-creator/agents/grader.md — clarify OpenCode usage if needed
- ai-resources/skills/opencode-coder-skill-creator/agents/comparator.md — clarify OpenCode usage if needed
- ai-resources/skills/opencode-coder-skill-creator/agents/analyzer.md — clarify OpenCode usage if needed

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] Every bundled agent instruction file has an explicit OpenCode runtime mapping
- [ ] The skill no longer implies that `agents/*.md` are native Claude Code agents
- [ ] SKILL.md explains how to invoke the mapped OpenCode agents in practice
- [ ] The documented mappings only use agent types actually available in OpenCode
close_reason: Folded into opencode-coder-a1p.5 per reviewer guidance to avoid overlapping SKILL.md edits and simplify the plan.

comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text:
## Task 1 is the easy task and it's overscoped — agent mapping is trivial, not a full task

**What**: Task opencode-coder-a1p.1 treats agent mapping as though it requires a significant audit and rewrite. In reality, the SKILL.md already treats agents/*.md as instruction documents that get read by subagents, not as native agent definitions. Line 461-463 of SKILL.md says: "The agents/ directory contains instructions for specialized subagents. Read them when you need to spawn the relevant subagent." The mapping is straightforward:
- agents/grader.md → reviewer or verifier agent (reads grader.md as instruction context)
- agents/comparator.md → reviewer agent (reads comparator.md for blind comparison workflow)  
- agents/analyzer.md → reviewer agent (reads analyzer.md for post-hoc analysis)

This mapping takes about 10 lines of documentation edits. Making it a full task with 4 acceptance criteria and 4 files-to-modify is overengineered.

**Why**: By inflating this into a full task, it absorbs execution budget that should go to the hard problem (task 2). It also creates the illusion of progress — closing task 1 would feel like half the epic is done, when the hard 90% hasn't been touched.

**Suggested action**: Fold this work into task 2 as a prerequisite step ("Step 0: document agent mappings") or reduce to a small standalone task with 1-2 acceptance criteria. The current 4 acceptance criteria are redundant — they all say the same thing in different words ("agents are mapped to OpenCode agents").

comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text:
## Task 1 lists wrong agent types — "general" and "explore" don't exist in this project

**What**: The instructions say "Use only existing OpenCode agent types for the mapping (for example reviewer, verifier, general, explore, tasker)." The actual OpenCode agents defined in ai-resources/agents/ are: orchestrator, tasker, reviewer, verifier. There is no "general" agent and no "explore" agent in this project.

**Why**: A tasker following these instructions would either invent mappings to non-existent agents, or waste time searching for agents that don't exist. This causes confusion and rework.

**Suggested action**: Replace the example agent types with the actual available agents: orchestrator (primary mode), tasker (subagent), reviewer (subagent), verifier (subagent). These are the only four that exist.

comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text:
## Prior comment to merge .1 into .2 is now wrong — merge .1 into .5 instead

**What**: A prior comment (019d1c3c-827f) suggested folding a1p.1 (agent mapping) into a1p.2 (CLI/eval pipeline). This made sense when there were only 2 implementation tasks. Now that a1p.5 exists (general workflow rewrite), the merge target should change. Agent mapping (grader.md → reviewer, comparator.md → reviewer, analyzer.md → reviewer) is a documentation edit that naturally belongs in the general workflow rewrite, not in the hard eval pipeline design task.

**Why**: The agent mapping directly affects how SKILL.md instructs users to invoke subagents — that is general workflow guidance, which is .5's scope. Merging into .2 would force the eval pipeline task to also handle prose that has nothing to do with CLI dependencies.

**Suggested action**: Merge a1p.1 into a1p.5. Add the agent-mapping work as Step 0 of .5's instructions. Remove a1p.1 as a standalone task. This reduces the epic from 5 tasks to 4 (plus the smoke test task I recommend adding, bringing it back to 5 with better coverage).

comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text: Reviewer-guided restructure: this task's agent-mapping scope has been folded into opencode-coder-a1p.5 so the main SKILL.md rewrite owns agent mapping, packaging/presentation wording, environment-specific prose, and other overlapping workflow edits in one place.

title: Port skill-creator to OpenCode with full feature parity
description:
## Description
Port the copied `opencode-coder-skill-creator` skill so it works in OpenCode by changing only what is necessary for OpenCode compatibility, preserving generic upstream Anthropic skill content wherever it is still valid, and closing the remaining capability gap until the port offers all core features of the original skill.

## Goals
- Adapt the vendored skill content under `ai-resources/skills/opencode-coder-skill-creator` only
- Remove or replace Claude-specific/runtime-specific content that does not work in OpenCode
- Preserve generic upstream guidance, structure, and pedagogical content unless a concrete incompatibility requires change
- Match the original skill's feature set in OpenCode, including a credible replacement for the description-optimization / trigger-eval workflow rather than permanent deferral
- Prove the ported skill works in practice and does not regress generic functionality/content from upstream

## Success Criteria
- [ ] All implementation work is done in `ai-resources/skills/opencode-coder-skill-creator` rather than by editing `.opencode/skills/*`
- [ ] The final SKILL.md preserves all generic (non-Claude-specific) upstream content, or documents a specific reason for each removed or materially rewritten section
- [ ] A section-by-section diff exists between upstream and the OpenCode port, classifying each change as: Claude-specific incompatibility fix, OpenCode-specific addition, or intentional change with rationale
- [ ] The upstream `Skill Writing Guide` and `How to think about improvements` guidance are preserved substantially intact
- [ ] The description-optimization and trigger-eval workflow has a real OpenCode-capable replacement path; explicit permanent deferral is not sufficient for epic closure
- [ ] The ported skill is smoke-tested in OpenCode using the project's documented testing infrastructure
- [ ] Packaging/install verification documents how to use the already-published `skill/opencode-coder-skill-creator` via `aimgr`
- [ ] A parity comparison shows the OpenCode port is not worse than the original for realistically comparable workflows, and any residual differences are justified
- [ ] Acceptance review confirms both: (a) no Claude-specific incompatibilities remain for OpenCode, and (b) no generic upstream content was unnecessarily changed, removed, or regressed
close_reason: all steps complete

comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text:
## Epic goal "fully in OpenCode" is misleading — scope needs honest narrowing

**What**: The epic title is "Support skill creator **fully** in OpenCode" and the success criteria say "the skill can be followed end-to-end in OpenCode." After reading every script and the SKILL.md, this is not achievable with the current two-task decomposition. The skill's core eval loop depends on capabilities OpenCode does not have equivalents for:

1. **Trigger evaluation** (run_eval.py) — creates temp .claude/commands/*.md files, shells out to `claude -p --output-format stream-json --include-partial-messages`, and detects skill triggering by parsing Claude's internal tool-use stream events (content_block_start, content_block_delta, message_stop). OpenCode has no `opencode -p` headless CLI, no stream-json output, and no way to programmatically test whether a skill gets triggered. This is not a "replace the CLI call" problem — the concept of automated trigger testing does not exist in OpenCode.

2. **Description improvement** (improve_description.py) — shells out to `claude -p` to use Claude as a subprocess for generating improved descriptions. OpenCode agents are interactive session agents, not headless one-shot subprocess engines. There is no `opencode -p "prompt"` equivalent.

3. **Subagent spawning with timing capture** — SKILL.md Step 1 says "spawn two subagents in the same turn" and Step 3 says "when each subagent task completes, you receive a notification containing total_tokens and duration_ms." OpenCode agents (orchestrator, tasker, reviewer, verifier) can be spawned, but the SKILL.md's assumption of receiving structured completion notifications with token/timing data is a Claude Code-specific feature. Whether OpenCode exposes this is unverified and not addressed.

**Why**: If the epic ships with "fully" in the title but the actual deliverable is "partially, with some flows documented as deferred," the acceptance review task (opencode-coder-a1p.3) will either pass dishonestly or fail and need rework. The scope promise must match reality.

**Suggested action**: Rename the epic to "Port skill creator to OpenCode with honest scope boundaries" or similar. Rewrite the success criteria to explicitly state: (1) which workflows will work natively in OpenCode, (2) which workflows will be documented as not-yet-supported with explicit rationale, (3) which workflows need a fundamentally different design (not just CLI swaps). The current success criteria treat this as a find-and-replace job when it's actually a design problem.

comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text:
## Missing task: SKILL.md has extensive Claude Code-specific prose that needs rewriting

**What**: The SKILL.md body is 485 lines and deeply embedded with Claude Code assumptions that neither task 1 nor task 2 explicitly covers:

1. **Line 13**: "run claude-with-access-to-the-skill on them" — Claude Code-specific invocation pattern
2. **Lines 60**: "research in parallel via subagents if available" — assumes Claude Code subagent spawn capability
3. **Lines 170-175**: "spawn two subagents in the same turn" — Claude Code Task tool semantics
4. **Lines 209-219**: "subagent task completes, you receive a notification containing total_tokens and duration_ms" — Claude Code-only notification model
5. **Lines 329**: "This is optional, requires subagents" for blind comparison
6. **Lines 420-456**: Entire "Claude.ai-specific instructions" and "Cowork-Specific Instructions" sections that reference Claude Code/Cowork environments
7. **Line 476**: "run claude-with-access-to-the-skill on test prompts" (repeated)
8. **Line 483**: "Please add steps to your TodoList, if you have such a thing" — TodoList is a Claude Code concept

Task 1 covers agent mapping. Task 2 covers script CLI dependencies. But nobody owns rewriting the ~50 lines of SKILL.md prose that assume Claude Code session model, subagent spawning semantics, TodoList, and environment-specific sections. Both tasks list SKILL.md in files-to-modify but for different reasons — this creates ownership ambiguity.

**Why**: After both tasks close, the SKILL.md will still contain Claude Code-specific instructions in sections neither task explicitly addresses. The acceptance review (a1p.3) will catch this and fail, causing rework.

**Suggested action**: Either (a) create a dedicated task "Rewrite SKILL.md prose for OpenCode session model" or (b) expand task 2's instructions to explicitly include a SKILL.md prose audit covering subagent references, environment sections, and Claude Code-specific workflow language. Option (b) is simpler since task 2 already touches SKILL.md.

comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text:
## The installed skill at .opencode/skills/skill-creator/ is a separate copy — dual-maintenance risk

**What**: There are two copies of the skill:
1. ai-resources/skills/opencode-coder-skill-creator/ (the "source" copy the epic targets)
2. .opencode/skills/skill-creator/ (the installed/active copy that OpenCode actually loads)

Both tasks list files under ai-resources/ as their modification targets. But the live skill that OpenCode uses is at .opencode/skills/skill-creator/. After the epic completes, the ai-resources copy will be updated but the .opencode copy will still contain the old Claude Code-specific content.

**Why**: The installed skill (.opencode/skills/) is what actually runs. Updating only the ai-resources copy means the fixes don't take effect. Users will still see the Claude Code-specific SKILL.md when the skill triggers.

**Suggested action**: Either (a) add a step to each task to sync changes to .opencode/skills/skill-creator/, (b) create a final task to sync, or (c) restructure so only one copy exists and the other is a symlink/generated artifact. This dual-copy problem needs to be explicitly addressed — it's currently invisible in the epic.

comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text:
## Simplification opportunity: the entire epic could be 2 tasks, not 3

**What**: The current epic has 3 children: agent mapping (a1p.1), CLI replacement (a1p.2), and acceptance review (a1p.3). As noted in my comment on a1p.1, the agent mapping work is trivial — it's ~10 lines of documentation edits. It should be folded into the main porting task. This would leave:
- Task 1: "Port skill-creator to OpenCode (agent mapping + script audit + SKILL.md rewrite + scope boundaries)"
- Task 2: Acceptance review

Or if task 2 is genuinely too large after absorbing agent mapping, split by problem domain (see my comment on a1p.2 about the three distinct problems), not by artificial "agents vs scripts" boundary:
- Task 1: "Adapt skill-creator core workflow for OpenCode (agent mapping + subagent eval execution + SKILL.md prose)"
- Task 2: "Resolve description optimization pipeline for OpenCode (run_eval/improve_description/run_loop — design, defer, or replace)"
- Task 3: Acceptance review

The second split is better because it isolates the hard design decision (description optimization) from the more straightforward porting work.

**Why**: The current task 1 / task 2 boundary splits by symptom (agents vs CLI) rather than by difficulty. This means task 1 will close quickly giving false progress, while task 2 will stall on the design problem. A difficulty-based split gives more honest progress tracking.

**Suggested action**: Restructure as described above — either 2 tasks (fold a1p.1 into a1p.2) or 3 tasks split by difficulty (core workflow adaptation + description optimization design + acceptance review).

comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text:
## No dependency between task 1 and task 2 — should one block the other?

**What**: Tasks a1p.1 and a1p.2 are both parent-child of the epic but have no explicit dependency on each other. They both modify SKILL.md. If a tasker works on a1p.1 and rewrites SKILL.md's agent references, and a separate tasker works on a1p.2 and rewrites SKILL.md's CLI references, they will create merge conflicts.

**Why**: Concurrent modification of the same file without coordination guarantees conflicts. Since both tasks claim SKILL.md as a files-to-modify, they should either be sequenced or their SKILL.md scopes should be non-overlapping (which is hard to guarantee for a 485-line file).

**Suggested action**: If the tasks remain separate, make a1p.1 block a1p.2 (a1p.1 completes first since it's simpler, then a1p.2 can work on a clean base). Or better: merge them as suggested in my simplification comment.

comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text: Reviewer findings applied: exact Claude Code parity is not a safe assumption. The copied description-optimization pipeline depends on nested claude -p, temporary .claude/commands injection, stream-json tool-event parsing, and browser-open flows that OpenCode does not currently expose. Epic scope and task 2 were narrowed to require honest replacement or explicit deferral. Added task opencode-coder-a1p.4 to define the authoritative live-skill copy and sync path so work does not land in a non-live vendor copy.

comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text: Scope clarified during discussion: porting this skill is not only about validation/eval plumbing. We also need to rewrite the general user-facing skill-creator workflow for OpenCode, including new-skill creation, existing-skill improvement, test-case decisions, review loops, and explanation/output guidance. Added task opencode-coder-a1p.5 for that work.

comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text:
## OVERALL VERDICT: Plan is 70% there — covers porting, but has no quality verification strategy

**What**: The epic and its 5 tasks cover the mechanics of porting (agent mapping, CLI replacement, workflow rewrite, packaging) but contain zero plan for verifying the ported skill actually works well. The epic goal says "support the core skill-creation workflow" but no task includes running the skill end-to-end, even once. The acceptance review (a1p.3) is a document-consistency check, not a functional test. There is no comparison against the original Anthropic skill and no definition of what "as good or better" means.

**Why**: A port that reads correctly but has never been executed is a theory, not a product. The original Anthropic skill has presumably been used and refined by real users. Our port will be untested prose modifications. Without at least one smoke test ("use the ported skill to create a simple skill from scratch"), we cannot know whether the rewritten SKILL.md actually guides an OpenCode agent through a coherent workflow.

**Suggested action**: Add a new task (see separate finding) for functional smoke-testing the ported skill. This task should come after all implementation tasks and before or alongside the acceptance review. It should include: (1) use the skill to create a trivial test skill, (2) use the skill to improve an existing skill, (3) document what worked and what didn't. This is not expensive — it is 2-3 manual test runs — but without it the epic delivers untested documentation.

comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text:
## Missing task: Functional smoke test of the ported skill

**What**: No task in the epic requires actually running the ported skill. All five implementation tasks produce documentation/code changes. The acceptance review (a1p.3) verifies document consistency ("the skill can be followed entirely within OpenCode's available agent and tool model") but this is a paper review, not an execution test. After all tasks close, nobody will have used the skill to create or improve a real skill in OpenCode even once.

**Why**: The core value proposition is "this skill helps OpenCode users create and iterate on skills." If we have never tested that proposition, we are shipping on faith. The original Anthropic skill was presumably battle-tested by Anthropic's own users. Our port strips out Claude Code-specific machinery and rewrites guidance — both changes that could easily break the workflow in subtle ways (wrong agent invocation patterns, instructions that don't match OpenCode's actual behavior, missing steps). A single end-to-end smoke test would catch the most egregious problems.

**Suggested action**: Create a new task "Smoke test the ported skill-creator in OpenCode" with these acceptance criteria:
1. Used the ported skill to create a new trivial skill from scratch (e.g., a simple code formatter skill) — skill was successfully created with SKILL.md, description, and at least one test case
2. Used the ported skill to improve an existing skill (e.g., the self-reflection skill) — at least one iteration of the review/improve loop completed
3. Documented what worked, what broke, and what guidance was confusing or wrong
4. Any bugs found during smoke testing are filed as follow-up beads

This task should block the acceptance review (a1p.3) and depend on all implementation tasks (.1, .2, .4, .5).

comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text:
## No definition of "as good or better" — the stronger goal has no success criteria

**What**: The stated ambition is making the OpenCode skill "as good as or better than the original Anthropic skill where parity is realistic." The epic success criteria do not mention quality comparison, parity benchmarks, or any mechanism to judge relative quality. The criteria are all structural: "agent mapping is defined," "workflows are rewritten," "CLI flows are replaced/deferred," "sync path is documented." These verify the port was done, not that it was done well.

**Why**: "As good as or better" requires a comparison framework. Without one, the goal is aspirational but unverifiable. After the epic closes, if someone asks "is our skill as good as the Anthropic one?" the honest answer will be "we don't know — we never compared." This matters because: (a) the ported skill will replace the Anthropic skill in this project (a1p.4 removes it from ai.package.yaml), and (b) if the replacement is worse, users lose capability with no recourse.

**Suggested action**: Either (a) add a comparison task that runs both skills through the same scenario and documents the results, or (b) honestly downgrade the goal to "port the skill so it works in OpenCode" without the "as good or better" aspiration. Option (a) is more work but honest. A lightweight version: create 3-5 benchmark prompts, run them against the Anthropic skill in Claude Code (or document what the Anthropic skill would do from reading its instructions), then run the same prompts against the ported skill in OpenCode, and document the comparison. This produces an artifact that can be referenced later.

comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text:
## Tasks .1, .2, and .5 all modify SKILL.md with overlapping scope — collision is guaranteed

**What**: Three tasks list SKILL.md as a primary modification target:
- a1p.1: "rewrite agent usage instructions for OpenCode" in SKILL.md
- a1p.2: "replace Claude CLI workflow instructions and parity claims" in SKILL.md
- a1p.5: "rewrite general workflow and user guidance for OpenCode" in SKILL.md

The SKILL.md is 485 lines. These three scopes overlap heavily. For example: lines 169-175 ("spawn two subagents in the same turn") are simultaneously an agent-mapping concern (a1p.1), a Claude Code-specific execution concern (a1p.2), and general workflow guidance (a1p.5). Lines 420-456 (Claude.ai/Cowork sections) are CLI-specific (a1p.2) but also general guidance (a1p.5). The existing comment on the epic noted this for a1p.1 vs a1p.2; now a1p.5 adds a third overlapping editor.

**Why**: If these tasks execute sequentially, the second and third tasker will be working against a SKILL.md that the previous tasker already modified, but their instructions reference the original file structure. If they execute in parallel, merge conflicts are certain. Either way, rework is likely.

**Suggested action**: Establish a clear execution order with explicit scope boundaries:
1. a1p.1 goes first (smallest scope, agent mapping only)
2. a1p.5 goes second (rewrites the general workflow prose — the bulk of SKILL.md)
3. a1p.2 goes third (handles the hard eval/description pipeline — can work against a1p.5's output)

Add blocking dependencies: a1p.1 blocks a1p.5, a1p.5 blocks a1p.2. This prevents parallel SKILL.md edits. Alternatively, merge a1p.1 into a1p.5 (the agent mapping is trivial — see prior comments) and keep a1p.5 → a1p.2 sequence.

comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text:
## Epic title still says "fully" — prior comment flagged this but it was not addressed

**What**: A prior comment (019d1c3a-63ff) correctly identified that the epic title "Support skill creator fully in OpenCode" overpromises relative to what is achievable. The comment recommended renaming. A follow-up comment (019d1c3f-e548) says "Reviewer findings applied: exact Claude Code parity is not a safe assumption" and mentions narrowing scope — but the title and success criteria were never actually changed. The title still says "fully" and the success criteria still do not distinguish between natively supported and deferred capabilities.

**Why**: The title sets expectations for everyone who reads the backlog. "Fully" means everything works. The actual deliverable will be a partial port with some capabilities deferred. If the title stays, someone reading the backlog will reasonably expect full feature parity and be confused when they discover deferred features.

**Suggested action**: Rename the epic to something like "Port skill-creator to OpenCode with honest scope boundaries" or "Adapt skill-creator for OpenCode (core workflow + deferred eval automation)". Update success criteria to explicitly list: (1) what will work natively, (2) what will be explicitly deferred with rationale.

comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text:
## Simplification opportunity: with .5 absorbing .1, the epic is cleaner as 4+1 tasks

**What**: The current 5-task structure can be simplified to a cleaner 4+1:

1. **a1p.4** (aimgr swap) — runs first, sets up packaging pipeline, independent
2. **a1p.5+a1p.1 merged** (general workflow + agent mapping rewrite) — the bulk of SKILL.md rewriting
3. **a1p.2** (eval/description pipeline resolution) — the hard design task, works against the rewritten SKILL.md from step 2
4. **NEW: Smoke test** — functional verification that the ported skill works
5. **a1p.3** (acceptance review) — final gate

Dependency chain: a1p.4 → merged(.5+.1) → a1p.2 → smoke test → a1p.3

This gives: clear execution order, no parallel SKILL.md edits, functional testing before acceptance, and the aimgr pipeline set up before content changes begin.

**Why**: The current structure has 3 tasks editing SKILL.md with unclear ordering, no functional testing, and the packaging task running last when it should run first. The simplified structure eliminates all three problems.

**Suggested action**: Implement this restructure. Specific changes:
- Merge a1p.1 into a1p.5 (add agent mapping as Step 0)
- Close a1p.1 with a note pointing to a1p.5
- Raise a1p.4 priority to 1 and make it the first task
- Add blocking dependencies: a1p.4 → a1p.5 → a1p.2 → new-smoke-test → a1p.3
- Create the smoke test task

comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text: Second reviewer pass found the plan still lacked functional verification and any credible path to support the stronger goal of being as good as or better than the Anthropic skill. Added explicit smoke-test and parity-comparison tasks, tightened acceptance review to inspect actual execution results, and sequenced overlapping SKILL.md and packaging tasks to reduce conflicts and make the plan executable.

comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text: Applied reviewer-recommended restructure: renamed the epic for honest scope, promoted the aimgr packaging task to the first-class setup step, folded agent mapping into the main SKILL.md rewrite task, closed the redundant standalone mapping task, tightened eval/acceptance criteria, and sequenced the work as packaging -> general workflow rewrite -> eval/defer decisions -> smoke test -> comparison -> acceptance review.

comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text: User clarified additional planning decisions: (1) the general workflow should map bundled skill instruction docs onto the standard OpenCode agents already available in the project, not invent separate custom agent types; (2) model selection should be considered explicitly because OpenCode can use non-Anthropic models as well; (3) implementation work must stay inside ai-resources/skills/opencode-coder-skill-creator and not treat .opencode/skills as an editing target; (4) the aimgr packaging/install task should happen later, mainly for final packaging and test/install verification; (5) smoke testing must use the project's testing infrastructure from docs/TESTING.md.

comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text: Discussion update: current port appears to have diverged too far from the upstream Anthropic skill structure/content without runtime validation to justify that level of rewrite. New direction under discussion: preserve upstream structure and guidance by default, keep sections like 'Skill Writing Guide' unless incompatibility is proven, and minimize edits to only what OpenCode actually requires.

comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text:
## The ported SKILL.md is a ground-up rewrite, not a port — this is the root cause of all content regressions

**What**: Comparing the upstream (`.opencode/skills/skill-creator/SKILL.md`, 485 lines, 327 non-empty) against the port (`ai-resources/skills/opencode-coder-skill-creator/SKILL.md`, 305 lines, 205 non-empty), the port is 37% shorter and shares essentially zero sentences with the upstream. This is not a port — it is a rewrite that uses the same section topics but replaces all prose. Specific high-value upstream content that was deleted with no equivalent:

1. **"Skill Writing Guide" section** (upstream lines 71-161, ~90 lines) — Anatomy of a Skill, Progressive Disclosure, Principle of Lack of Surprise, Writing Patterns, Writing Style, Test Cases. This is the most valuable section in the upstream skill: it teaches the agent HOW to write good skills. The port has nothing equivalent.

2. **"Improving the skill" / "How to think about improvements"** (upstream lines 292-322, ~30 lines) — 4 detailed principles on generalization vs overfitting, keeping prompts lean, explaining the why, looking for repeated work. The port's "Workflow B" covers the mechanics but drops all the reasoning guidance.

3. **"Description Optimization" full flow** (upstream lines 333-404, ~70 lines) — detailed eval query writing guidance with good/bad examples, explanation of how skill triggering works, the optimization loop. The port replaces this with a 27-line "Trigger Description Review" section that drops all the query-writing guidance and triggering explanation.

4. **"What the user sees in the viewer"** (upstream lines 253-265) — explains the viewer tabs, navigation, feedback mechanism. Port has no equivalent.

5. **"Advanced: Blind comparison"** (upstream lines 325-330) — brief but useful. Port drops it entirely.

6. **The conversational tone and metacognitive guidance** — The upstream uses deliberate, personality-rich prose ("Cool? Cool.", "This task is pretty important... take your time and really mull things over"). The port replaces this with dry bullet lists. This isn't just style — the upstream tone is a deliberate pedagogical choice that helps the agent internalize the guidance. Replacing it with imperative lists may reduce comprehension.

**Why**: The user's stated policy is: "change only what is needed — only content that is clearly Claude-specific or otherwise does not work in OpenCode." The upstream content listed above is entirely generic. None of it references Claude Code, `claude -p`, subagents, or any Claude-specific runtime. It was deleted during the rewrite not because it was incompatible but because the rewrite chose to restructure instead of preserve.

**Suggested action**: The port approach must change from "rewrite for OpenCode" to "fork upstream, apply minimal patches." The correct workflow is:
1. Start from the upstream SKILL.md verbatim
2. Identify each line/section that references Claude-specific features
3. Replace ONLY those lines/sections with OpenCode equivalents
4. Add OpenCode-specific sections (environment assumptions, agent mapping, model selection) as NEW sections, not replacements for generic content
5. Every deletion must have a documented reason

This is a fundamental direction change for the epic.

comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text:
## Epic success criteria need a "no-regression" gate — currently they only measure forward compatibility

**What**: The current success criteria are all forward-looking: "workflow matches OpenCode," "eval pipeline is replaced/deferred," "smoke-tested," "parity comparison exists." None of them enforce preservation of upstream content. A tasker could delete every section of the upstream skill, replace it with a 10-line stub that works in OpenCode, and pass all current criteria.

The missing gate: "The ported SKILL.md preserves all generic upstream content that is not Claude-specific, and every deletion or rewrite of upstream content has a documented justification."

**Why**: Without a no-regression criterion, the epic's incentive structure rewards rewriting over preserving. Task a1p.5 ("Rewrite the general skill-creator workflow") even has "rewrite" in its title — it was designed to produce a rewrite, not a minimal patch. The acceptance review (a1p.3) checks consistency ("the documented workflow is internally consistent") but not preservation ("the upstream content wasn't needlessly lost").

**Suggested action**: Add these success criteria to the epic:
- [ ] The ported SKILL.md preserves all generic (non-Claude-specific) upstream content from the installed skill, or documents a specific reason for each removed/rewritten section
- [ ] A section-by-section diff between upstream and port exists, with each change classified as: (a) Claude-specific fix, (b) OpenCode addition, or (c) intentional content change with rationale
- [ ] The "Skill Writing Guide" section from upstream is preserved intact (it contains zero Claude-specific content)
- [ ] The "How to think about improvements" guidance from upstream is preserved intact (it contains zero Claude-specific content)

comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text:
## Task a1p.5 (closed) produced the rewrite that caused all content regressions — it needs to be superseded, not patched

**What**: Task a1p.5 ("Rewrite the general skill-creator workflow and user guidance for OpenCode") is closed and was the task that produced the current 305-line port. Its acceptance criteria explicitly asked for rewrites: "SKILL.md contains a step-by-step OpenCode workflow for creating a new skill," "every reference to Claude Code... is removed or replaced." The task was correctly executed against its own criteria — the problem is that the criteria encouraged wholesale replacement instead of minimal patching.

The new direction ("change only what is needed") fundamentally contradicts a1p.5's mandate. You cannot achieve "minimal upstream-preserving port" by patching the output of a task designed to produce a "rewrite." The rewrite changed the document structure, section names, content ordering, prose style, and level of detail. Reverse-engineering which parts to keep and which to revert is harder than starting fresh from upstream.

title: Private opt-in manual-launcher integration fails for --project-path socket preservation
description:
## Summary
While verifying opencode-coder-0a8, the explicit private opt-in integration suite does not fully pass.

## Evidence
Command:
OPENCODE_CODER_PRIVATE_TESTS=true bun test tests/integration/manual-launcher.test.ts

Observed failure:
- Test: manual launcher non-interactive mode > runs one-shot command with external --project-path directly in place
- Assertion: expect(await sourceBeadsSocket.exists()).toBe(true)
- Actual: false
- Location: tests/integration/manual-launcher.test.ts:493

## Impact
This means the private/auth/opencode-dependent coverage is not fully available behind the documented explicit opt-in control, so opencode-coder-0a8 cannot yet be verified closed.

## Reproduction
1. In repo root, run:
   OPENCODE_CODER_PRIVATE_TESTS=true bun test tests/integration/manual-launcher.test.ts
2. Observe the failing assertion in the --project-path scenario.
close_reason: Root cause: Bun.file().exists() returns false for Unix domain sockets because it checks isFile(), which is false for socket inodes. The bd.sock socket was always preserved — the test assertion method was wrong. Fix: replaced Bun.file().exists() with fs.stat().isSocket() for the socket check. Private opt-in suite now passes: 22 pass, 0 fail.

title: Rework manual testing workflow to run project-path scenarios in place
description:
## Description
The current manual testing workflow and documentation are not aligned with how humans and agents actually need to validate slash commands and other agent-mediated behavior.

Two problems are now clear:
1. `docs/TESTING.md` needs a stronger manual-testing guide for humans and agents, including what to run, when to use it, and which scenarios exist.
2. The current manual launcher uses a copy-based `--project-path` flow that copies the source project into `.manual-test-runs/...` under the source tree. That breaks with `cannot copy <src> to a subdirectory of self <dest>` and makes realistic project-path validation unreliable.

The manual testing system should support scenario-driven validation directly against another project path without copying it, while still preserving diagnostics and keeping fixture-based flows where they remain useful.

Discovered while working on `opencode-coder-5d2` and trying to manually validate `/opencode-coder/docs`.

## Instructions
1. Update `docs/TESTING.md` so it becomes a practical manual-testing guide for both humans and agents.
2. Explain when to use direct-in-project manual testing, when to use fixtures, and when to use deterministic integration/e2e coverage.
3. Change the manual testing system so `--project-path` runs against the provided project directly instead of copying it into a nested workspace.
4. Keep or adapt fixture behavior as appropriate, but remove the broken self-copy assumption for real project paths.
5. Document the available manual-testing scenarios and when each one should be used.
6. Update tests around the manual launcher to match the new in-place project-path behavior.
7. Verify the updated launcher and docs with relevant tests and at least one manual self-check.

## Files to Modify
- `docs/TESTING.md`
- `scripts/manual-test/index.ts`
- `tests/e2e/helpers/harness.ts`
- `tests/integration/manual-launcher.test.ts`
- `tests/e2e/fixtures/README.md` (if scenario/launcher docs need alignment)
- other manual-launcher docs or helpers as needed

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] `docs/TESTING.md` clearly explains manual testing for humans and agents.
- [ ] `docs/TESTING.md` documents available scenarios and when to use them.
- [ ] `--project-path` manual runs no longer rely on copy-into-self behavior.
- [ ] Manual launcher tests reflect the new direct project-path behavior.
- [ ] At least one real manual validation path is exercised successfully after the change.
- [ ] Relevant automated tests pass.

## Description
Several published slash-command resources under `ai-resources/commands/opencode-coder/` need a full quality cleanup so they behave like strong user-facing command contracts instead of leaking maintainer/meta implementation notes.

The originally identified defect is most obvious in `docs.md` and `improve-doc.md`, but the requested follow-through is broader: review **all** published opencode-coder commands, remove weak/internal phrasing where present, tighten instructions for clarity and actionability, and verify the resulting command quality with the project's testing system.

## Scope
Review and improve these published commands:
- `ai-resources/commands/opencode-coder/docs.md`
- `ai-resources/commands/opencode-coder/improve-doc.md`
- `ai-resources/commands/opencode-coder/init.md`
- `ai-resources/commands/opencode-coder/status.md`
- `ai-resources/commands/opencode-coder/report-bug.md`
- `ai-resources/commands/opencode-coder/doctor.md`

## Current Findings
- `docs.md` and `improve-doc.md` contain explicit maintainer/meta phrasing such as `Dispatcher Flow (thin)` and instructions about where lifecycle logic should live.
- `init.md` is stronger overall, but still deserves cleanup for wording quality and any remaining internal-architecture leakage.

- Runtime command templates in `src/index.ts` must stay aligned with the published docs-lifecycle commands.

## Why This Matters
These files are the agent-facing contracts behind user-invoked slash commands. They should focus on helping with the user's task, not on documenting how we organized our internal resource architecture. Weak command contracts directly reduce command quality.

## Instructions
1. Audit every published command under `ai-resources/commands/opencode-coder/` for user-facing quality, clarity, and maintainability.
2. Rewrite commands that contain maintainer/meta leakage so they are purely task-oriented and user-facing.
3. Improve weaker wording, structure, and actionability across the remaining commands even where no explicit bug phrase exists.
4. Keep runtime docs-lifecycle command templates in `src/index.ts` aligned with the published command contracts.
5. Add or update focused tests that lock in the intended command quality where practical.
6. Run the relevant project test commands to verify the updated command contracts and runtime alignment.

- `ai-resources/commands/opencode-coder/init.md`

- [ ] `docs.md` and `improve-doc.md` no longer contain maintainer/meta architecture instructions.
- [ ] `init.md` and the other published commands are clearer, more actionable, and free of unnecessary internal wording.
- [ ] Runtime templates in `src/index.ts` remain aligned with the published docs-lifecycle command contracts.
- [ ] Focused tests cover the command-quality expectations that should not regress.
- [ ] Relevant test commands pass after the cleanup.

title: Make /init docs prompt inspect-first and state-aware
description:
## Description
Update the `/opencode-coder/init` docs follow-through so it inspects the repo's docs state before asking the user anything, then asks a different plain-language question for bootstrap, refresh, or migration scenarios.

## Instructions
1. Treat `ai-resources/commands/opencode-coder/init.md` Step 4 / 4a as the inspect-first reference model, then rewrite `src/templates/init-install-guide.ts` Step 5 so the template matches that model instead of maintaining a second, divergent flow.
2. Require inspection of the active AGENTS/docs paths and standard topic docs before asking the user what to do.
3. Distinguish at least these states in the instructions and resulting prompt guidance:
   - no standard baseline exists yet
   - standard AGENTS/docs layout already exists
   - docs exist but use non-standard names/layout that may need migration or routing changes
4. Define the migration scenario concretely so implementation does not improvise. Treat it as cases where project-specific guidance exists outside the standard topic files or is mixed into broader files (for example `README.md`, `CONTRIBUTING.md`, or non-standard docs filenames) and should be inspected before proposing extraction, relocation, renaming, or routing updates.
5. Replace internal capability wording with user-facing descriptions of the likely outcome, including AGENTS routing and standard docs structure when relevant.
6. Include sketch-level example wording guidance for each scenario so there is a positive bar for "user-facing":
   - bootstrap/setup: explain that the repo does not yet have the standard docs structure and that init can inspect the project and create topic docs plus an AGENTS routing document where there is real project-specific guidance
   - review/update: explain that the standard layout already exists and init can review, refresh, verify, and improve those docs and the AGENTS routing
   - migration/proposal: explain that documentation exists but is not organized in the standard layout, and init can inspect what exists and propose how to reorganize or route it before making changes
7. Clarify the fallback path when `/opencode-coder/docs` is unavailable in the current session. Keep that path in plain language and explicitly scope whether the inspect-first branching applies only when docs follow-through can run, while the fallback should explain that project-doc setup/update is unavailable right now and init will continue without that step.
8. Update `ai-resources/commands/opencode-coder/init.md` so the command contract matches the same inspect-first, state-aware behavior.
9. Preserve the shared docs lifecycle model (`inspect -> decide -> apply -> verify/report`) and do not invent a second docs workflow inside init.

## Files to Modify
- `src/templates/init-install-guide.ts` — reorder and rewrite Step 5 guidance
- `ai-resources/commands/opencode-coder/init.md` — align command contract with inspect-first prompt behavior

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] Init guidance requires inspection before the project-doc question is asked.
- [ ] Bootstrap, refresh, and migration scenarios each have distinct user-facing question guidance.
- [ ] The migration scenario is defined concretely enough that an agent can implement it without guessing.
- [ ] The wording no longer relies on terms like "docs lifecycle support" or "runtime" for the user-facing question.
- [ ] The template and command contract converge on the same inspect-first behavior rather than diverging.
- [ ] The fallback path is described in plain language and does not break the no-skill/no-resource path.

comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text:
## Template and command contract already diverge on Step numbering and content — task must reconcile both

**What**: The init-install-guide.ts template calls this "Step 5: Optional Docs Lifecycle Follow-through" and uses a runtime availability check (`/opencode-coder/docs` command presence). The init.md command contract calls the equivalent "Step 4: Optional project-doc setup/refresh" and already includes an explicit inspect phase (4a) with topic classification before writing. The task says to update both files, but does not call out that the command contract (init.md) already has significant inspect-first logic that the template lacks.

**Why**: A tasker who reads only the task instructions may not realize that init.md Step 4 already implements much of the inspect-first requirement (4a: inspection with topic classification). The real gap is primarily in init-install-guide.ts Step 5, which has zero inspection logic and just asks "Set up project docs now / Skip for now" with no state awareness. If the tasker treats both files as equally needing the same new logic, they'll duplicate what init.md already has or, worse, create a conflicting second version of the inspection flow.

**Suggested action**: Add a note to the instructions clarifying: "The command contract (init.md Step 4) already contains inspect-first logic with topic classification. The primary implementation gap is in init-install-guide.ts Step 5, which needs to be rewritten to match the init.md model. Reconcile both to use the same inspect-first, state-aware question structure, using init.md 4a as the reference."

comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text:
## Missing: the third user scenario — docs exist but not in standard layout (migration case)

**What**: The user explicitly requested three distinct states: (1) no standard docs layout, (2) standard layout already exists, (3) docs exist but not in standard layout — inspect and propose migration. The task instructions mention "bootstrap, refresh, or migration scenarios" in criterion 2, but the instructions don't describe what the migration scenario prompt should actually say or do. The existing init.md Step 4 classifies topics as "existing doc / skill-only / neither" but never considers "docs exist under non-standard names/paths that could be migrated."

**Why**: This is the user's most distinctive requirement — the one that doesn't exist at all in the current code. Without concrete guidance, a tasker will implement bootstrap and refresh (which roughly map to existing code) but will likely punt or improvise on migration. The prompt wording for migration is the hardest to get right because it needs to explain what will happen without overwhelming the user.

**Suggested action**: Add explicit instructions for the migration scenario: Define what "non-standard layout" means concretely (e.g., README.md contains testing guidance that should be in TESTING.md, or a contributing.md exists but no CODING.md). Specify the user-facing question for this scenario should explain what was found AND what the proposed migration would do. Clarify whether migration means file renames, content extraction, or both.

comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text:
## The "unavailable command" fallback path is not addressed

**What**: The current template Step 5 has a fallback for when /opencode-coder/docs is not available in the session (missing aimgr resources, etc.). The task says "Preserve the shared docs lifecycle model and keep the unavailable-command fallback in plain language when it must be mentioned." But the task does not specify what the inspect-first, state-aware behavior should look like in the fallback path. Does the template still do a lightweight inspection even when the full docs command is not available? Or does it skip the question entirely?

**Why**: The init-install-guide.ts template is specifically the fallback template — it runs when the skill/command may not be loaded. If the tasker rewrites Step 5 to depend on inspection capabilities that only exist in the full docs lifecycle command, the fallback path breaks. The user's requirement for state-aware prompting should apply in both paths or the task needs to explicitly scope it to the available path only.

**Suggested action**: Clarify in the instructions whether the inspect-first behavior applies to: (a) only the "docs command available" path (keeping the fallback simple), or (b) both paths, with a lightweight inspection embedded in the template itself for the fallback case. Option (a) is simpler and probably sufficient since the full docs command already has the inspection logic.

comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text:
## Acceptance criteria lack positive examples of what "user-facing" means

**What**: Criterion 3 says the wording must no longer rely on terms like "docs lifecycle support" or "runtime." This is a good negative constraint but lacks a positive definition. There is no example of what the user-facing question SHOULD say for each of the three scenarios.

**Why**: Without at least one example per scenario, the tasker and the acceptance reviewer have no shared standard for "good enough." The user specifically said they want the prompt to explain what will happen — that is a positive standard, not just the absence of jargon.

**Suggested action**: Add at least sketch-level example wording for each scenario. For example — Bootstrap: "This project does not have a standard docs structure yet. I can inspect your project and create topic docs (like CODING.md, TESTING.md) with real project-specific content, plus an AGENTS.md routing document. Want me to do that now?" Refresh: "This project already has a standard docs layout. I can review and update your existing docs and AGENTS routing. Want me to do that now?" Migration: "I found existing documentation but it is not organized in the standard layout. I can inspect what you have and propose reorganizing it into standard topic docs. Want me to show you a migration plan?" These do not have to be final copy — they are implementation guidance so the tasker knows the bar.

title: Improve /init project docs follow-through prompts
description:
## Description
Make `/opencode-coder/init` ask a user-facing project-docs question instead of exposing internal terms like "docs lifecycle support" or "runtime". The init flow should inspect the current docs/AGENTS state first, then explain whether it will set up a standard project-docs structure, review/update an existing standard layout, or inspect and propose migration from non-standard docs before changing files. The template guidance and the command contract must converge on one inspect-first model rather than drift as separate sources of truth.

## Goals
- The init prompt explains the user-visible outcome in plain language.
- The question changes based on whether the standard docs layout already exists.
- The flow stays aligned with the shared docs lifecycle and AGENTS routing model.
- The fallback path remains understandable when docs follow-through cannot run in the current session.

## Success Criteria
- [ ] Child tasks define the inspect-first, state-aware init docs flow.
- [ ] Copy clearly explains AGENTS routing and standard docs structure where relevant.
- [ ] Tests cover the new wording/decision contract, including fallback wording.
- [ ] Acceptance review confirms the prompt is understandable for first-time, existing-standard, and non-standard-layout repos.
- [ ] The template guidance and init command contract describe the same behavior.
close_reason: All child tasks closed. Init docs prompt now uses inspect-first, state-aware, plain-language questions.

comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text:
## Plan structure is solid — epic and children are well-scoped

**What**: The epic correctly captures the user's three requirements (inspect-first, state-aware branching, plain-language prompting). The three-task breakdown (implementation, regression tests, acceptance review) is proportional to the work. Dependencies flow correctly: gnx.1 → gnx.2 → gnx.3.

**Why**: Good news first — this plan is executable as-is for the core requirement. The separation of implementation from test coverage and acceptance review is clean.

**Suggested action**: No structural changes needed to the epic itself.

comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text:
## Simplification opportunity: consider whether init.md and init-install-guide.ts should diverge at all

**What**: The codebase has two parallel descriptions of the init flow: init.md (the command contract, 233 lines) and init-install-guide.ts (the fallback template, 313 lines). Both describe the same Steps 1-5/6 workflow with overlapping but subtly different content. This task adds state-aware logic to both, which will widen the divergence surface.

**Why**: Two parallel sources of truth for the same workflow is an ongoing maintenance burden. Every future change to the init flow must update both files and keep them consistent. The existing test (init-install-guide.test.ts) only covers the template, not the command contract. The more logic is added to both, the more likely they drift.

**Suggested action**: Consider whether the template (init-install-guide.ts) should be simplified to defer to the command contract (init.md) for docs lifecycle decisions rather than embedding its own version of the inspect-first logic. This is not a blocker for gnx.1, but it is worth flagging: if the template's only job in the fallback path is "skip docs gracefully," it does not need to replicate the three-scenario state machine. File this as a follow-up simplification if the current approach proceeds.

comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text: Reviewer completed plan review and found material gaps. The implementation, test, and acceptance-review tasks were updated to reflect: (1) init.md Step 4a as the inspect-first reference model, (2) a concrete definition of the migration scenario, (3) explicit fallback-path behavior in plain language, and (4) manual acceptance validation against representative repo states.

title: Temporarily skip GitHub workflow integration gates for v0.35.0 release
description:
## Description
Temporarily bypass GitHub-hosted integration gating in the CI and release workflows so v0.35.0 can be shipped while the auth-enabled private package registry issue is tracked separately.

## Scope Notes
- GitHub workflows currently do **not** run e2e tests, so this task is mainly about the integration test steps.
- The temporary bypass must be explicit in the workflow definitions so maintainers can see it is intentional and temporary.
- The real workflow coverage restoration is tracked separately in the follow-up bug.

## Instructions
1. Update `.github/workflows/ci.yml` to stop running the integration suite temporarily.
2. Update `.github/workflows/release.yml` to stop running the integration suite temporarily so release dispatch can proceed.
3. Make the temporary bypass obvious in the workflow step names or commands.
4. Keep unit, typecheck, and build gates intact.
5. Push the workflow change, confirm CI passes, then continue the release.

## Files to Modify
- `.github/workflows/ci.yml`
- `.github/workflows/release.yml`

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] CI workflow no longer runs integration tests temporarily
- [ ] Release workflow no longer runs integration tests temporarily
- [ ] The temporary nature of the bypass is visible in the workflow definitions
- [ ] Remaining GitHub workflow gates still pass
close_reason: Temporarily bypassed GitHub workflow integration gates for the v0.35.0 release unblock and pushed workflow changes in 2c72c76.

comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text: Implemented temporary v0.35.0 workflow bypass by replacing the integration-test steps in  and  with explicit temporary skip notices referencing follow-up bug opencode-coder-0a8. Commit: 2c72c76.

title: Restore GitHub workflow integration coverage after v0.35.0 release
description:
## Description
Restore GitHub workflow integration coverage after the temporary v0.35.0 release bypass, but do it in a way that is sustainable for both maintainers and external contributors.

## Current Status
- `.github/workflows/ci.yml` and `.github/workflows/release.yml` currently skip the integration step explicitly as a temporary release unblock.
- `tests/integration/manual-launcher.test.ts` now has a mixed suite:
  - public/preflight checks that do **not** need `opencode` or private package access
  - auth/private-plugin/opencode-dependent checks that are currently inferred from environment state
- `tests/e2e/helpers/harness.ts` still contains helper paths that prepare the pinned `@hk9890/opencode-dynatrace` package during some launcher scenarios.
- The short-term business reality is that the Dynatrace plugin migration may take 1-2 weeks, so we need a supported temporary model instead of pretending everyone can run the full private-capability suite today.

## Design Goal
The default repository test experience must be runnable by external users without private plugin access. Private-registry / opencode-binary coverage should remain available, but only through an explicit opt-in capability path.

## Proposal Direction
1. Split repository test coverage into **public-default** vs **capability-dependent** layers.
2. Make default integration coverage public-safe and restore that to GitHub workflows.
3. Keep private plugin / authenticated package install / local opencode coverage behind explicit opt-in flags or dedicated scripts.
4. Stop inferring "run private tests" merely from ambient auth variables or incidental local setup.
5. Document the contract clearly in `docs/TESTING.md` and workflow definitions.

## Concrete Outcome We Want
- `bun run test:integration` works for external contributors by default.
- A separate opt-in command/profile runs private/auth/opencode-dependent launcher coverage.
- GitHub CI/release workflows run the public-safe integration suite again.
- Extended/private coverage can run in a dedicated environment once registry/migration setup is ready.

## Instructions
1. Separate public-safe manual-launcher/integration checks from private/auth/opencode-dependent checks.
2. Introduce an explicit capability model (for example dedicated env flags or test profile scripts) instead of relying on ambient auth detection alone.
3. Restore GitHub workflow integration coverage using the public-safe suite.
4. Define a deliberate strategy for extended coverage (manual, nightly, self-hosted, or dedicated secret-backed workflow) while the plugin migration is incomplete.
5. Update testing docs so external contributors know what is expected to work by default and how to enable the extended suite.

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] Default integration tests are runnable without private plugin access
- [ ] GitHub workflows restore intentional public-safe integration coverage
- [ ] Private/auth/opencode-dependent coverage is available behind explicit opt-in controls
- [ ] Test/docs/workflow behavior is documented clearly for maintainers and external contributors
close_reason: All 4 acceptance criteria now pass. The only blocker was the socket preservation test (opencode-coder-nzl, now closed). Root cause was Bun.file().exists() returning false for Unix domain sockets — fixed by using fs.stat().isSocket(). Full private opt-in suite: 22 pass / 0 fail. Public-safe suite: 37 pass / 5 skip / 0 fail.

comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text: Discussion update: scope is now broader than simply restoring the skipped workflow step. The real requirement is a capability-based testing model: public-default integration coverage for everyone, plus explicit opt-in private/auth/opencode coverage while the Dynatrace plugin migration is still in progress.

comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text:
## Overall direction is sound but the split point needs to be more precise

**What**: The proposal correctly identifies the public/private boundary, but the description does not specify exactly which tests in manual-launcher.test.ts are private. After careful analysis, the boundary is:

**Public-safe (no auth, no opencode binary, no private registry)**:
- Lines 87-316: All of describe("manual launcher preflight") EXCEPT the single .skipIf(!githubPackagesAuthCheck) test at line 335

**Private/capability-dependent**:
- Line 335-358: "prepares pinned Dynatrace package deterministically..." — needs GitHub Packages auth (already .skipIf-guarded)
- Lines 361-661: All of describe("manual launcher non-interactive mode") — needs BOTH opencode binary AND GitHub Packages auth (already .skipIf-guarded)

The existing .skipIf guards already implement most of the proposed capability model. The real problem is NOT that the tests run when they should not — it is that GitHub CI cannot even load the test file without the bun test tests/integration step failing for other environmental reasons, or that the entire step was skipped as a blunt workaround.

**Why**: The proposal risks over-engineering a solution for a problem that is primarily "the CI step was sledgehammered off." If the only actual failure mode was the integration step itself, we need to identify exactly what broke — was it an import-time failure? A runtime auth probe? A test framework error? — before designing a file-split or env-flag system.

**Suggested action**: Before implementing the split, run bun test tests/integration in a clean GitHub Actions environment (no private auth, no opencode binary) and capture the EXACT failure. The .skipIf guards may already make this pass. If they do, the fix is just restoring the workflow step — no file splitting needed.

comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text:
## The skipIf guards already exist but the config fixture has an embedded private package reference

**What**: The isolated opencode config fixture at tests/e2e/fixtures/_shared/opencode-config/opencode.json contains:

  "plugin": ["@hk9890/opencode-dynatrace@0.6.0"]

And createIsolatedOpenCodePaths() in harness.ts (line 801) calls buildSharedConfiguredPluginSpecs() which reads this fixture and injects the pinned Dynatrace spec. The test at line 154-167 ("copies the committed OpenCode config fixture into isolated config") asserts the isolated config contains the Dynatrace plugin spec.

This test does NOT actually install the private package — it only asserts the config JSON was written correctly. But it does assert on a string that references a private package name. This is a latent coupling: the test itself is public-safe (no network, no auth), but its fixture and assertions are tightly bound to the private package naming.

Similarly, test at line 169-174 ("reads isolated test manifest pins") directly asserts on @hk9890/opencode-dynatrace pin values.

**Why**: These tests will pass in CI without auth — they are pure JSON/file assertions. But they will break when the Dynatrace plugin migration changes the package name. This is a maintenance risk, not a CI blocker. The proposal should acknowledge that "public-safe" tests still reference private-ecosystem names, and plan for that migration path.

**Suggested action**: Accept these tests as public-safe for now (they do not need auth), but add a note to the issue that the Dynatrace plugin migration will require updating fixture names and assertions in these tests. Do not block the CI restoration on this.

comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text:
## Simplification opportunity: file splitting is unnecessary if skipIf guards work in CI

**What**: The proposal suggests splitting coverage into two layers and potentially two separate commands or scripts. But examining the actual test code:

1. plugin.test.ts (732 lines) — fully public-safe, uses mocks, zero external deps
2. manual-launcher.test.ts (662 lines) — already has .skipIf guards on every private test

The private tests are already guarded by:
- .skipIf(!githubPackagesAuthCheck) on line 335
- .skipIf(!opencodeCheck.available || !githubPackagesAuthCheck) on line 361

These guards run async checks at module load time (lines 84-85) and skip the describe/it blocks cleanly. Bun test will report them as skipped, not failed.

If these guards work correctly in a clean CI environment (no auth, no opencode binary), then the ENTIRE proposal collapses to: restore the "bun run test:integration" step in CI workflows.

**Why**: Adding separate commands, env flags, or file splits for something that already works via skipIf is unnecessary complexity. The proposal should validate the simple path first.

**Suggested action**: 
1. First: manually verify that bun test tests/integration passes in a clean env with the skipIf guards doing their job (should show skipped tests, zero failures).
2. If it passes: restore the CI step. Done. No new scripts, no env flags, no file splits.
3. If it does NOT pass: identify the specific failure, and fix THAT — which is likely a much smaller change than the full proposal.
4. Only if the tests fundamentally cannot run in CI (e.g., module-level import failure from a missing dep) should you escalate to file splitting.

comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text:
## Risk: hasGitHubPackagesAuthConfig probes the filesystem at module load time

**What**: Lines 26-56 of manual-launcher.test.ts define hasGitHubPackagesAuthConfig() which reads .npmrc files from HOME and PROJECT_ROOT. Line 85 calls this at module top level:

  const githubPackagesAuthCheck = await hasGitHubPackagesAuthConfig();

This is an async function called at module scope. In a CI environment, this will:
1. Check env vars (NODE_AUTH_TOKEN, NPM_TOKEN, GITHUB_TOKEN) — these may be set in CI for package operations
2. Try to read ~/.npmrc and <project-root>/.npmrc

If GITHUB_TOKEN is set in CI (which it always is in GitHub Actions via secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN or the default token), hasGitHubPackagesAuthConfig() will return true, and the skipIf guards will NOT skip the private tests. Those private tests will then attempt network operations (bun add @hk9890/opencode-dynatrace@0.6.0) and may fail because the token does not have read:packages scope for the private registry.

**Why**: This is the most likely actual failure mode. The GITHUB_TOKEN in standard GitHub Actions has limited scope. If it triggers auth detection but cannot actually install the private package, you get a runtime failure in a test that should have been skipped. This would explain why the entire step was disabled.

**Suggested action**: The capability detection in hasGitHubPackagesAuthConfig must be more precise. Options:
1. Check for a dedicated opt-in env var like OPENCODE_CODER_PRIVATE_TESTS=true instead of inferring capability from ambient auth
2. Actually validate the auth works (try a lightweight npm whoami or registry ping) before enabling private tests
3. At minimum, exclude GITHUB_TOKEN from the auth candidate list since it is always present in Actions but rarely has the right scope

Option 1 is the cleanest — it directly implements "explicit opt-in" from the proposal and makes the contract unambiguous for both CI and local dev.

comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text:
## Recommended concrete contract for test commands

**What**: The proposal asks for "default integration command" and "opt-in extended/private command" but does not specify the exact contract. Here is a concrete recommendation:

**Default (public-safe, runs in CI):**
  bun run test:integration

Behavior: runs all integration tests. Private/auth-dependent tests skip automatically via capability detection. No env vars needed.

**Opt-in private/extended (maintainer local, dedicated workflow):**
  OPENCODE_CODER_PRIVATE_TESTS=true bun run test:integration

Behavior: same command, but the env flag signals that the environment has been explicitly prepared with private registry auth. The skipIf guards check for this flag instead of (or in addition to) probing for ambient auth.

**Why**: This avoids introducing new package.json scripts, separate test files, or complex workflow matrices. One command, one codepath, one env flag. External contributors run the same command as CI and see skipped tests. Maintainers set one flag. The workflow files restore the step with zero additional config.

**Suggested action**: Implement this contract:
1. Replace hasGitHubPackagesAuthConfig() probing with a check for OPENCODE_CODER_PRIVATE_TESTS env var
2. Keep the opencodeCheck.available guard for tests that need the opencode binary (this is already correct and does not suffer from the ambient-auth problem)
3. Restore the CI workflow step as just: bun run test:integration
4. If a dedicated private workflow is wanted later, add a separate GitHub Actions workflow with OPENCODE_CODER_PRIVATE_TESTS=true and appropriate secrets — but this is not blocking

comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text:
## The harness.ts installWorkspacePluginDependencies is the actual CI-breaking call path

**What**: When private tests are NOT skipped (due to ambient GITHUB_TOKEN detection), the test at line 335 calls prepareWorkspacePluginSource which calls wireBuiltPluginArtifact (line 728-741 of harness.ts) which calls installWorkspacePluginDependencies (line 360-392). This function runs:

  bun add --exact @hk9890/opencode-dynatrace@0.6.0

This is a network call to npm.pkg.github.com that requires read:packages scope on a token configured for that registry. In GitHub Actions with a default GITHUB_TOKEN, this will fail because:
1. The default token is scoped to the current repository
2. @hk9890/opencode-dynatrace lives in a different org/user namespace

The non-interactive mode tests (line 361+) are even worse — they call runLauncher which spawns a child process that runs the full launcher setup flow including package installation.

**Why**: This confirms the root cause hypothesis from my previous comment. The fix is upstream of all these call paths: change the skip-guard to use explicit opt-in rather than ambient auth detection.

**Suggested action**: This comment reinforces that the single most impactful change is replacing hasGitHubPackagesAuthConfig with an explicit OPENCODE_CODER_PRIVATE_TESTS check. Everything else in the proposal (file splits, separate commands, dedicated workflows) is optional follow-up that can be deferred.

comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text:
## Workflow restoration should be identical in ci.yml and release.yml

**What**: Both ci.yml (line 34-35) and release.yml (line 54-55) have the same skip placeholder. The proposal should restore both identically to:

  - name: Run integration tests
    run: bun run test:integration

No conditional logic, no env flags in the workflow itself. The test suite handles its own skip logic internally.

**Why**: Having different integration test behavior between CI and release pipelines is a maintenance risk and a source of confusion. The test suite should be the single source of truth for what runs where — the workflow just invokes it.

**Suggested action**: Restore both workflow files with the same simple step. Do not add workflow-level env vars or conditional steps for the integration suite. If private coverage needs a dedicated workflow later, create a new workflow file rather than bolting conditions onto ci.yml or release.yml.

comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text:
## Acceptance criteria are mostly testable but criteria 3 needs clarification

**What**: The acceptance criteria are:
1. Default integration tests are runnable without private plugin access — testable, verify by running in clean env
2. GitHub workflows restore intentional public-safe integration coverage — testable, verify workflow file change and a passing CI run
3. Private/auth/opencode-dependent coverage is available behind explicit opt-in controls — partially testable, but "available" is vague. Does this mean the tests exist and can be run with the flag? Or that there is a documented workflow/command? Or that a dedicated CI job runs them?
4. Test/docs/workflow behavior is documented clearly — testable only by review

**Why**: Criteria 3 has different implementation costs depending on interpretation. If it just means "the tests skip by default and run when OPENCODE_CODER_PRIVATE_TESTS=true", that is trivial. If it means "there is a dedicated GitHub Actions workflow with proper secrets that runs nightly", that is significantly more work and probably not needed for the initial fix.

**Suggested action**: Narrow criteria 3 to: "Private tests are gated behind explicit OPENCODE_CODER_PRIVATE_TESTS=true env var and documented in TESTING.md." Defer dedicated CI pipeline for private coverage to a follow-up if needed.

comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text:
## Summary: recommended minimal implementation path

**What**: After reviewing all files, here is the recommended implementation in priority order:

**Step 1 (fixes CI, ~30 min)**:
- Replace hasGitHubPackagesAuthConfig() check with: process.env.OPENCODE_CODER_PRIVATE_TESTS === "true"
- Keep checkOpencodeAvailability() as-is (it is already correct for the opencode binary gate)
- Restore "bun run test:integration" step in both ci.yml and release.yml
- Verify CI passes with private tests skipped

**Step 2 (documentation, ~15 min)**:
- Add a "Private/extended integration tests" section to TESTING.md explaining:
  - What OPENCODE_CODER_PRIVATE_TESTS=true enables
  - What prerequisites are needed (GitHub Packages auth, opencode binary)
  - How maintainers run it locally

**Step 3 (optional follow-up, separate issue)**:
- Dedicated GitHub Actions workflow for private tests with proper secrets (nightly or manual dispatch)
- Migration path when @hk9890/opencode-dynatrace becomes a public package

**What NOT to do**:
- Do not split manual-launcher.test.ts into separate files — the skipIf guards already handle this
- Do not add new package.json scripts for private tests — the env flag is sufficient
- Do not add workflow-level conditional logic — keep it simple

**Why**: This is the minimum viable fix that unblocks CI, establishes the explicit opt-in contract, and avoids unnecessary structural changes. The proposal as written is directionally correct but oversized for the actual problem.

**Suggested action**: Implement steps 1 and 2 as the scope of this issue. File a separate follow-up for step 3 if dedicated private CI coverage is wanted.

comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text: Implemented the minimal explicit-capability fix. Changes: removed ambient auth detection from manual-launcher integration gating; private launcher/package-install scenarios now require ; restored bun test v1.3.11 (af24e281) in both CI and release workflows; documented the public-safe default vs private opt-in contract in docs/TESTING.md. Local verification: bun test v1.3.11 (af24e281) => 37 pass / 5 skip / 0 fail; bun test v1.3.11 (af24e281) => 18 pass / 4 skip / 0 fail in current local environment.

title: Fix release-workflow integration failure for private package setup
description:
## Description
The v0.35.0 release workflow failed during `Run integration tests` after the manual-launcher stabilization work was pushed.

Failed workflow:
- `release.yml` run `23435509346`
- job `68172461834`

Observed failure excerpt:
- `installWorkspacePluginDependencies (...)`
- `bun add --exact @hk9890/opencode-dynatrace@0.6.0`
- `error: GET https://registry.npmjs.org/@hk9890%2fopencode-dynatrace - 404`
- stack points to `tests/integration/manual-launcher.test.ts` local-build/manual-launcher path

## Root Cause
The normal CI workflow currently passes because the auth-sensitive/manual-launcher cases are skipped unless GitHub Packages auth is configured. The release workflow runs with package-publish auth, which makes the auth gate pass, but the manual-launcher dependency install still resolves the pinned `@hk9890/opencode-dynatrace` package from the wrong registry during integration tests.

So the release environment is materially different from plain CI:
- it has auth available
- but the harness install path still is not configured robustly for the pinned package registry expectation

## Instructions
1. Reproduce and confirm the release-workflow-only integration failure locally if possible, without broadening scope.
2. Fix the manual-launcher dependency install path so auth-enabled release/CI environments resolve the pinned package from the intended registry.
