comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text:
## Fix strategy: use allowlist env, not blocklist — this is the root bug of all three

**What**: The env construction at `scripts/manual-test/index.ts` line 338-341 does `{ ...process.env, ...isolatedPaths.env }` which starts from the full host env and overlays 6 isolation vars. The automated harness `runOpencodeCli` (harness.ts line 394-397) does the opposite: `{ ...options.env, PATH: process.env.PATH }` — starting from ONLY isolation vars + PATH. This means the manual launcher and the automated harness have fundamentally different env contracts. The manual launcher leaks ~150 host env vars including secrets (JIRA_TOKEN, BITBUCKET_TOKEN, LANGDOCK_API_KEY, MISE_GITHUB_TOKEN, GITHUB_NPM_REGISTRY_KEY are all visible in the evidence dump).

**Why**: This is not just an isolation parity gap — it's a credential exposure vector. The entire env dump in the bug evidence contains multiple real API tokens and secrets from the host environment. When the manual launcher is used to test plugin behavior, those secrets are visible to the child process and anything it spawns. Beyond security, this makes the manual launcher fundamentally non-comparable to automated e2e: a plugin that works under manual testing might fail under e2e (or vice versa) because the env contexts are different. The story goal of "comparable and collaborative" testing is broken.

**Suggested action**: Replace line 338-341 with an allowlist-based env construction that matches `runOpencodeCli`'s contract. The fix is one line change:

```typescript
const childEnv: Record<string, string | undefined> = {
  ...isolatedPaths.env,
  PATH: process.env.PATH ?? "",
};
```

However — see my next comment on the TUI/shell mode pitfall. This simple fix works for `command` mode but will break interactive modes. The fix needs to be mode-aware.

comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text:
## Mode-specific env policy: same base for all modes, with documented TERM passthrough for interactive

**What**: The question is whether TUI/shell modes need more env passthrough than command mode. My position: they do, but only a small, explicit set — not the full host env.

The absolute minimum viable allowlist for all modes is:
- `PATH` (to find binaries — required)
- `isolatedPaths.env` (the 6 OpenCode isolation vars)
- `USER` / `LOGNAME` (some tools need a username)
- `LANG` / `LC_*` (locale — affects terminal rendering)

For interactive modes (TUI and shell) additionally:
- `TERM` / `COLORTERM` / `TERMINFO` (terminal capability detection — TUI will render garbage without TERM)
- `DISPLAY` / `WAYLAND_DISPLAY` / `XDG_RUNTIME_DIR` (if clipboard/GUI integration matters)
- `SHELL` (only for shell mode, to know which shell to spawn)

**Why**: The right contract is "isolated by default, explicit passthrough for usability." The harness uses isolated-env-only for automated runs because those never need terminal rendering. The manual launcher needs a few more vars because a human is staring at the terminal. But "a few more" is 8-12 vars, not 150. The full host env inheritance was never the right default — it just happened to be easier to code.

**Suggested action**: Extract a `buildChildEnv(mode, isolatedPaths)` helper in the launcher (or better, in harness.ts so it's shared). Use an explicit allowlist. The allowlist should be a named constant so it's auditable and testable. Document the policy in TESTING.md under the manual launcher section.

comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text:
## Hidden pitfall: TUI mode will break if you naively strip the env

**What**: If the fixer applies the minimal env fix (`isolatedPaths.env + PATH`) uniformly to all modes, `--mode=tui` will likely break or render incorrectly. The OpenCode TUI is a terminal application that needs `TERM` at minimum to detect terminal capabilities (color depth, alternate screen support, mouse protocol). Without `TERM`, Bubble Tea (the Go TUI framework OpenCode uses) will fall back to dumb terminal mode or panic. Similarly, `--mode=shell` without `SHELL` will fall back to `/bin/sh` (the code at line 351 already handles this, but it reads from `process.env.SHELL` of the launcher process, not the child env — which is correct).

**Why**: The fixer might test the env fix with `--mode=command -- env` (the repro from this very bug), see it working, and ship. Then TUI mode silently degrades or crashes. This is the most likely regression from fixing this bug.

**Suggested action**: The fix PR must include a manual smoke test of `--mode=tui` after the env change. The automated test can't easily verify TUI rendering, but it can at minimum assert that `TERM` is present in the child env when mode is tui/shell. Add a comment in the code explaining why TERM/COLORTERM/TERMINFO are allowlisted — so the next person doesn't remove them thinking they're unnecessary passthrough.

comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text:
## Pitfall not yet filed: OPENCODE_DEFAULT_OPTIONS leaks through and changes CLI behavior

**What**: The bug evidence shows `OPENCODE_DEFAULT_OPTIONS=--log-level DEBUG` in the child env. This is a host-level OpenCode configuration variable that changes CLI behavior (enables debug logging). Under the current `...process.env` approach, this means manual test runs produce different log output than automated e2e runs, and may trigger different code paths in the plugin. Specifically, `OPENCODE_LOG_RETENTION=100` and `OPENCODE_PID=168162` also leak — the child process sees the host's OpenCode PID and log retention settings.

**Why**: Even if someone only cares about auth/config isolation and not general env hygiene, these three vars (`OPENCODE_DEFAULT_OPTIONS`, `OPENCODE_LOG_RETENTION`, `OPENCODE_PID`) directly affect OpenCode's own behavior inside the isolated environment. `OPENCODE_PID` in particular could cause IPC confusion if the OpenCode TUI tries to talk to the host's running OpenCode process. The allowlist fix from 874 will eliminate all of these, but this deserves explicit mention in the TESTING.md policy to explain WHY even OPENCODE_* vars from the host must be blocked (except the ones the harness explicitly sets).

**Suggested action**: In the TESTING.md env policy section, add a note: "The launcher intentionally does NOT inherit OPENCODE_* vars from the host environment — it sets only the isolation-controlled ones (OPENCODE_CONFIG_DIR, OPENCODE_DISABLE_DEFAULT_PLUGINS). Host vars like OPENCODE_DEFAULT_OPTIONS, OPENCODE_LOG_RETENTION, and OPENCODE_PID are excluded to prevent cross-talk."

comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text: Reviewer summary: this bug is the root cause. The launcher currently builds child env as { ...process.env, ...isolatedPaths.env }, which leaks host OpenCode/plugin-affecting env like OPENCODE_DEFAULT_OPTIONS, OPENCODE_PID, OPENCODE_CODER_DEBUG and many unrelated secrets. Recommended fix is an allowlist-based child env, not full env inheritance. Policy recommendation: all modes get isolated HOME/XDG/OpenCode vars plus PATH, USER/LOGNAME, LANG/LC_*; interactive TUI/shell also get TERM/COLORTERM/TERMINFO and display/session vars needed for terminal usability; everything else stays out.

comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text:
## Fix strategy: use allowlist env, not blocklist — this is the root bug of all three

**What**: The env construction at `scripts/manual-test/index.ts` line 338-341 does `{ ...process.env, ...isolatedPaths.env }` which starts from the full host env and overlays 6 isolation vars. The automated harness `runOpencodeCli` (harness.ts line 394-397) does the opposite: `{ ...options.env, PATH: process.env.PATH }` — starting from ONLY isolation vars + PATH. This means the manual launcher and the automated harness have fundamentally different env contracts. The manual launcher leaks ~150 host env vars including secrets (JIRA_TOKEN, BITBUCKET_TOKEN, LANGDOCK_API_KEY, MISE_GITHUB_TOKEN, GITHUB_NPM_REGISTRY_KEY are all visible in the evidence dump).

**Why**: This is not just an isolation parity gap — it's a credential exposure vector. The entire env dump in the bug evidence contains multiple real API tokens and secrets from the host environment. When the manual launcher is used to test plugin behavior, those secrets are visible to the child process and anything it spawns. Beyond security, this makes the manual launcher fundamentally non-comparable to automated e2e: a plugin that works under manual testing might fail under e2e (or vice versa) because the env contexts are different. The story goal of "comparable and collaborative" testing is broken.

**Suggested action**: Replace line 338-341 with an allowlist-based env construction that matches `runOpencodeCli`'s contract. The fix is one line change:

```typescript
const childEnv: Record<string, string | undefined> = {
  ...isolatedPaths.env,
  PATH: process.env.PATH ?? "",
};
```

However — see my next comment on the TUI/shell mode pitfall. This simple fix works for `command` mode but will break interactive modes. The fix needs to be mode-aware.

comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text:
## Mode-specific env policy: same base for all modes, with documented TERM passthrough for interactive

**What**: The question is whether TUI/shell modes need more env passthrough than command mode. My position: they do, but only a small, explicit set — not the full host env.

The absolute minimum viable allowlist for all modes is:
- `PATH` (to find binaries — required)
- `isolatedPaths.env` (the 6 OpenCode isolation vars)
- `USER` / `LOGNAME` (some tools need a username)
- `LANG` / `LC_*` (locale — affects terminal rendering)

For interactive modes (TUI and shell) additionally:
- `TERM` / `COLORTERM` / `TERMINFO` (terminal capability detection — TUI will render garbage without TERM)
- `DISPLAY` / `WAYLAND_DISPLAY` / `XDG_RUNTIME_DIR` (if clipboard/GUI integration matters)
- `SHELL` (only for shell mode, to know which shell to spawn)

**Why**: The right contract is "isolated by default, explicit passthrough for usability." The harness uses isolated-env-only for automated runs because those never need terminal rendering. The manual launcher needs a few more vars because a human is staring at the terminal. But "a few more" is 8-12 vars, not 150. The full host env inheritance was never the right default — it just happened to be easier to code.

**Suggested action**: Extract a `buildChildEnv(mode, isolatedPaths)` helper in the launcher (or better, in harness.ts so it's shared). Use an explicit allowlist. The allowlist should be a named constant so it's auditable and testable. Document the policy in TESTING.md under the manual launcher section.

comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text:
## Hidden pitfall: TUI mode will break if you naively strip the env

**What**: If the fixer applies the minimal env fix (`isolatedPaths.env + PATH`) uniformly to all modes, `--mode=tui` will likely break or render incorrectly. The OpenCode TUI is a terminal application that needs `TERM` at minimum to detect terminal capabilities (color depth, alternate screen support, mouse protocol). Without `TERM`, Bubble Tea (the Go TUI framework OpenCode uses) will fall back to dumb terminal mode or panic. Similarly, `--mode=shell` without `SHELL` will fall back to `/bin/sh` (the code at line 351 already handles this, but it reads from `process.env.SHELL` of the launcher process, not the child env — which is correct).

**Why**: The fixer might test the env fix with `--mode=command -- env` (the repro from this very bug), see it working, and ship. Then TUI mode silently degrades or crashes. This is the most likely regression from fixing this bug.

**Suggested action**: The fix PR must include a manual smoke test of `--mode=tui` after the env change. The automated test can't easily verify TUI rendering, but it can at minimum assert that `TERM` is present in the child env when mode is tui/shell. Add a comment in the code explaining why TERM/COLORTERM/TERMINFO are allowlisted — so the next person doesn't remove them thinking they're unnecessary passthrough.

comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text:
## Pitfall not yet filed: OPENCODE_DEFAULT_OPTIONS leaks through and changes CLI behavior

**What**: The bug evidence shows `OPENCODE_DEFAULT_OPTIONS=--log-level DEBUG` in the child env. This is a host-level OpenCode configuration variable that changes CLI behavior (enables debug logging). Under the current `...process.env` approach, this means manual test runs produce different log output than automated e2e runs, and may trigger different code paths in the plugin. Specifically, `OPENCODE_LOG_RETENTION=100` and `OPENCODE_PID=168162` also leak — the child process sees the host's OpenCode PID and log retention settings.

**Why**: Even if someone only cares about auth/config isolation and not general env hygiene, these three vars (`OPENCODE_DEFAULT_OPTIONS`, `OPENCODE_LOG_RETENTION`, `OPENCODE_PID`) directly affect OpenCode's own behavior inside the isolated environment. `OPENCODE_PID` in particular could cause IPC confusion if the OpenCode TUI tries to talk to the host's running OpenCode process. The allowlist fix from 874 will eliminate all of these, but this deserves explicit mention in the TESTING.md policy to explain WHY even OPENCODE_* vars from the host must be blocked (except the ones the harness explicitly sets).

**Suggested action**: In the TESTING.md env policy section, add a note: "The launcher intentionally does NOT inherit OPENCODE_* vars from the host environment — it sets only the isolation-controlled ones (OPENCODE_CONFIG_DIR, OPENCODE_DISABLE_DEFAULT_PLUGINS). Host vars like OPENCODE_DEFAULT_OPTIONS, OPENCODE_LOG_RETENTION, and OPENCODE_PID are excluded to prevent cross-talk."

comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text: Reviewer summary: this bug is the root cause. The launcher currently builds child env as { ...process.env, ...isolatedPaths.env }, which leaks host OpenCode/plugin-affecting env like OPENCODE_DEFAULT_OPTIONS, OPENCODE_PID, OPENCODE_CODER_DEBUG and many unrelated secrets. Recommended fix is an allowlist-based child env, not full env inheritance. Policy recommendation: all modes get isolated HOME/XDG/OpenCode vars plus PATH, USER/LOGNAME, LANG/LC_*; interactive TUI/shell also get TERM/COLORTERM/TERMINFO and display/session vars needed for terminal usability; everything else stays out.

title: Implement shared manual isolated plugin test launcher
description:
## Description
Implement a reusable manual testing launcher that creates the same isolated temp fixture environment used by the real-CLI e2e harness, so humans and automated tests can exercise the current plugin under comparable conditions.

## Instructions
1. Review the current e2e harness under `tests/e2e/helpers/` and reuse its setup logic as much as possible rather than reimplementing fixture copy, plugin wiring, auth seeding, and isolated path creation from scratch.
2. Add a user-facing launcher entrypoint (script, Bun script, or equivalent) that supports at least these workflows:
   - launch OpenCode TUI in the isolated temp project using inherited stdio
   - open an interactive shell in the isolated temp project using inherited stdio
   - run a one-shot command in the isolated temp project and capture/report results
3. Support choosing a committed fixture (at minimum the existing e2e fixtures) and default to a sensible fixture if none is provided.
4. Seed auth with the same precedence model as e2e:
   - explicit path input
   - fallback to `~/.local/share/opencode/auth.json` if present
   Copy auth into isolated `XDG_DATA_HOME/opencode/auth.json`; do not use host-global auth in place during runtime.
   Do not require raw auth JSON on command-line arguments where it could leak to shell history or process lists.
5. Add explicit preflight checks and helpful errors for at least:
   - missing `opencode` binary
   - unknown fixture name
   - missing usable auth source when auth is requested/expected
6. Make the launcher print useful information for manual use:
   - temp project path
   - isolation root paths
   - fixture used
   - plugin path used
   - whether auth was seeded and from which source category
   - whether the environment will be cleaned up or kept
7. Add a `--keep` option and preserve the temp environment automatically on failure/non-zero exit so users can inspect it.
8. Handle Ctrl+C / child-process termination cleanly enough that interactive use does not leave the user confused about whether the temp env was preserved or cleaned.
9. Add automated verification for the launcher in a realistic non-interactive mode with concrete assertions about setup parity/output.
10. Update docs with examples for user/manual workflows and explain that this shares the same environment model as automated e2e tests.

## Files to Modify
- scripts/** or equivalent user-facing entrypoint — add launcher
- tests/e2e/helpers/** — extract/reuse shared setup logic if needed
- tests/** — add coverage for launcher non-interactive flow
- docs/TESTING.md — document user/manual launcher workflow

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] Manual launcher reuses or shares the automated harness setup model
- [ ] Launcher supports TUI, shell, and one-shot command workflows
- [ ] Fixture selection works for committed e2e fixtures
- [ ] Auth and config are copied into isolated temp roots, not used in place
- [ ] Launcher reports enough information for a human to use/debug it
- [ ] Preflight errors are clear for missing opencode / bad fixture / missing auth
- [ ] Temp environments are preserved on failure and optionally via `--keep`
- [ ] Non-interactive automated verification passes
- [ ] Docs clearly describe how both the assistant and the user can use the shared setup
close_reason: Implemented shared manual isolated launcher with fixture/auth isolation, interactive modes, preflight checks, cleanup semantics, automated non-interactive verification, and TESTING docs updates.

comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text:
## TUI/shell mode requires `stdin: "inherit"` — harness API gap

**What**: The existing `runOpencodeCli()` in `harness.ts` hardcodes `stdout: "pipe"` and `stderr: "pipe"` (lines 361-362) with no `stdin` config. This captures output for automated assertions but kills interactive use. The TUI mode needs `stdin: "inherit"`, `stdout: "inherit"`, `stderr: "inherit"` — the shell mode needs the same plus proper signal forwarding. The task instructions say "reuse harness setup logic" but the harness's *execution* function is fundamentally non-interactive.

**Why**: If a tasker tries to reuse `runOpencodeCli()` for TUI/shell mode, either the TUI will hang waiting for piped stdin that never comes, or they'll need to fork/copy the function anyway — defeating the "reuse" goal. This is the single biggest API gap between the automated harness and the launcher.

**Suggested action**: Clarify in the task instructions that the launcher should reuse the *setup* helpers (`createFixtureWorkspace`, `wireBuiltPluginArtifact`, `createIsolatedOpenCodePaths`, `seedIsolatedOpenCodeAuth`, `resolveCopilotAuthSeedFromEnv`) but should NOT reuse `runOpencodeCli()` for interactive modes. The launcher needs its own execution path that uses `Bun.spawn` with `{ stdin: "inherit", stdout: "inherit", stderr: "inherit" }` for TUI and shell, and the existing pipe-based `runOpencodeCli()` (or something similar) only for one-shot mode.

comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text:
## Signal handling for interactive modes is unspecified

**What**: The task says "launch OpenCode TUI" and "open a shell" but says nothing about signal handling. When a user Ctrl+C's the TUI, the launcher process needs to forward SIGINT to the child and wait for graceful exit. When the user `exit`s a shell, the launcher needs to handle cleanup vs. `--keep`. The existing harness uses a `setTimeout`-based kill (line 366-369) which is fine for automated tests but wrong for interactive use — there's no predefined timeout for a human session.

**Why**: Without signal handling, Ctrl+C will kill the launcher but may orphan the child OpenCode/shell process, leaving temp dirs and possibly port bindings behind. This is a predictable user frustration in the primary use case.

**Suggested action**: Add to the instructions: "For interactive modes (TUI, shell), the launcher must forward signals (SIGINT, SIGTERM) to the child process and wait for child exit before performing cleanup. No timeout should be applied to interactive sessions. Cleanup (or preservation with `--keep`) should run after the child process exits."

comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text:
## Cleanup-vs-keep semantics are under-specified for interactive failure

**What**: The task says "Add a `--keep` option so users can preserve the temp environment for inspection." But it doesn't specify what happens when the child process crashes or when the user Ctrl+C's without `--keep`. Three cases need explicit rules:
1. Normal exit without `--keep` → cleanup temp (clear)
2. Normal exit with `--keep` → preserve temp, print path (clear)
3. Abnormal exit / signal without `--keep` → cleanup? Or preserve for debugging?

Case 3 is the most important for the user: if the TUI crashes, the user almost certainly wants to inspect the environment. Auto-deleting it on failure is hostile.

**Why**: A tasker will have to make this choice, and the wrong default (clean up on crash) will frustrate users at exactly the moment they need the temp dir most.

**Suggested action**: Add to acceptance criteria: "On abnormal child exit (non-zero exit code or signal), the launcher should preserve the temp environment by default and print the path, regardless of `--keep`. Only clean up on successful exit when `--keep` is not set."

comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text:
## `wireBuiltPluginArtifact` runs `bun install` — slow and fragile for manual launcher

**What**: The existing `wireBuiltPluginArtifact()` (harness.ts lines 179-209) creates `.opencode/package.json`, symlinks the built plugin, and runs `bun install` inside the temp `.opencode/` directory. This works in automated tests because the test waits for it. But for a user-facing launcher, this means every launch has a `bun install` step that:
- Takes several seconds even with cached deps
- Can fail if Bun is not installed or if network is unavailable
- Writes a `bun.lock` file that pollutes the temp workspace

The `existing-active-project` fixture already ships committed `node_modules` (I can see `@opencode-ai/sdk` and `@opencode-ai/plugin` vendored in the fixture), but the other fixtures do not.

**Why**: A manual testing launcher should start fast. If the user is iterating on plugin behavior and relaunching repeatedly, a multi-second `bun install` on every launch is friction. Also, `bun install` failure messages are confusing for users who just want to test the plugin.

**Suggested action**: Consider whether `wireBuiltPluginArtifact` can be refactored to skip `bun install` when the target fixture already has `node_modules`, or whether a pre-warmed approach (copy from the fixture that already has node_modules) would be faster. At minimum, the launcher should print a clear "installing plugin dependencies..." message so the user knows what's happening. This isn't a blocker but should be called out in implementation.

comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text:
## Auth seed raw-content mode is a security surface — task should acknowledge this

**What**: The task instruction #4 says "explicit raw auth content input if appropriate/safe" and the harness supports `authJsonContent` as a string. For an automated test, this is fine — the content comes from `E2E_COPILOT_AUTH_JSON_CONTENT` env var which is under CI control. But for a user-facing launcher, accepting raw auth content as a CLI argument means it appears in shell history, `ps` output, and process listings.

**Why**: Auth tokens in `ps aux` output or `.bash_history` are a credential leak vector. The harness function `seedIsolatedOpenCodeAuth` doesn't care about this because it's an internal API, but a user-facing launcher is different.

**Suggested action**: For the launcher, support only file-path-based auth seeding (explicit path or default local fallback). Do NOT expose raw auth content as a CLI flag. The "if appropriate/safe" qualifier in the current instructions is too vague — make it explicit: "The launcher must NOT accept raw auth content as a command-line argument. Use file paths only."

comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text:
## Entrypoint format is unspecified — Bun script vs shell wrapper matters

**What**: The task says "Add a user-facing launcher entrypoint (script, Bun script, or equivalent)" but doesn't specify which. The existing project convention shows: `scripts/` contains Python scripts (session sanitizer, DB vacuum, etc.) and TypeScript scripts (log-analyzer). The `package.json` defines `"scripts"` entries for dev workflows like `opencode:dev`. There is no precedent for a `bun run scripts/...` launcher intended for human use from the command line.

**Why**: The choice matters because:
1. A `package.json` script entry (e.g. `bun run test:manual`) is discoverable and consistent with existing patterns
2. A standalone TypeScript file in `scripts/` needs documentation for users to know it exists
3. A shell wrapper script is more portable but adds a different language to maintain
4. The tasker will pick something arbitrary without guidance

**Suggested action**: Specify that the launcher should be a TypeScript file in `scripts/` (matching the log-analyzer precedent) with a corresponding `package.json` script entry (e.g. `"test:manual": "bun run scripts/manual-test-launcher/index.ts"` or similar). This keeps the entrypoint discoverable via `bun run` and consistent with the project's existing script patterns.

comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text:
## Missing acceptance criterion: launcher must fail fast if `opencode` not on PATH

**What**: The automated harness has `checkOpencodeAvailability()` which returns diagnostics when `opencode` is not found, and tests skip via `describe.skipIf`. But the task instructions don't mention pre-flight checks for the launcher. A user launching the manual test environment expects a clear error if OpenCode isn't installed — not a cryptic `spawn opencode ENOENT` from Bun.

**Why**: The harness already solved this problem with good diagnostics (harness.ts lines 79-117). The launcher should reuse this check. If it doesn't, users will hit a confusing error on the most basic prerequisite failure.

**Suggested action**: Add to acceptance criteria: "Launcher must check `opencode` availability on PATH before attempting to launch and show actionable diagnostics on failure (reuse `checkOpencodeAvailability()` from the harness)." Similarly, the launcher should verify the plugin builds successfully before creating the temp workspace.

comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text:
## "Automated verification for the launcher in a realistic non-interactive mode" is vague

**What**: Task instruction #7 says "Add automated verification for the launcher in a realistic non-interactive mode." This is the weakest instruction in the task. What does "realistic non-interactive mode" mean concretely? Is this a Bun test? A script that runs the launcher in one-shot mode and checks exit code? What assertions? Against which fixture?

**Why**: A tasker will either skip this, write a trivially passing smoke test, or over-engineer a test suite. The instruction needs to specify: (a) what test framework/location, (b) what mode to test (one-shot command is the only one that's automatable without a PTY), (c) what to assert (exit code, env isolation, fixture copy, auth seeded).

**Suggested action**: Replace instruction #7 with: "Add a Bun test in `tests/e2e/` that exercises the launcher in one-shot command mode (e.g. `bun run test:manual -- --mode=command -- pwd`). Assert: (a) exit code 0, (b) temp workspace was created with the expected fixture, (c) isolated env vars were set, (d) auth was seeded if available. This test should reuse the same skip-guard as existing e2e tests (`checkOpencodeAvailability`)."

comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text:
## Shell mode's env export needs to be explicit about WHAT to export

**What**: The task says "open a shell in the isolated temp project with the isolated env exported" but doesn't specify which env vars to export vs. inherit from the parent process. The harness's `createIsolatedOpenCodePaths()` returns an `env` map with HOME, XDG_CONFIG_HOME, XDG_DATA_HOME, XDG_CACHE_HOME, OPENCODE_CONFIG_DIR, and OPENCODE_DISABLE_DEFAULT_PLUGINS. But `runOpencodeCli()` merges this with only `PATH` from the parent process — it does NOT inherit the full parent environment.

This is intentional for automated isolation, but for a manual shell the user probably expects tools like `git`, `vim`, `ssh`, etc. to work, which requires inheriting most of the parent env. The question is: should the shell get `{ ...process.env, ...isolatedPaths.env }` (inherit everything, override isolation vars) or `{ PATH: process.env.PATH, ...isolatedPaths.env }` (minimal, like the harness)?

**Why**: If the shell inherits the full parent env with overrides, isolation is partial — other OpenCode-sensitive env vars the user has set (like OPENCODE_HOME or provider API keys) will leak through. If the shell uses minimal env, basic tools may not work.

**Suggested action**: Specify in the instructions: "Shell mode should inherit the full parent environment and override with the isolated path env vars. Document that this means the shell is isolated for OpenCode state but inherits other env from the host. This is the right tradeoff for manual testing — full isolation is for automated tests only."

comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text:
## Suggested implementation shape (if caveats above are addressed)

**What**: After reviewing the full harness API surface and the task instructions, here is the safest implementation shape:

**Structure**:
- `scripts/manual-test/index.ts` — launcher entrypoint
- `package.json` script: `"test:manual": "bun run scripts/manual-test/index.ts --"`
- Arg parsing: minimal, use `process.argv` or `parseArgs` (no new deps). Modes: `--tui` (default), `--shell`, `--command <cmd>`. Options: `--fixture <name>`, `--auth <path>`, `--keep`, `--no-build`.

**Execution flow**:
1. Parse args
2. `checkOpencodeAvailability()` — fail fast with diagnostics
3. `ensurePluginBuilt()` (skip if `--no-build` and dist exists)
4. `createFixtureWorkspace(fixture)` — copy fixture to temp
5. `wireBuiltPluginArtifact()` — symlink + install deps
6. `createIsolatedOpenCodePaths()` — create isolated HOME/XDG
7. `resolveCopilotAuthSeedFromEnv()` or `--auth <path>` — seed auth if available
8. Print summary banner (temp path, fixture, plugin, auth source, isolation roots)
9. Mode dispatch:
   - `--tui`: `Bun.spawn(["opencode"], { cwd, env: { ...process.env, ...isolatedEnv }, stdin: "inherit", stdout: "inherit", stderr: "inherit" })` — wait for child exit
   - `--shell`: `Bun.spawn([process.env.SHELL ?? "/bin/sh"], { cwd, env: { ...process.env, ...isolatedEnv }, stdin: "inherit", stdout: "inherit", stderr: "inherit" })` — wait for child exit
   - `--command`: Use `runOpencodeCli()`-like pipe mode, print output, report exit code
10. Signal handler: forward SIGINT/SIGTERM to child, wait for exit
11. Cleanup: if `--keep` or non-zero exit → print path, skip cleanup. Otherwise → `rm -rf tempRoot`.

**Test coverage**: One Bun test exercising `--command pwd` against `cli-smoke-project` fixture, asserting exit 0, isolated env, and auth seeding.

**Why**: This shape maximizes harness reuse (steps 2-7 are direct function calls), keeps the interactive execution path separate from the automated one, and handles the signal/cleanup edge cases.

**Suggested action**: Use this shape as a reference during implementation. It's not prescriptive — the tasker can deviate — but it covers the gaps identified in the other review comments.

title: Add reusable manual plugin test environment launcher
description:
## Description
Create a reusable manual testing entrypoint that uses the same isolated fixture-copy/plugin-injection/auth-seeding setup as the automated real-CLI e2e harness, so both the assistant and the user can run ad-hoc OpenCode manual tests against the currently developed plugin without drifting from the verified test environment model.

## Goals
- Manual testing reuses the same fixture-copy and isolated OpenCode environment model as automated e2e tests
- Users can launch either an interactive OpenCode TUI session, a subshell inside the isolated temp project, or a one-shot command against the isolated environment
- The launcher defaults to the current built plugin and current local OpenCode auth when available, while preserving runtime isolation by copying state into temp XDG roots
- Manual and automated testing become comparable and collaborative because they share setup assumptions and fixture inputs

## Success Criteria
- [ ] A documented launcher exists for manual isolated plugin testing
- [ ] Launcher reuses shared harness logic rather than duplicating setup behavior
- [ ] Launcher supports interactive/manual workflows (TUI, shell, one-shot command)
- [ ] Launcher copies auth/config into isolated temp roots instead of using host-global state in place
- [ ] Automated verification covers the launcher enough to trust parity with the e2e harness
- [ ] Acceptance review confirms user-facing workflow is clear and reproducible
close_reason: Completed reusable manual plugin test environment launcher that shares the automated e2e harness setup model for fixture copy, plugin injection, isolated HOME/XDG/OpenCode paths, copied auth seeding, and manual TUI/shell/command workflows.

comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text:
## Story structure is well-scoped — verdict: viable with caveats

**What**: The feature/task/acceptance-review triangle is correct. One feature, one implementation task, one acceptance review with the right blocking dependency. The goals and success criteria are clear and non-overlapping. The task instructions are specific enough for a tasker to begin work without ambiguity.

**Why**: Documenting this so the "what's good" baseline is on record before the caveats that follow.

**Suggested action**: No changes to story structure needed. See comments on opencode-coder-ism.2 for the implementation-level caveats.

comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text:
## Simplification opportunity: shell mode may be unnecessary scope

**What**: The task defines three modes: TUI, shell, and one-shot command. But "open a shell in the isolated temp project with the isolated env exported" is functionally equivalent to the user running `--tui` and then using OpenCode's built-in shell/terminal, or to the user running `--command bash` (one-shot mode with `bash` as the command). A dedicated `--shell` mode adds a separate code path, separate signal handling, separate documentation, and separate test coverage — for something the other two modes can already achieve.

**Why**: Each mode triples the surface area for bugs and documentation. If shell mode is cut, the launcher has two modes (TUI and command), which is simpler to implement, test, and document. The user who wants a raw shell can run `--command bash` or `--command $SHELL`.

**Suggested action**: Consider cutting `--shell` as a dedicated mode. If kept, the tasker should know that `--shell` is just `--command $SHELL` with `stdin: "inherit"` — and should implement it that way rather than as a separate code path.

comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text: Reviewer verdict: viable with caveats. Main implementation adjustments before coding: interactive TUI/shell modes need separate inherited-stdio spawn handling rather than the pipe-based test runner helper; preserve temp environments on failure (and ideally by explicit --keep), avoid raw auth JSON on CLI surfaces where it could leak to shell history/process lists, add explicit preflight checks, and define concrete non-interactive automated verification. The task body has been tightened to reflect these risks so tasker execution is not guessing.

comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text: Reviewer verdict on the bug set: 3 bugs are effectively 1.5 independent problems. Main fix strategy is (1) implement allowlist-based env construction with mode-specific minimal terminal/display passthrough, and strengthen automated tests/docs to lock that contract; then (2) fix invalid-auth preflight handling. This keeps manual and automated testing aligned on the same setup model without over-inheriting host state.

title: Acceptance Review: Add reusable manual plugin test environment launcher
description:
## Description
Verify that the manual plugin test environment launcher uses the same isolation/setup model as the automated real-CLI e2e harness and is practical for both user-driven and assistant-driven ad-hoc testing.

## Instructions
1. Run the documented launcher in at least one non-interactive mode and one interactive-oriented mode if feasible.
2. Confirm the launcher uses committed fixtures copied into temp workdirs.
3. Confirm the launcher injects the current built plugin and uses isolated HOME/XDG/OpenCode paths.
4. Confirm auth seeding follows the documented precedence and copies into isolated storage rather than using host-global auth in place.
5. Confirm the docs explain how the user can start TUI, shell, or one-shot command workflows.
6. Confirm the launcher output tells the user where the temp environment lives and how to inspect or keep it.

## Files to Inspect
- scripts/**
- tests/e2e/helpers/**
- docs/TESTING.md

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] Launcher behavior matches the automated harness model closely enough for shared use
- [ ] Interactive and non-interactive workflows are documented and at least minimally validated
- [ ] Auth/config isolation is preserved
- [ ] Failure/help output is sufficient for a human user
- [ ] All implementation tasks for the story are closed before this task closes

## Owner
verifier
close_reason: Acceptance review passed after bug-fix round: manual launcher now uses allowlist-based isolated child env with no host OPENCODE/env leakage in command mode, invalid --auth preflight returns concise user-facing errors without stack traces, strengthened automated launcher tests catch env-isolation regressions, docs describe the shared manual/automated setup model, and interactive-oriented shell/help smoke checks succeeded.

comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text:
## Acceptance review should verify signal handling and crash-preserve behavior

**What**: The current acceptance criteria cover "Interactive and non-interactive workflows are documented and at least minimally validated" and "Failure/help output is sufficient for a human user." These are good but miss the edge cases that matter most for a manual tool:
1. What happens when the user Ctrl+C's the TUI?
2. What happens when the TUI/shell crashes?
3. Does the temp dir survive for inspection on failure?

**Why**: These are the scenarios where a manual test launcher either earns trust or becomes a source of frustration. The acceptance review should explicitly check them.

**Suggested action**: Add to acceptance criteria:
- "Ctrl+C during TUI/shell mode exits cleanly without orphan processes"
- "Non-zero child exit preserves temp environment and prints its path"
- "Launcher reports auth source category (explicit path vs. default local fallback vs. none)"

comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text: Acceptance review failed. Verified launcher setup reuse and manual modes, but found three concrete defects: (1) launcher command/shell/TUI child env inherits full host process.env, so OpenCode-sensitive host vars can leak and isolation no longer matches the automated harness; (2) invalid --auth path throws a raw stack trace instead of a friendly preflight error; (3) automated launcher tests do not assert env-isolation parity, so the regression was not caught. Review task remains open until those bugs are fixed and re-verified.

comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text:
## Critical review verdict: 3 bugs are really 1.5 bugs — recommended fix order and grouping

**What**: After reviewing all three bugs in context of the source code:

- **opencode-coder-874** (env leakage) is the root cause. It's also the only P1. Fix this first.
- **opencode-coder-316** (test gap) is the verification half of 874. It should be fixed in the same PR as 874, not separately.
- **opencode-coder-8c8** (auth stack trace) is independent and trivial — a 5-line try/catch wrap plus one test case. Fix this second, in its own small PR.

So the work is: **PR 1** = 874 + 316 (env isolation + test assertions), **PR 2** = 8c8 (preflight error handling).

**Why**: Fixing 874 and 316 together is both safer (the test guards the fix) and simpler (no ordering dependency). 8c8 is orthogonal — it's a preflight UX bug that doesn't interact with env isolation at all. Keeping it separate makes both PRs reviewable in isolation.

**Suggested action**:
1. PR 1: Fix env allowlist in launcher + add env-minimality assertions in test + update TESTING.md env policy section + manual TUI smoke. Closes 874 and 316.
2. PR 2: Wrap `resolveAuthSeedPath` in try/catch + add preflight test for bad auth path. Closes 8c8.
3. After both PRs merge, re-verify the acceptance review task (opencode-coder-ism.1) — the acceptance criteria for "auth/config isolation is preserved" and "failure/help output is sufficient" are the two that these bugs blocked.

The TESTING.md update in PR 1 should add a subsection under "Manual Isolated Launcher" documenting the env allowlist policy per mode and explicitly stating that the manual launcher uses a stripped env, not `process.env`.

title: Default isolated Copilot auth seeding to current OpenCode auth
description:
## Description
Make the optional GitHub Copilot-backed LLM e2e scenario runnable in a normal developer environment without requiring extra seed env vars when the developer already has OpenCode GitHub Copilot credentials configured locally.

## Instructions
1. Update the e2e harness so isolated auth seeding supports this precedence order:
   - explicit test seed env input (`E2E_COPILOT_AUTH_JSON_PATH`)
   - explicit raw auth JSON content (`E2E_COPILOT_AUTH_JSON_CONTENT`)
   - fallback to the default local OpenCode auth file at `~/.local/share/opencode/auth.json` if it exists
2. Keep the runtime isolated: even when using the default local auth file as the source, copy its content into `XDG_DATA_HOME/opencode/auth.json` inside the temp isolated environment and do not rely on host-global OpenCode config during the actual CLI run.
3. Update the optional Copilot-backed scenario so it can run automatically in environments that already have local Copilot auth configured, while still skipping cleanly when no usable auth source exists.
4. Keep explicit env overrides supported for CI or custom test inputs.
5. Update `docs/TESTING.md` to document the precedence order and default-local-auth fallback behavior.
6. Run the e2e suite and typecheck. If the current environment has working local Copilot auth, verify the optional scenario executes rather than skipping.

## Files to Modify
- tests/e2e/helpers/** — add default auth discovery helper and fallback behavior
- tests/e2e/opencode.test.ts — use fallback-capable auth seed resolution
- docs/TESTING.md — document default auth fallback and precedence

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] Optional Copilot-backed scenario can use the default local OpenCode auth file when explicit env inputs are absent
- [ ] The actual CLI run still uses isolated copied auth under XDG data, not host-global auth in place
- [ ] Explicit env-based auth seeding still works
- [ ] The scenario skips only when no usable auth source exists
- [ ] e2e tests and typecheck pass
close_reason: Implemented fallback auth seed precedence (path > content > ~/.local/share/opencode/auth.json), preserved isolated auth copy into XDG_DATA_HOME, updated optional scenario skip logic/docs, and verified e2e+typecheck pass with scenario 5 executing in this environment.

title: Validate real CLI isolation and plugin discovery assumptions
description:
## Description
Empirically validate the core assumptions behind the real OpenCode CLI e2e plan before expanding scenario coverage, because the current harness may appear isolated while still loading config or plugins from unexpected locations.

## Instructions
1. Verify which project-local plugin directory the real OpenCode CLI honors during startup (`.opencode/plugin/` vs `.opencode/plugins/`) and update the harness/docs to use the confirmed path.
2. Add an explicit assertion that the plugin actually loaded in the baseline scenario; the suite must fail if the plugin is absent.
3. Ensure temp fixture workdirs cannot escape upward into the real repository when OpenCode searches for project root markers. If needed, initialize a temp git repo or otherwise prove root detection stays inside the temp workspace.
4. Empirically test whether isolating `HOME`, `XDG_CONFIG_HOME`, `XDG_DATA_HOME`, and `XDG_CACHE_HOME` is sufficient to hide host-global OpenCode config/plugin state for the real CLI. Treat `OPENCODE_HOME` as untrusted unless verified from documentation or observed behavior.
5. Determine the minimum supported strategy for LLM-capable CLI runs in isolated mode, including where auth/config must live (for example synthetic config content, env vars, or isolated auth files) and which parts are undocumented and need defensive checks.
6. Add or update helper code/docs so these assumptions are enforced or clearly documented before broader scenario coverage is built.

## Files to Modify
- tests/e2e/helpers/** — harden harness behavior and add proof-oriented helpers
- tests/e2e/**/*.ts — add isolation and plugin-loaded assertions
- docs/TESTING.md — document verified assumptions and any caveats

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] Real CLI plugin search path is verified and the harness uses the verified path
- [ ] Tests explicitly fail when the plugin is not loaded
- [ ] Temp workspaces are proven not to resolve back to the host repo during startup
- [ ] Host-global config isolation is verified empirically for the real CLI
- [ ] LLM auth/config strategy for isolated tests is documented with concrete supported inputs

title: Implement fixture-backed CLI smoke tests for startup scenarios
description:
## Description
Implement real OpenCode CLI tests that execute this plugin through fixture projects and cover the agreed startup scenarios using commands such as `opencode run "hi"` and/or `opencode serve`.

## Execution Strategy
Start with one basic end-to-end smoke test through the real CLI/hardened harness, validate that the approach is stable, then expand to additional scenarios.

## Instructions
1. Create committed fixture projects for the targeted scenarios and keep them minimal.
2. Add helper utilities to copy a fixture into a temp project, wire in the built plugin, and run OpenCode commands.
3. First implement one basic smoke test through the real CLI/hardened harness for an active project path and use it to validate plugin loading, isolation, and diagnostics.
4. After the smoke path is stable, implement broader scenario coverage for:
   - existing real-server startup path (current e2e baseline, adapted if needed)
   - CLI smoke startup path using `opencode run "hi"` or equivalent
   - local startup parity path that uses the actual CLI startup entrypoint instead of SDK-only boot
   - fresh project startup where the plugin should remain inactive and expose only init behavior
5. For scenarios that require a real model call, write the minimum isolated OpenCode user config needed inside the synthetic HOME/XDG roots and source auth from test-controlled env/config rather than the developer's host config.
6. Assert that the plugin is loaded exactly once, or otherwise assert via logs/config/command list that no duplicate plugin registration occurred.
7. Make test output include enough context to debug startup failures quickly.

## Files to Modify
- tests/e2e/**/*.ts — add or reorganize scenario tests
- tests/e2e/helpers/** — add execution helpers
- tests/e2e/fixtures/** — add committed fixture inputs
- docs/TESTING.md — document isolated config/auth expectations for real CLI tests if needed

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] A basic real-CLI smoke test exists and passes through the hardened isolated harness
- [ ] Real CLI tests exist for scenarios 1-4 or follow-up work is clearly identified after the initial smoke path
- [ ] Tests run from committed fixture setups copied to temp workdirs
- [ ] Tests protect against plugin double-load behavior
- [ ] LLM-capable scenarios use isolated config/auth and do not rely on host global OpenCode config
- [ ] Failures report captured stdout/stderr and relevant logs
- [ ] The suite is runnable with documented commands

comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter

The harness will run OpenCode with a synthetic HOME/XDG/OPENCODE_HOME rooted inside the temp workspace so ~/.config/opencode and related global state are invisible. The only plugin made discoverable will be the repo-built dist/opencode-coder.js linked into the temp fixture's .opencode/plugin directory. comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text:
## CRITICAL: Plugin directory is .opencode/plugins/ (plural), not .opencode/plugin/ (singular)

**What**: The harness (wireBuiltPluginArtifact in harness.ts line 154) creates .opencode/plugin/opencode-coder.js. OpenCode's official plugin documentation at https://opencode.ai/docs/plugins/ says the project-level plugin directory is .opencode/plugins/ (plural). The config docs add: "Singular names (e.g., agent/) are also supported for backwards compatibility."

**Why**: If the backwards-compat singular form works, this is fine. If it doesn't (or if OpenCode drops backwards compat), the plugin won't be discovered at all and every test will silently pass without the plugin loaded — a false-green disaster. The current e2e test (opencode.test.ts) doesn't actually assert that the plugin WAS loaded, so this failure mode is invisible.

**Suggested action**: 
1. Change the harness to use .opencode/plugins/ (plural) to match canonical documentation
2. Add an assertion in each test that the plugin was actually loaded (e.g., check for a known command or tool registered by the plugin)
3. If backwards compat is relied upon, add an explicit test that verifies singular directory loading works, and document that dependency

comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text:
## CRITICAL: OPENCODE_HOME env var does not appear in OpenCode's documented environment variables

**What**: The harness (createIsolatedOpenCodePaths, line 212) sets OPENCODE_HOME as part of the isolation strategy. However, OPENCODE_HOME does not appear in OpenCode's official CLI environment variable documentation (https://opencode.ai/docs/cli/#environment-variables). The documented env vars are: OPENCODE_CONFIG, OPENCODE_TUI_CONFIG, OPENCODE_CONFIG_DIR, OPENCODE_CONFIG_CONTENT, and various feature flags. OPENCODE_HOME is not among them.

**Why**: If OpenCode ignores OPENCODE_HOME entirely (which the docs strongly suggest), then setting it does nothing for isolation. It becomes a placebo — giving a false sense that OpenCode's data/state paths are redirected when they're not. The real isolation relies entirely on HOME, XDG_CONFIG_HOME, XDG_DATA_HOME, and XDG_CACHE_HOME. If the isolation plan was counting on OPENCODE_HOME to redirect something that XDG doesn't cover, there's a gap.

**Suggested action**: 
1. Remove OPENCODE_HOME from the harness unless you can confirm OpenCode reads it (test empirically or check the Go source)
2. Document that isolation relies on XDG vars + HOME, not OPENCODE_HOME
3. If you need additional path isolation, use OPENCODE_CONFIG_DIR which IS documented and controls the config directory search path

comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text:
## Auth credentials live at XDG_DATA_HOME/opencode/auth.json — isolation strategy must account for this

**What**: OpenCode stores provider credentials at ~/.local/share/opencode/auth.json (i.e., XDG_DATA_HOME/opencode/auth.json). The harness correctly isolates XDG_DATA_HOME. This means the isolated environment will have NO auth credentials at all — no API keys for any provider.

**Why**: For LLM-capable scenarios (like opencode run "hi"), the test needs valid provider credentials. The task description says "write a synthetic minimal config inside the isolated HOME/XDG roots and source auth from test-controlled env/config" — but this is under-specified. Specifically:
- Some providers (Anthropic, OpenAI) accept env vars like ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, OPENAI_API_KEY
- Others require auth.json entries created by /connect
- GitHub Copilot uses an OAuth device flow that CANNOT be provisioned via config alone
- The OPENCODE_CONFIG_CONTENT mechanism can inject provider.X.options.apiKey but it's unclear if that bypasses the need for auth.json entirely

**Suggested action**: 
1. For LLM-capable tests, use a provider that supports plain env-var auth (e.g., ANTHROPIC_API_KEY or OPENAI_API_KEY) and inject that env var in the test
2. Alternatively, write a synthetic auth.json to XDG_DATA_HOME/opencode/auth.json inside the isolated root
3. Use OPENCODE_CONFIG_CONTENT to set the model and provider config inline — the SDK already uses this mechanism when spawning opencode serve
4. Document which provider is expected for CI/dev testing and what env var must be set
5. For tests that don't need real LLM responses, consider if opencode serve even starts successfully without any configured provider — this needs empirical testing

comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text:
## SDK createOpencodeServer spawns child process with process.env — withEnvironment approach works but has a subtle race

**What**: Reviewing the SDK source (node_modules/@opencode-ai/sdk/dist/server.js), createOpencodeServer spawns opencode serve as a child process with { env: { ...process.env, OPENCODE_CONFIG_CONTENT: ... } }. The harness uses withEnvironment() to temporarily set process.env before calling createOpencodeServer. This works because spawn captures env at call time.

**Why**: This approach is sound for the SDK path (opencode serve). However, for opencode run "hi" CLI tests (which the task explicitly requires), there's no SDK wrapper. The implementer will need to spawn opencode run directly via Bun.$ or child_process.spawn. When using Bun.$, the env handling is different — Bun.$ inherits the current process.env automatically, but you need to verify it doesn't snapshot env at module load time.

**Suggested action**: 
1. For opencode run tests, spawn the process explicitly with a controlled env object (like the SDK does), rather than relying on withEnvironment + Bun.$
2. Example: use spawn("opencode", ["run", "hi"], { env: { ...isolatedPaths.env, PATH: process.env.PATH, OPENCODE_CONFIG_CONTENT: ... } })
3. Be explicit about which env vars from the host are passed through (PATH is needed, TERM may be needed, others should be blocked)

comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text:
## No test asserts that the plugin was actually loaded — false-green risk for ALL scenarios

**What**: The current e2e test (opencode.test.ts) starts a server and checks that agents are available, but the agent assertion was weakened: "Plugin no longer ships agents via knowledge-base. Agents are now provided by ai-resources/... Verify the agents list is available (may be empty from plugin's perspective)." The test logs agent names but doesn't fail if the plugin isn't loaded. There's no assertion on commands, tools, or any other artifact that proves this specific plugin loaded.

**Why**: This is the single most dangerous gap in the test design. If the plugin isn't loaded (wrong directory name, broken symlink, missing dependency, incompatible SDK version), every test passes green because none of them check for plugin-specific behavior. The entire e2e suite becomes a test of "does opencode serve start?" rather than "does our plugin work?"

**Suggested action**: 
1. Add a hard assertion that a known plugin artifact is present. The plugin registers a "coder" tool — assert it appears in the tool list
2. Use client.app.tools() or equivalent SDK call to verify the coder tool is registered
3. This assertion should be in the beforeAll or a top-level describe block that gates all other tests
4. Every fixture scenario should have at least one assertion that distinguishes "plugin loaded" from "plugin absent"

comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text:
## opencode run has no SDK wrapper — task needs to define its own CLI execution helper

**What**: The task requires testing via opencode run "hi" but the @opencode-ai/sdk only provides createOpencodeServer (which wraps opencode serve) and createOpencodeTui. There is no createOpencodeRun or equivalent. The implementer must write a raw process.spawn wrapper.

**Why**: This isn't a blocker but it's unacknowledged complexity. The opencode run path starts a server internally, runs the prompt, and exits. The test needs to: (a) capture stdout/stderr, (b) detect success/failure, (c) handle timeouts, (d) pass isolated env. This is different from the server-based flow where you get a persistent client.

**Suggested action**: 
1. Write a helper like runOpencodeCommand(args: string[], opts: { env, cwd, timeout }) that spawns opencode with the given args and returns { exitCode, stdout, stderr }
2. Use explicit env construction (not withEnvironment) since this is a child process
3. Set a reasonable timeout (opencode run with a real LLM call could take 30-60s)
4. Consider whether opencode run --format json gives parseable output for assertions
5. Document this helper in the testing docs

comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text:
## OpenCode npm plugin cache at XDG_CACHE_HOME/opencode/ needs isolation attention

**What**: OpenCode caches npm plugin packages at ~/.cache/opencode/node_modules/ (XDG_CACHE_HOME/opencode/). The harness isolates XDG_CACHE_HOME. This means the isolated environment starts with an empty cache.

**Why**: Two implications:
1. If the opencode.json config in the fixture lists any npm plugins (via the "plugin" array), OpenCode will try to bun install them at startup, adding startup latency and an internet dependency to tests.
2. More importantly: if the developer's global cache contains a DIFFERENT version of this plugin installed via npm, and the cache somehow leaks (e.g., XDG_CACHE_HOME isolation isn't respected by bun), the test could load the wrong version.

The fixtures don't appear to use the "plugin" config array (they use local file discovery), so this is low risk. But it's worth confirming.

**Suggested action**: 
1. Explicitly verify that fixture opencode.json files (if they exist) do NOT list this plugin in the "plugin" array
2. If fixtures don't have opencode.json, confirm OpenCode doesn't auto-discover npm plugins without config
3. Consider setting OPENCODE_DISABLE_DEFAULT_PLUGINS=true (it's a documented env var) to eliminate any default plugin loading behavior

comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text:
## process.chdir in test setup is fragile for parallel test execution

**What**: The current e2e test (opencode.test.ts lines 46/74) uses process.chdir(workspace.workdir) before calling createOpencodeServer, then restores the original cwd in a finally block. This mutates global process state.

**Why**: If multiple e2e test suites or describe blocks run in the same Bun process (which bun:test does by default), chdir creates a race condition. One test's chdir affects all other concurrent tests. Even sequential execution is fragile — if the finally block doesn't run (e.g., process crash), the cwd stays wrong for all subsequent tests.

For the opencode run path, the --project flag or cwd option on spawn is better than process.chdir.

**Suggested action**: 
1. For createOpencodeServer, check if the SDK accepts a cwd/project option — the createOpencodeTui function accepts --project, but createOpencodeServer doesn't seem to
2. For opencode run, spawn with { cwd: workspace.workdir } instead of chdir
3. If createOpencodeServer truly requires cwd (because OpenCode uses os.Getwd()), wrap each server lifecycle in its own subprocess to avoid global state mutation
4. At minimum, document this limitation and ensure tests never run in parallel

comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text:
## "Duplicate plugin loading" assertion needs clarification — what does "loaded exactly once" look like?

**What**: Task acceptance criterion #3 says "Tests protect against plugin double-load behavior" and instruction #5 says "Assert that the plugin is loaded exactly once, or otherwise assert via logs/config/command list that no duplicate plugin registration occurred." The harness isolates global plugin paths, which prevents the global copy from loading. But the task doesn't specify HOW to assert single-loading.

**Why**: There's no obvious SDK API to query "how many times was plugin X loaded?" Options include:
- Check that the plugin's tool appears exactly once in the tool list (not duplicated)
- Check OpenCode logs for duplicate registration warnings
- Check that plugin hooks don't fire twice for a single event

Without a concrete assertion strategy, the "double-load prevention" criterion is untestable and becomes a documentation-only claim.

**Suggested action**: 
1. The most reliable assertion: query the tool list and verify the "coder" tool appears exactly once
2. Additionally, capture OpenCode's startup logs (available via stderr when using --log-level DEBUG or --print-logs) and grep for plugin loading messages
3. Define what "double-loaded" looks like concretely so the test can detect it
4. Update the acceptance criteria to specify the assertion method

comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text:
## OpenCode database (opencode.db) lives at XDG_DATA_HOME — isolation creates fresh state, which may change startup behavior

**What**: OpenCode stores its SQLite database at ~/.local/share/opencode/opencode.db. With XDG_DATA_HOME isolated, the test gets a fresh database with no sessions, no history, no saved state.

**Why**: This is mostly a positive (clean test state). But OpenCode may have first-run behaviors that differ from subsequent runs — prompting for provider setup, running migrations, creating default state. The test needs to handle this gracefully. If opencode serve blocks waiting for provider configuration on first run (before the server emits "listening"), the 30-second timeout will fire and the test will fail with an unhelpful timeout error.

**Suggested action**: 
1. Test empirically whether opencode serve starts successfully with an empty data directory and no configured provider
2. If it does, document that behavior
3. If it doesn't (e.g., it prompts for setup), use OPENCODE_CONFIG_CONTENT to pre-configure a provider or use a flag to skip first-run flows
4. Consider setting OPENCODE_DISABLE_AUTOUPDATE=true (or autoupdate: false in config) to prevent update checks during tests

comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text:
## XDG isolation is sound for Linux but needs verification for OpenCode's Go runtime behavior

**What**: The isolation strategy sets HOME, XDG_CONFIG_HOME, XDG_DATA_HOME, and XDG_CACHE_HOME. On Linux, well-behaved XDG-aware applications respect these. OpenCode is written in Go and likely uses os.UserHomeDir() and XDG paths.

**Why**: The strategy is sound IF OpenCode's Go code respects these env vars. Most Go XDG libraries do. However, some Go functions (like os.UserConfigDir on macOS) use platform-specific paths that don't respect XDG vars. Since this project appears to run on Linux, this is lower risk. But:
1. Go's os.UserHomeDir() reads HOME on Linux — so that's covered
2. Go's os.UserConfigDir() reads XDG_CONFIG_HOME on Linux — covered
3. Go's os.UserCacheDir() reads XDG_CACHE_HOME on Linux — covered
4. But auth.json at ~/.local/share/opencode/ depends on Go respecting XDG_DATA_HOME — which it should on Linux

The key risk is: does OpenCode use a Go XDG library or does it hardcode paths?

**Suggested action**: 
1. Test empirically: run opencode serve with isolated XDG vars and check if it creates files in the isolated paths (not the real home)
2. Add a diagnostic assertion that checks no files were created in the REAL ~/.config/opencode or ~/.local/share/opencode during test execution
3. This empirical test should be the FIRST thing implemented — if XDG isolation doesn't work, the entire approach needs redesign

comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text:
## Simplification opportunity: The 4 fixture scenarios can likely share more harness code

**What**: The task defines 4 scenarios: (1) existing real-server startup, (2) CLI smoke via opencode run, (3) local startup parity via CLI, (4) fresh project inactive startup. The current harness has separate fixture directories for each. However, the differences between fixtures are minimal — the main distinction is whether .coder/opencode-coder.yaml exists and what mode it sets.

**Why**: 4 separate fixture directories with nearly identical content (a README, a .gitkeep, and maybe a yaml file) adds maintenance burden without proportional value. When the fixture layout needs updating, you update 4 places.

**Suggested action**: Consider whether scenarios 1-3 (which all need an active plugin) can share a SINGLE fixture directory and differentiate only via:
- The OPENCODE_CONFIG_CONTENT passed at runtime
- Whether .coder/opencode-coder.yaml is written by the test setup (not committed)
This would reduce to 2 fixtures: "active project" and "fresh project". The test setup code handles the rest.

This is a suggestion, not a blocker — if the team prefers explicit fixtures per scenario for clarity, that's defensible. But consider it.

comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text:
## Fixtures use .gitkeep but temp workdirs are NOT git repos — opencode may require git

**What**: The fixtures contain .gitkeep files and the existing-active-project fixture has git.initialized: true in project.yaml. However, the harness (createFixtureWorkspace) copies the fixture to a temp dir using fs.cp — it does NOT run git init. The temp workdir is NOT a git repository.

**Why**: OpenCode documentation says: "When OpenCode starts up, it looks for a config file in the current directory or traverse up to the nearest Git directory." If OpenCode requires a git directory to anchor the project root, running from a non-git temp dir may cause OpenCode to traverse up and find the REAL project root (this repo's own .git), which would break isolation entirely — OpenCode would load THIS repo's .opencode/plugins instead of the fixture's.

This is a critical isolation failure mode. The fixture exists in /tmp/opencode-coder-xxx/project/ with no .git, so OpenCode walks up to / looking for .git, finds nothing (good) or finds an ancestor .git (bad if /tmp is under a git worktree, unlikely but possible).

**Suggested action**: 
1. Add git init to the fixture workspace setup (after cp, before running tests)
2. This is a one-liner: await $\`git init\`.cwd(workdir).quiet()
3. This ensures OpenCode anchors to the temp workdir and doesn't escape
4. The existing-active-project fixture's project.yaml already claims git.initialized: true — make that true in reality

comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text:
## Summary: Overall feasibility verdict — VIABLE WITH CAVEATS

**What**: After reviewing the harness code, SDK internals, OpenCode's official documentation (plugins, config, CLI, providers), and the epic/task descriptions, here is my overall assessment.

**What definitely seems sound**:
1. The fixture-copy-to-temp model is solid and well-implemented
2. XDG env var isolation is the RIGHT approach for preventing global config/plugin leakage on Linux
3. OPENCODE_CONFIG_CONTENT is the correct mechanism for injecting synthetic config (highest precedence per docs)
4. The symlink-to-built-plugin approach avoids copying large files
5. The failure artifact capture (writeFailureArtifacts) is good practice
6. The SDK's createOpencodeServer correctly passes env through to the child process

**What is risky or unsupported**:
1. OPENCODE_HOME is not a documented env var — likely a no-op (see separate comment)
2. Plugin directory uses singular "plugin" vs documented plural "plugins" (see separate comment)  
3. No assertion anywhere that the plugin actually loaded (see separate comment)
4. Temp workdirs are not git repos — OpenCode may escape to find the real project root (see separate comment)
5. Auth credential path needs explicit provisioning strategy for LLM tests (see separate comment)
6. XDG isolation is unverified empirically against the actual OpenCode binary (see separate comment)

**Gaps in the current task descriptions**:
1. No definition of what "plugin loaded" looks like as a test assertion
2. No specification of which LLM provider to use in tests or what env var supplies the key
3. No mention of git init in temp workdirs
4. No mention of OPENCODE_DISABLE_DEFAULT_PLUGINS or autoupdate/snapshot disabling
5. "Duplicate load" acceptance criterion has no concrete assertion strategy

**Recommendations for implementation order**:
1. FIRST: Empirically test XDG isolation (does opencode serve respect isolated paths?)
2. SECOND: Fix plugin dir to "plugins" (plural), add git init, add plugin-loaded assertion
3. THIRD: Implement the simplest scenario (existing-active-project via createOpencodeServer)  
4. FOURTH: Add opencode run helper and CLI smoke test
5. FIFTH: Add LLM-capable scenario with OPENCODE_CONFIG_CONTENT + env-var auth
6. LAST: Fresh inactive project scenario

**Suggested action**: Address the individual findings in separate comments before starting implementation. The approach is viable but needs these fixes to avoid building on a foundation that silently doesn't work.

comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text: Reviewer found the plan is viable with caveats, not yet proven. Main risks: plugin path may be  rather than ; current tests do not prove the plugin loaded; temp workdirs may let OpenCode walk back to the real repo unless rooted explicitly;  may be undocumented/no-op; and LLM-capable runs need a concrete isolated auth/config strategy. This task now depends on a dedicated validation/hardening task for those assumptions.

comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text: Correction to prior reviewer-summary comment: the specific risky assumptions are (1) the real CLI plugin path may be .opencode/plugins/ rather than .opencode/plugin/, (2) current tests do not prove the plugin loaded, (3) temp workdirs may let OpenCode walk back to the host repo unless rooted explicitly, (4) OPENCODE_HOME may be undocumented or ignored, and (5) LLM-capable runs need a concrete isolated auth/config strategy.

comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text: Progress update: implemented the first hardened real-CLI smoke path. The harness now uses .opencode/plugins, initializes git inside temp fixtures to anchor project root detection, runs the real CLI via an explicit spawn helper, verifies isolated XDG/OpenCode state creation, and includes a no-plugin control path. Current e2e smoke test proves plugin startup by checking that .coder/project.yaml changes from the fixture placeholder pluginVersion to a real plugin-generated value. Remaining work for this task is broader scenario coverage (additional startup paths), stronger duplicate-load assertions across scenarios, and an isolated LLM-capable run strategy in executable test form.

title: Design fixture layout and isolated OpenCode harness
description:
## Description
Define the reusable fixture structure and test harness for running this plugin against a real OpenCode CLI instance without loading a second plugin copy from an existing global or legacy coder installation.

## Instructions
1. Inspect the current e2e test and how OpenCode discovers local plugins.
2. Design a fixture directory layout under `tests/e2e/fixtures/` (or similar) for at least:
   - existing/active project
   - cli-smoke project
   - fresh inactive project
   - local startup parity project
3. Define a harness strategy that copies fixtures into a temp workdir before execution so tests can mutate files safely.
4. Define how the harness injects only this repository's built plugin into the temp project.
5. Explicitly prevent duplicate loading from any globally installed or old `coder` plugin by controlling OpenCode home/config/plugin search paths or environment.
6. Define the minimal logs/artifacts the harness should capture on failure.

## Files to Modify
- tests/e2e/README.md or docs/TESTING.md — document the fixture/harness model
- tests/e2e/fixtures/** — create initial layout
- tests/e2e/helpers/** — add shared harness helpers as needed

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] Fixture directory structure is explicitly defined
- [ ] Double-loading prevention strategy is explicitly defined
- [ ] Temp-copy execution model is explicitly defined
- [ ] Failure diagnostics strategy is explicitly defined
- [ ] Plan is specific enough for implementation without further scoping

title: Add real OpenCode CLI startup test coverage
description:
## Description
Build fixture-based end-to-end coverage that exercises this plugin against a real OpenCode instance across the startup scenarios we want to validate now: existing real-server coverage, CLI smoke startup, local-startup equivalence via the CLI entrypoint, and fresh-project inactive startup.

## Goals
- Add reproducible project fixtures under `tests/` instead of constructing every scenario ad hoc
- Run OpenCode through real CLI paths such as `opencode serve` and `opencode run "hi"`
- Ensure test isolation so a globally installed or older `coder` plugin is not loaded alongside this plugin
- Ensure LLM-capable scenarios do not depend on the developer's existing global OpenCode config by using a synthetic isolated config/auth path
- Make startup failures diagnosable from test output and fixture logs

## Success Criteria
- [ ] Fixture project directories exist under `tests/` for the targeted scenarios
- [ ] Tests can run against a real OpenCode instance using committed fixture setup plus temp copies
- [ ] The harness prevents double-loading from globally installed plugin resources
- [ ] LLM-capable scenarios use isolated OpenCode config/auth instead of the host user's config
- [ ] Scenario coverage exists for items 1-4 discussed with the user
- [ ] Acceptance review confirms reproducibility and clear local test instructions
close_reason: Completed real OpenCode CLI startup test coverage with committed fixture-based isolated harness, scenario coverage for real server/CLI/fresh inactive paths, and verified live isolated GitHub Copilot-backed LLM scenario execution in this environment.

comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text:
## Epic success criteria are missing a "plugin actually loaded" gate

**What**: The epic's success criteria focus on fixture existence, harness isolation, and scenario coverage. None of them require proving the plugin was actually loaded and functional in the test. "Tests can run against a real OpenCode instance" could pass with the plugin absent.

**Why**: The whole point of these tests is to verify the plugin works through real CLI paths. If the test passes without the plugin loaded, the entire epic delivers false confidence. This is the highest-risk gap in the plan.

**Suggested action**: Add to epic success criteria: "Each test scenario includes at least one assertion that verifies a plugin-specific artifact (tool, command, or config hook output) is present, confirming the plugin was loaded and functional."

comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text:
## Epic should require an empirical smoke test of XDG isolation BEFORE implementing all 4 scenarios

**What**: The entire harness rests on the assumption that OpenCode CLI respects HOME/XDG_CONFIG_HOME/XDG_DATA_HOME/XDG_CACHE_HOME when discovering config, plugins, and auth. This assumption is reasonable but unverified.

**Why**: If this assumption is wrong (e.g., OpenCode hardcodes some paths, or Bun runtime behavior differs from the Go binary behavior), all 4 scenario implementations are wasted work. The risk is concentrated at the foundation.

**Suggested action**: The implementation task (opencode-coder-a9g) should start with a single empirical test: start opencode serve with isolated env vars and verify it does NOT touch the real ~/.config/opencode or ~/.local/share/opencode directories. Only after this passes should the 4 scenarios be built out. This de-risks the entire approach early.

comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text: Reviewer verdict: viable with caveats. Critical de-risking items emerged before broader scenario coverage: confirm real CLI plugin search path, add explicit plugin-loaded assertions, prevent temp workdir root escape into the host repo, empirically verify XDG/HOME isolation against the real CLI, and define concrete isolated auth/config provisioning for LLM-capable runs. Created a dedicated task to harden these assumptions before the main scenario-coverage task proceeds.

comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text: Discussion update: the harness can and should eventually cover all plugin startup modes, not only the initial startup-path scenarios. Existing integration tests already cover resolved modes such as team, stealth, saved disabled, hard-disabled, not-enabled/fresh, and legacy migration behavior at the plugin level. Real CLI e2e coverage can be expanded to exercise those same modes in fixture projects once the isolation/plugin-discovery validation task is complete.

comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text: Implementation update: the blocking validation task is complete and the epic now has a working basic real-CLI smoke test through the hardened isolated harness. Broader scenario coverage is still open, but the current state already proves a real CLI startup path can load the in-repo plugin in an isolated fixture and avoid host-global config/plugin leakage.

comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter

Current blocker is environmental rather than code-completion: the optional credential-gated LLM e2e path exists and is documented, yet it was skipped during verification because `E2E_OPENAI_API_KEY` was not set. title: Expand automated coverage for explicit enablement, migration, and env override behavior
description:
## Description
Add or update automated tests so the new startup and init behavior is verified end-to-end across saved `disabled`, `stealth`, and `team` modes, plus upgrade migration and env-var precedence. The change is risky because it alters plugin exposure, startup side effects, upgrade behavior, and init flow, so strong regression coverage is required.

## Instructions
1. Update integration tests for `src/index.ts` startup behavior to cover:
   - fresh startup with no explicit mode and no `.coder/` side effects

   - saved `disabled` startup with no active plugin features
   - `stealth` and `team` startup preserving active behavior
