title: Implement project log sink and retention
description:
## Description
Extend the plugin logger so every log entry is still sent to OpenCode and is also appended to a project-local daily log file under `.coder/logs/`.

## Instructions
1. Update the logger implementation in `src/core/logger.ts` to support dual logging.
2. Add a project-local file sink that writes synchronously to `.coder/logs/coder-YYYY-MM-DD.log` using the project workdir.
3. Ensure the file sink creates `.coder/logs/` lazily if it does not exist.
4. Format each log line as a readable single line that includes at least timestamp, level, pid, service, message, and serialized `extra` fields when present.
5. Keep the existing OpenCode logging behavior unchanged.
6. Add retention logic that removes project log files older than 7 days.
7. Use filename-based retention against `coder-YYYY-MM-DD.log` rather than filesystem mtime.
8. Ensure retention runs safely during startup and does not crash plugin initialization if pruning fails.
9. File logging must include the same emitted log events as OpenCode logging, including debug messages when they are enabled by `OPENCODE_CODER_DEBUG`.
10. Wire any required workdir parameter changes through logger creation call sites.
11. Update related logger test helpers or mocks so unit tests can construct the logger with the new inputs.

## Files to Modify
- `src/core/logger.ts` — add file sink, line formatting, retention, and dual-write behavior
- `src/core/index.ts` — update exports if needed
- `src/index.ts` — pass workdir into logger creation if required
- `tests/helpers/mock-logger.ts` — update logger test helper if the logger contract changes
- `.coder/.gitignore` and/or logger setup logic — ensure project-local log files stay out of git

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] Logs are appended to `.coder/logs/coder-YYYY-MM-DD.log`
- [ ] Existing OpenCode logging still works
- [ ] Each log line includes pid and serialized metadata needed to debug multiple processes
- [ ] Logs older than 7 days are pruned automatically using filename-based retention
- [ ] Logger/file-sink failures do not prevent plugin startup
- [ ] Unit tests cover daily log path selection and retention behavior
- [ ] Unit tests or focused tests cover file log line formatting and extra-field serialization
close_reason: Implemented dual logger with project-local file sink, safe retention, call-site wiring, gitignore update, and focused tests

comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text:
## .gitignore must be updated to cover .coder/logs/

**What**: The .gitignore currently only ignores `.coder/project.yaml` (line 39). The new `.coder/logs/` directory is not gitignored. If an implementer forgets this, project logs will be tracked by git and committed into the repo.

**Why**: Log files containing PIDs, timestamps, and debug output should never be committed. This is the kind of thing that slips through because .gitignore isn't listed in "Files to Modify" and the implementer is focused on logger.ts.

**Suggested action**: Add `.gitignore` to the Files to Modify section and add an acceptance criterion: ".coder/logs/ is gitignored". Consider also broadening the existing `.coder/project.yaml` ignore to `.coder/` entirely, since nothing in .coder/ should ever be committed.

comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text:
## createLogger signature change will break mock-logger and all test call sites

**What**: The current `createLogger(client)` takes only a `PluginInput["client"]`. Adding `workdir` changes the signature. The task says "Wire any required workdir parameter changes through logger creation call sites" but does not mention updating `tests/helpers/mock-logger.ts` or the test files that use `createMockLogger()`. The mock logger has no concept of a workdir or file sink.

**Why**: The mock logger (`tests/helpers/mock-logger.ts`) directly implements the `Logger` type. If the `createLogger` function signature changes, the mock must be updated too — otherwise unit tests for every service that uses a logger will fail. This is the #1 cause of "it works in my head but breaks in CI" for this kind of change.

**Suggested action**: Add `tests/helpers/mock-logger.ts` to "Files to Modify". The mock logger should remain in-memory-only (no file sink in tests) but must match the updated `Logger` type. Also, if `createLogger` now requires `workdir`, all existing `createMockLogger()` call sites may need updating.

comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text:
## Log line format is underspecified — implementer will guess

**What**: The task says "include at least timestamp, level, service, message, and pid" but doesn't specify the actual format. Is this structured JSON per line (greppable, parseable by the existing log-analyzer)? Or human-readable like `2026-03-14T18:39:13.000Z [INFO] [opencode-coder] (pid=12345) Plugin loading...`? The acceptance review task says "readable format" which implies human-readable, but the existing MONITORING.md describes structured log parsing.

**Why**: If the format isn't pinned, the implementer picks one and the verifier may reject it. Worse, if someone later wants to parse these logs with the log-analyzer tooling, an incompatible format means rework. This decision should be made upfront.

**Suggested action**: Add an explicit line format to the instructions. Recommendation: human-readable structured text like `YYYY-MM-DDTHH:mm:ss.sssZ LEVEL [service] (pid=NNNNN) message [extra as JSON if present]`. This is greppable, readable, and the `extra` field preserves structured data for tooling.

comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text:
## Sync vs async file writes: the task doesn't specify and the choice matters

**What**: The task says "appended to a project-local daily log file" but doesn't specify whether writes should be synchronous (`fs.appendFileSync`) or asynchronous (`fs.promises.appendFile`). The current `createLogger` returns a synchronous-looking API (no promises returned from debug/info/warn/error). If async writes are used, the Logger type contract changes. If sync writes are used, every log call blocks the event loop for I/O.

**Why**: This is a real design decision with tradeoffs. Sync writes are simpler and guarantee ordering but add latency to every log call. Async writes are non-blocking but complicate error handling and the current Logger interface (callers don't await log calls). Fire-and-forget async writes silently swallow errors. The implementer needs guidance.

**Suggested action**: Specify sync writes (`appendFileSync`) in the instructions. Rationale: the logger is called infrequently (startup + a few runtime calls), the current API is synchronous, and sync writes guarantee log ordering and simplify error handling with try/catch. The performance cost is negligible for the ~20-30 log calls per plugin lifecycle.

comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text:
## Retention "older than 7 days" is ambiguous — file mtime or filename date?

**What**: The task says "removes project log files older than 7 days" but doesn't specify whether "older" means file modification time (mtime) or the date parsed from the filename (`coder-YYYY-MM-DD.log`). These behave differently: mtime depends on the OS clock and can be affected by file copies/restores; filename date is deterministic and matches the log rotation boundary.

**Why**: An implementer choosing mtime-based pruning would produce correct-looking code that breaks subtly when files are copied or backed up. Filename-based pruning is simpler, deterministic, and consistent with the daily rotation naming.

**Suggested action**: Specify that retention compares the YYYY-MM-DD in the filename against today's date, not file mtime. Delete files where `today - fileDate > 7 days`.

comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text:
## Missing: what happens with the extra field in file logs?

**What**: The current OpenCode logger accepts an optional `extra?: Record<string, unknown>` parameter on every log call. Many call sites pass structured data like `{ durationMs: 42 }` or `{ error: String(err) }`. The task says to include "timestamp, level, service, message, and pid" but says nothing about `extra`.

**Why**: If `extra` is silently dropped from file logs, you lose the most useful debugging data (error details, timing, context). If it's included, the format needs to handle it (e.g., JSON-serialized at end of line). This should be an explicit decision, not left to implementer discretion.

**Suggested action**: Add to the instructions: "Include the `extra` field in file log lines. Serialize it as JSON at the end of the line when present."

comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text:
## Debug log filtering: should file sink respect OPENCODE_CODER_DEBUG?

**What**: The current logger gates debug messages behind the `OPENCODE_CODER_DEBUG` env var — when it's falsy, debug calls are no-ops that never reach OpenCode logging. The task doesn't specify whether the file sink should also respect this gate or write all levels unconditionally.

**Why**: If the file sink respects the debug gate, project-local logs in production will be missing debug entries (which is where most startup diagnostic value lives). If it ignores the gate, you get richer project logs but the behavior differs between the two sinks, which could confuse people. This is a deliberate design choice.

**Suggested action**: Specify in the instructions: "The file sink should write ALL log levels including debug, regardless of the OPENCODE_CODER_DEBUG environment variable. Project-local logs are explicitly for debugging and should contain maximum detail."

title: Project-local dual logging for opencode-coder
description:
## Description
Add project-local log files for the opencode-coder plugin so plugin activity can be inspected from the repository without relying on OpenCode's unlinked per-process log files.

## Goals

- Use one project log file per day with predictable names
- Keep only the most recent 7 days of project-local logs
- Preserve current logging behavior to OpenCode so existing diagnostics keep working

## Success Criteria

- [ ] Log files are created lazily and stored under `.coder/logs/`
- [ ] Log retention prunes project-local logs older than 7 days
- [ ] File logging failures do not break OpenCode logging or plugin startup
- [ ] Documentation explains where to find project-local logs and retention behavior
- [ ] Acceptance review confirms the feature works from a real startup flow

## Notes
This work should make it easy to inspect plugin startup behavior for a project even when OpenCode's current-process log file is only reachable through `/proc/<pid>/fd/...`.

comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text:
## Simplification opportunity: doc task could be folded into implementation task

**What**: The documentation task (opencode-coder-hev) is 4 acceptance criteria that amount to "add a section to docs/MONITORING.md". This is ~15-30 lines of markdown. Having a separate beads issue, dependency chain, and review cycle for this is overhead that exceeds the work itself.

The doc task creates scheduling overhead (dependency ordering, separate claiming, separate closing) for work that takes 5 minutes and is naturally done at the end of the implementation task.

**Suggested action**: Consider merging the documentation criteria into opencode-coder-pul as an additional acceptance criterion: "docs/MONITORING.md updated with project-local log section covering path, rotation, retention, and coexistence with OpenCode logs." Then close opencode-coder-hev as unnecessary. This reduces the plan to: 1 epic, 1 implementation task, 1 acceptance review — which matches the actual scope.

title: Release v0.33.1
description: Complete GitHub release workflow for version 0.33.1
close_reason: v0.33.1 released and verified

comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text:
## BLOCKER: Commit 055d2f9 has not been pushed to origin/main

**What**: `git log origin/main..HEAD` shows commit `055d2f9 feat: improve startup readiness and release validation` exists only locally. The remote `main` does not have it.

**Why**: The release workflow checks out `main` from GitHub. If this commit is not on `origin/main`, the workflow will run quality gates and build against stale code, then create a release that does not contain the changes you're releasing. The version bump commit and tag will be on top of v0.33.0 code, not on top of 055d2f9. The entire release would be wrong.

**Suggested action**: Push before executing this epic: `git push origin main`. Task .3 (Version Bump) does include `git push origin main`, but that only works if no force push or rebase conflict intervenes. Consider adding an explicit pre-flight check in task .1 that verifies `origin/main` matches `HEAD`, not just that the working tree is clean.

comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text:
## Quality gates task (.1) runs `bun test` but RELEASING.md says `test:unit` + `test:integration`

**What**: Task .1 runs `bun test`, which executes ALL tests including e2e. The release workflow (release.yml) runs `test:unit` and `test:integration` specifically. The RELEASING.md pre-release checklist says `bun run test:unit && bun run test:integration`. These are three different test scopes.

**Why**: If e2e tests are flaky and block the local gate unnecessarily, the local quality gate doesn't match what the workflow will actually run. More practically: `bun test` will be slower than needed. The local pre-flight should match the workflow's gates.

**Suggested action**: Align task .1 commands with the workflow: use `bun run test:unit && bun run test:integration` instead of `bun test`. If you want e2e too, add it explicitly and accept the time cost.

comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text:
## CHANGELOG.md is not updated for v0.33.1

**What**: The pre-release checklist in `docs/RELEASING.md` line 56 says "CHANGELOG.md updated with new version and changes". The current CHANGELOG.md has `[Unreleased]` as an empty section and no `[0.33.1]` entry. Neither the quality gates task (.1) nor the docs task (.2) mentions updating CHANGELOG.md.

**Why**: This is a documented prerequisite in RELEASING.md. Skipping it means the project's changelog drifts from the release history. The workflow itself doesn't enforce or auto-generate it, so it will be silently skipped.

**Suggested action**: Either (a) add a CHANGELOG.md update step to task .2 (Documentation Check), or (b) explicitly decide to skip it for this patch and document that decision as a task .2 stop-condition exception. Don't leave it as an unmarked gap.

comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text:
## Tasks .4 and .5 overlap — release notes are passed twice with divergence risk

**What**: Task .4 (Create GitHub Release) passes `release_notes` inline to `gh workflow run`. Task .5 (Write Release Notes) then edits the release with `gh release edit --notes-file release-notes.md`. The release notes content appears in both task descriptions, and they're supposed to be the same text, but the inline version in .4 uses escaped newlines while .5 uses a markdown code block.

**Why**: Two tasks writing the same content creates a divergence risk. If someone edits the notes in .5 but not in .4, the workflow creates a release with notes A, then .5 immediately overwrites with notes B. If .5 fails (e.g., `release-notes.md` doesn't exist because nobody wrote the file), the release ships with the .4 version and nobody notices the inconsistency.

**Suggested action**: Merge .5 into .4. The workflow trigger command already contains the release notes, and `softprops/action-gh-release` writes them to the GitHub release. If notes need post-hoc editing, that's ad hoc, not a planned step. This eliminates a divergence-prone handoff and reduces the epic from 7 to 6 tasks.

comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text:
## Release notes miscategorize changes — most "Fixed" items are not fixes

**What**: The proposed release notes list 4 items under "Fixed":
1. "startup readiness now waits for aimgr initialization" — this is a behavioral change/feature. The old code worked (fire-and-forget init); this deliberately changes startup sequencing.
2. "project detection no longer carries unused git platform/remote metadata" — this is refactoring (dead code removal). Nothing was broken.
3. "/coder/status now detects supported plugin install scopes correctly" — this IS a fix.
4. "release verification docs now distinguish package visibility from auth failures" — this is a docs improvement, already listed under Docs.

**Why**: Mislabeling changes as "Fixed" misleads consumers about what changed. Users reading "Fixed: startup readiness waits for aimgr init" may think there was a startup bug. The semver implications also matter: removing exported interface fields and changing startup behavior are not patch-level fixes.

**Suggested action**: Recategorize:
- **Changed**: startup readiness now sequences aimgr initialization before project detection, with automatic resource repair
- **Changed**: removed unused `git.platform` and `git.remote` fields from project context
- **Fixed**: /coder/status now probes multiple plugin install scopes (@dynatrace-oss, @hk9890)
- Remove item 4 from Fixed (it's already in Docs)

comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text:
## Verification task (.6) should separate hard gates from soft gates

**What**: Task .6 includes an installation check using `TOKEN="<token-with-read:packages>"` as a placeholder. The task's stop condition says "stop if install checks fail."

**Why**: The task as written doesn't distinguish between "publication failed" and "I don't have a token with read:packages scope." If the executor hits this step without a PAT, the stop condition fires and the release appears failed when it may actually be fine. The `npm view` check (which is separate from authenticated install) is the better existence proof and is already in the checklist.

**Suggested action**: Restructure the verification checklist into:
- **Hard gates** (must pass): tag exists, GitHub release is not draft, `npm view` shows the version
- **Soft gate** (informational): authenticated `npm install` succeeds — note this requires a PAT with `read:packages` and may be skipped if unavailable

This way the task can be closed on hard gates alone.

comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text:
## Version semantics question: is 0.33.1 correct for these changes?

**What**: The diff removes `git.platform` and `git.remote` from the exported `ProjectContext` interface and changes startup from fire-and-forget to sequential await. Both are observable behavioral changes.

**Why**: Under strict semver, removing fields from an exported interface is a breaking change. The startup sequencing change affects timing behavior. This argues for a minor bump (0.34.0), not a patch (0.33.1).

**Suggested action**: This is a judgment call, not a blocker. If no external consumers depend on the removed fields (likely — this is a plugin's internal project.yaml), 0.33.1 is pragmatically fine. But document the decision: "Removed git.platform and git.remote from project context — no known external consumers." If there ARE consumers of that YAML structure, bump to 0.34.0.

comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text:
## 738-line Scion brainstorming doc is unusual for a patch release

**What**: The diff includes `docs/brainstorming/scion-integration.md` — a 738-line speculative design document. It's mentioned in the release notes as "added Scion integration brainstorming notes" under Docs.

**Why**: Brainstorming documents are not typically shipped as part of a patch release. Including a large speculative architecture document in 0.33.1 may confuse consumers about the release's purpose. It's not harmful, but it's unusual and muddies what's a focused fix/improvement release.

**Suggested action**: Not a blocker. If you want to include it, acknowledge it clearly: "Added Scion integration brainstorming document (design exploration only, no implementation changes)." Consider whether this would be better in a 0.34.0 release.

comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text:
## No CI run exists for commit 055d2f9

**What**: `gh run list --limit 5` shows the latest CI run was for `docs: prepare changelog for v0.33.0`. Commit `055d2f9` was never pushed, so there is no CI run for the code that will be released.

**Why**: Task .1 checks "Latest CI on main is green" but the latest CI was for a different commit. The quality gates task will run tests locally, which is good, but the release workflow will ALSO run tests — and if there's an environment-specific failure (different Bun version, different Node 20 behavior), you'll only find out after the workflow starts. Pushing first and letting CI run gives you an early signal.

**Suggested action**: Push to `origin/main` first, wait for CI to go green, THEN start executing the epic. This de-risks the workflow execution step (.4).

comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text: Execution update: release is temporarily blocked by `opencode-coder-1eh` after CI on commit `f55c462` failed in `tests/integration/plugin.test.ts`. I have fixed the test locally and will push the repair before resuming the quality gates, CI check, and workflow dispatch.

title: Status command reports plugin not installed when package scope/path differs
description:
## Description
The `/coder/status` health output can falsely report that the plugin is not installed because it checks the wrong package scope/path.

Observed during investigation:
- OpenCode config uses `@dynatrace-oss/opencode-coder`
- actual installed package on disk was `~/.cache/opencode/node_modules/@hk9890/opencode-coder/package.json`
- plugin version `0.31.1` was present and loadable
- status output still said package metadata was unavailable / plugin not installed

## Expected Behavior
The status command should detect the installed plugin package correctly across supported package scopes and install locations, and should not report a false negative when the plugin is active and installed.

## Files to Modify
- `ai-resources/commands/opencode-coder/status.md` or corresponding implementation path
- any plugin/package-detection utility used by status/doctor flows
- related tests

## Acceptance Criteria

title: Release verification gh auth token flow fails for GitHub Packages because active token lacks package-read scope
description:
## Problem
The release verification/authentication guidance assumes that `gh auth token` can be used directly as the npm authentication token for reading `@dynatrace-oss/opencode-coder` from GitHub Packages.

In the current environment, that assumption is false: the active GitHub CLI token does not include the required package-read scope, so npm access to GitHub Packages fails even though the package is published correctly.

## Expected Behavior
If the documentation recommends using `gh auth token` for GitHub Packages verification, that flow should succeed with the documented prerequisites.

If additional token scopes are required, the documentation should say so explicitly and provide a working verification method.

## Actual Behavior
Using the active `gh auth token` in `.npmrc` causes package install from GitHub Packages to fail with `npm ERR! code E403`:

```text
npm error 403 Forbidden - GET https://npm.pkg.github.com/@dynatrace-oss%2fopencode-coder
npm error 403 Permission permission_denied: The token provided does not match expected scopes.
```

At the same time:
- `npm view @dynatrace-oss/opencode-coder@0.33.0 --registry=https://npm.pkg.github.com` succeeds
- a scoped install using existing working npm auth succeeds

That confirms the package exists and publication succeeded; the failure is specific to the `gh auth token` npm auth flow.

## Steps to Reproduce
1. Confirm GitHub CLI auth status:
   ```bash
   gh auth status
   ```
2. Observe that the active token scopes do **not** include `read:packages`
3. Create a clean temp directory and write `.npmrc` using the active GitHub CLI token:
   ```bash
   TOKEN=$(gh auth token)
   printf '@dynatrace-oss:registry=https://npm.pkg.github.com\n//npm.pkg.github.com/:_authToken=%s\n' "$TOKEN" > .npmrc
   ```
4. Attempt package installation:
   ```bash
   npm install --no-save @dynatrace-oss/opencode-coder@0.33.0
   ```
5. Observe `E403 permission_denied` from GitHub Packages

## Environment
- **Operating System**: Linux
- **Node.js Version**: v24.14.0
- **npm Version**: 11.9.0
- **bd CLI Version**: 0.59.0
- **Package under verification**: `@dynatrace-oss/opencode-coder@0.33.0`
- **Shell**: bash
- **Active gh token scopes**: `gist`, `read:org`, `repo`, `workflow` (no `read:packages`)

## Evidence
Reproduced locally on 2026-03-12.

Broken auth flow:
```bash
TOKEN=$(gh auth token)
printf '@dynatrace-oss:registry=https://npm.pkg.github.com\n//npm.pkg.github.com/:_authToken=%s\n' "$TOKEN" > .npmrc
npm install --no-save @dynatrace-oss/opencode-coder@0.33.0
```

Observed failure:
```text
npm error 403 Permission permission_denied: The token provided does not match expected scopes.
```

Working comparison:
```bash
printf '@dynatrace-oss:registry=https://npm.pkg.github.com\n' > .npmrc
npm install --no-save @dynatrace-oss/opencode-coder@0.33.0
```

The working comparison confirms publication is healthy and the broken part is the token-based authentication guidance.

## Root Cause Analysis
The documented `gh auth token` verification path assumes the active GitHub CLI token is authorized for GitHub Packages reads.

In this environment, the active token lacks the required package-read scope, so GitHub Packages rejects the request with `permission_denied`.

This is separate from `opencode-coder-isp`:
- `opencode-coder-isp` = wrong registry routing breaks transitive dependencies
- `opencode-coder-eb3` = the `gh auth token`-based auth method is not valid unless the token has package-read scope

## Affected Documentation / Flows
- release verification notes/tasks that recommend using `gh auth token` for npm auth
- troubleshooting guidance that implies `gh auth login` is sufficient for GitHub Packages verification
- any automation or manual verification flow that assumes `gh auth token` always grants package-read access

## Recommended Fix Direction
1. Update release/auth documentation to explicitly require a token with GitHub Packages read scope (for example `read:packages`)
2. Do not imply that `gh auth token` is universally sufficient for npm verification
3. Provide a known-good verification method using either:
   - a PAT/token with package-read scope, or
   - an existing npm auth configuration already known to work
4. Separate package existence verification from package-auth verification in release docs

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] Documentation explicitly states the token scope requirements for GitHub Packages npm verification
- [ ] The recommended auth flow succeeds in a clean temp directory when the documented prerequisites are met
- [ ] Release verification guidance distinguishes package publication success from auth misconfiguration/scope failures
- [ ] The docs no longer imply that any active `gh auth token` is sufficient for GitHub Packages reads
close_reason: Updated release docs to require read:packages-capable npm token, clarified metadata-vs-auth verification distinction, and removed implication that any gh auth token works

comments.text:
## .3 and .4 could be merged — the split adds overhead without reducing risk

**What**: Task .3 (package metadata, install docs, release workflow) and task .4 (runtime identity, tests, generated artifacts) are both blocked on .1, touch overlapping concerns, and must be done by the same person in the same session to avoid broken builds. For example: .3 updates `package.json` name, .4 updates `src/core/version.ts` fallback — but both reference the same package identity string, and the build/test quality gates in .4 will fail if .3's changes aren't committed yet.

**Why**: The current split means .4 depends on .3 being fully merged first, but in practice a single agent session would do both tasks atomically to get a green build. Splitting them creates artificial coordination overhead (two claims, two PRs, one depends on the other) for what is functionally one batch of find-and-replace work. The dependency chain .1 → .3 → .4 is serial anyway, so parallelization isn't a benefit.

**Suggested action**: Consider merging .3 and .4 into a single task: "Implement chosen package identity across metadata, docs, runtime, tests, and release workflow." The acceptance criteria from both tasks combine naturally. This would reduce the epic from 5 tasks to 4, which is the right size for this scope. If you prefer to keep them separate for review granularity, document explicitly that .4 should be done in the same branch/PR as .3 to avoid a broken intermediate state.

## Description

1. Create a new reference/workflow file under `ai-resources/skills/opencode-coder/references/` for simplify behavior.
2. Update `ai-resources/skills/opencode-coder/SKILL.md` so the skill description and routing table mention simplify as a supported use case.
3. Treat freeform command arguments as optional focus guidance.

   - staged files from `git diff --name-only --cached`
   - unstaged files from `git diff --name-only`

5. Instruct the workflow to spawn three parallel review passes focused on:
   - code reuse / duplication
   - code quality / readability / maintainability
   - efficiency / performance
6. Require aggregation and deduplication of findings, then apply safe fixes directly.
7. Require ask-first behavior for broad or risky refactors, while keeping the default flow streamlined.
8. Create `ai-resources/commands/simplify.md` as a thin wrapper that loads the `opencode-coder` skill and tells the agent to follow the simplify workflow with the user's arguments.
9. End with a concise summary of what changed, what was intentionally not changed, and any follow-up issues to file.

comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text:
Discussion outcome: user-centered `coder-docs` flow model should be organized around four primary use cases instead of the current workflow-decomposition-first surface.

Proposed primary use cases:
1. Create project docs — scan the repo, establish canonical docs, and create the baseline doc set from best practices.
2. Update docs to match project truth — inspect current docs against the current repo, validate commands/paths/claims, update docs only, and do not modify project source files.
3. Improve docs structure/quality — compare the current doc structure against best practices, propose or apply split/merge/slim/consolidation changes, and improve taxonomy/routing quality.
4. Review/validate docs without editing — produce a read-only summary of what is outdated, what is incorrect, and what should be improved structurally.

Secondary/specialized flow:
- AGENTS-only guidance should remain available, but as a specialized secondary path rather than a co-equal primary use case.

Observed overlap/confusion to resolve during cleanup:
- `Project-doc setup and taxonomy` vs `Initialize and set up project docs`
- `Initialize and set up project docs` vs `Docs lifecycle`
- `Improve-doc workflow` vs `Docs lifecycle`
- `Project-doc review` vs read-only discussion-first improvement
- `AGENTS generation guidance` is too prominent as a top-level route relative to the four user-centered use cases

Implication for the task: evaluate whether `coder-docs` should be rewritten so the routing table and description are centered on create / update / improve / review-validate, with AGENTS guidance handled as a specialized companion path.

comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text:
Use-case coverage analysis for `coder-docs` based on the user-centered model below.

Primary use cases to support:
1. Create project docs — scan the repo, establish canonical docs, and create a baseline doc set from best practices.
2. Update docs to match project truth — inspect current docs against the current repo, validate commands/paths/claims, update docs only, and do not modify project source files.
3. Improve docs structure/quality — compare current docs against best practices, propose or apply split/merge/slim/consolidation changes, and improve taxonomy/routing quality.
4. Review/validate without editing — produce a read-only summary of what is outdated, incorrect, or should be improved structurally.

Current support assessment:
- Use case 1 (create): supported, but split awkwardly across `project-setup.md`, `docs-init.md`, and `project-docs-lifecycle.md`.
- Use case 2 (update): supported in substance, but weakly expressed as a first-class route. "update" is buried inside lifecycle and the docs-only / verify-against-repo-truth boundary is not prominent enough.
- Use case 3 (improve): supported, but modeled confusingly because "Improve-doc workflow" is routed separately while its actual execution modes live inside `project-docs-lifecycle.md`.
- Use case 4 (review/validate): weakest support. `project-doc-review-guidelines.md` is reviewer-oriented, but there is no clean top-level read-only overview/validate flow that combines correctness findings and improvement suggestions without editing.

Main overlap/confusion points:
1. `Project-doc setup and taxonomy` vs `Initialize and set up project docs`
   - setup defines the model and ownership boundaries
   - init is mostly a wrapper that immediately delegates to setup + lifecycle
   - likely too much top-level separation for an agent-facing route table
2. `Initialize and set up project docs` vs `Docs lifecycle`
   - init already says: if baseline missing, use setup + lifecycle; if baseline exists, refresh using lifecycle
   - this makes init feel like a thin entry shim rather than a distinct flow
3. `Improve-doc workflow` vs `Docs lifecycle`
   - both route to lifecycle in practice
   - improve-doc appears to be a mode within lifecycle, not a truly separate top-level workflow
4. `Project-doc review` vs read-only discussion-first improvement
   - both can look like "review our docs before changing anything"
   - one is reviewer/checklist oriented, the other is proposal-oriented
   - the distinction is not sharp enough for reliable routing
5. `AGENTS generation guidance`
   - valid specialized path, but too prominent as a top-level route relative to the four primary user-centered use cases
   - AGENTS is usually part of create/update/improve, except when explicitly requested as a standalone task

Changes likely needed to support the four use cases properly:
1. Re-center the top-level routing table around the four primary user intents:
   - Create project docs
   - Update docs to match project truth
   - Improve docs structure/quality
   - Review/validate docs without editing
   - Keep AGENTS-only guidance as a secondary/specialized route
2. Make one primary runtime entrypoint own use case 1 (probably `docs-init.md`, but rewritten to be a full creation flow rather than a thin wrapper).
3. Make use case 2 explicit as its own runtime flow:
   - inspect docs against current repo
   - validate commands/paths/claims
   - update docs only
   - do not modify source files
   - report what was changed and what was verified
4. Make use case 3 explicit as a structure/quality improvement flow:
   - compare current doc set against best practices and taxonomy
   - identify split/merge/slim/consolidation candidates
   - default to proposal-first / ask-before-destructive changes
5. Add or refactor a dedicated read-only use case 4 flow:
   - inspect docs and repo
   - summarize outdated or incorrect guidance
   - summarize structural improvement opportunities
   - make no edits
6. Clarify that `project-doc-review-guidelines.md` is reviewer/checklist support, not automatically the full user-facing overview/validate workflow unless it is rewritten to serve that purpose.
7. Clarify that `project-doc-guidelines.md` is supporting guidance, not a top-level route on its own.
8. Reposition `agents-md-template.md` as a specialized companion or subflow that is usually invoked from create/update/improve rather than presented as a co-equal primary use case.

Practical implication for this task:
- Cleanup of non-runtime text is still in scope.
- But the task should also judge whether the current routing model itself needs restructuring so an agent can reliably choose the right flow for the four primary user intents without guessing.
- If that restructuring is too large for this cleanup task, file a focused follow-up issue for coder-docs workflow redesign.

comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text:
Reviewer assessment summary for `coder-docs` flow coverage:

Overall verdict: partial / structurally muddled. The skill substance covers the intended work, but the routing surface does not clearly present the four primary user-centered use cases. An execution agent is likely to default into the lifecycle reference because multiple routing rows overlap and several rows resolve to the same file.

Coverage by use case:
1. Create project docs — PARTIAL
   - Supported by `project-setup.md`, `docs-init.md`, and lifecycle Phase 2.
   - Weakness: split across three files with no single clear create flow.
2. Update docs to match project truth — WEAK/PARTIAL
   - Supported in substance by lifecycle inspect/refresh/audit/verify phases.
   - Weakness: not expressed as a first-class route; no strong docs-only / do-not-modify-source-files contract.
3. Improve docs structure/quality — PARTIAL
   - Supported by lifecycle consolidate/slim/split logic and improve-doc modes.
   - Weakness: improve-doc is modeled as a separate top-level route even though it is really a mode within lifecycle.
4. Review/validate without editing — WEAK
   - Supported partly by `project-doc-review-guidelines.md`.
   - Weakness: no explicit read-only contract; current decision rules can route the agent into discussion-first improve mode, which still leads to execution.

Key confusion/overlap findings:
- `SKILL.md` has multiple overlapping rows that resolve to the same lifecycle reference.
- `docs-init.md` is a thin wrapper that mostly delegates to setup + lifecycle.
- `project-setup.md` and `project-structure.md` overlap on taxonomy and AGENTS routing rules.

- AGENTS guidance is over-promoted as a top-level route even though it is usually a sub-step of create/update/improve.

1. Re-center the routing table around the four user intents:
   - Create baseline docs
   - Update docs against repo truth
   - Improve docs structure/quality
   - Review docs without editing
   - Keep AGENTS-only guidance as a specialized secondary route

title: Normalize external tool prerequisites for integration and e2e tests
description:
Current test setup treats external binaries inconsistently across suites. We need a shared prerequisite layer that (1) defines which host tools are required for integration/e2e/manual-launcher coverage, (2) resolves or verifies those binaries in the host environment before test execution, (3) fails fast or skips deterministically when required tools are unavailable, and (4) removes duplicated PATH/bootstrap logic across test files.

Scope:

title: bd create --deps rejects hierarchical issue IDs resolved by bd show
description:
## Discovered in
Acceptance verification follow-up filing on 2026-04-18 while creating bugs discovered during review of `opencode-coder-bwrr`.

## Expected
If `bd show <hierarchical-id>` resolves an issue successfully, that same hierarchical ID should also be accepted by `bd create --deps ...` when creating a dependency.

## Actual
`bd create --deps discovered-from:opencode-coder-bwrr.4 ...` warned that `opencode-coder-bwrr.4` was not found, even though `bd show opencode-coder-bwrr.4` resolved earlier in the same repository session.

## Repro
1. From `/home/hans/dev/github/opencode-coder`, run `bd show opencode-coder-bwrr.4`.
2. Then run `bd create --type bug --deps discovered-from:opencode-coder-bwrr.4 --title "tmp" --description "tmp"`.
3. Observe the dependency warning.

## Impact
Follow-up bugs discovered during acceptance cannot be linked cleanly to hierarchical acceptance/task IDs, which weakens tracker history and makes later review harder.

## Evidence
- Verification session on 2026-04-18 while creating follow-up issue `opencode-coder-axu`.
close_reason: Closing as duplicate/session artifact tied to non-resolving hierarchical IDs in the same session; reviewer judged it not a separate product defect.

comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text: Review verdict: LIKELY DUPLICATE / CONSEQUENCE OF oo5. What: if the hierarchical IDs stopped resolving (oo5), then of course --deps referencing those IDs would also fail. This is the same root cause, not a separate bug. The description even says 'bd show resolved earlier in the same session' — meaning it worked before the state corruption from oo5 happened. Why it matters: tracking a symptom separately from its cause creates duplicate work and confusing tracker history. Suggested action: close as duplicate of oo5, or if oo5 is closed as session artifact, close this too.

title: Team-mode beads init can exceed default 120s timeout
description:
## Discovered in
Manual Phase 2 acceptance validation for `opencode-coder-bwrr` on 2026-04-18.

## Expected
Team-mode Phase 2 beads initialization should complete within the default agent bash timeout, or the flow should explicitly allow a longer-running init step.

## Actual
During Phase 2 team-mode validation, the inner `bd init --skip-agents` step exceeded the 120000ms timeout. A later `bd status` check indicated the beads workspace eventually became healthy, so the operation appears to finish eventually but too slowly for the default execution budget.

## Repro
1. Prepare an `empty-project` launcher workspace with local working-tree resources.
2. Set `.coder/opencode-coder.yaml` to `mode: team`.
3. Install `package/coder-core`, `package/coder-beads`, `package/coder-docs`, and `package/complexity-review` into `.opencode/`.
4. Run `opencode run --command opencode-coder/init --format json`.
5. Observe the `coder-beads` Phase 2 step run `bd init --skip-agents` and exceed the default timeout.

## Impact
Phase 2 team-mode setup can appear to fail under normal agent time budgets even when the underlying beads init eventually succeeds. This can block or confuse setup automation.

## Evidence
- Manual launcher artifact: `/home/hans/dev/github/opencode-coder/.manual-test-runs/run-FHVtcp`
- Session output artifact: `/home/hans/.local/share/opencode/tool-output/tool_da11378ef001wxNuKJMxCbXXR2`

comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text: Review verdict: VALID bug, well-scoped. What: bd init --skip-agents exceeding 120s in a team-mode launcher environment is a real problem that will hit any agent-driven setup automation. The description, repro, and evidence are solid. Why it matters: if Phase 2 team-mode init reliably times out under default agent budgets, automated setup is broken for team mode. P2 is appropriate. Suggested action: keep as-is. This should be fixed as a near-term follow-up — either bd init needs to be faster, or the init command needs to set an explicit longer timeout for this step. Defer from the current install/setup commit but prioritize it next.

comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text: Reviewer follow-up: valid product bug with solid evidence. Keep open as a real follow-up; should be prioritized ahead of cosmetic bootstrap polish.

comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text: Epic relation review: reviewed against opencode-coder-wk0 and kept standalone. This is a separate team-mode bd init timeout/performance issue, not the prerequisite normalization work in the epic.

comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text: Validation 2026-04-19: could not cleanly revalidate the original timeout symptom in the current environment because the repro path now fails earlier for a different reason. Reproduced the documented setup (empty-project workspace, mode: team, aimgr-installed coder-core/coder-beads/coder-docs/complexity-review) and then ran 'opencode run --command opencode-coder/init --format json'. The command returned in ~9s with an upstream 'model_not_supported' API error before reaching the long-running Phase 2 beads init path, so the original >120s timeout was not observed in this environment. Bug remains unresolved from this validation pass because the original code path was blocked by a different failure.

title: Behavior eval planning prompts mutate live beads state
description:
## Description
Behavior evals for planning workflows are allowed to execute real `bd create` commands against the live repository tracker. When validation is run against the real repo, the eval creates actual beads issues instead of isolated artifacts.

## Why This Is Still Valid
The stray issues from the 2026-03-24 validation run were cleaned up, but the underlying eval prompts and execution model remain unchanged. Re-running the same planning-oriented evals can recreate live tracker pollution.

## Current Behavior
- Planning evals can create live issues such as `opencode-coder-s0xc` and related cleanup artifacts (`opencode-coder-o67c`, `opencode-coder-xf6y`, `opencode-coder-ue03`)
- Validation is not idempotent and leaves tracker noise unless someone manually cleans it up

## Expected Behavior
Running the full opencode-coder eval set should create zero new issues in the real repository tracker.

## Likely Affected Areas / Files
- `ai-resources/skills/opencode-coder/evals/evals.json` — planning-oriented eval prompts such as eval-0 and eval-1
- Any behavior-eval or manual-validation harness that currently runs those prompts against the real repository root instead of a disposable workspace
- `ai-resources/skills/opencode-coder-skill-creator/scripts/run_eval.py` or equivalent execution harness code

## Preferred Fix Direction
Prefer generic harness isolation over prompt-only suppression. The eval system should stay reusable across many projects, so the fix should not depend on a repo-specific fixture or the current repository's project tracker. Planning-oriented evals should run inside a disposable synthesized workspace (temporary git project plus isolated beads state), optionally seeded from eval metadata such as input files. Prompt wording can still clarify expected output, but isolation should be the primary protection.

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] Running the full eval set leaves the real repository tracker unchanged
- [ ] Planning evals run in an isolated temporary workspace with their own beads state instead of the live project tracker
- [ ] The isolated workspace approach is generic and reusable across many projects, not hardcoded to this repository
- [ ] Planning evals still demonstrate the intended epic/task/bug structure inside the disposable workspace
- [ ] Validation includes a before/after check proving the live tracker stayed unchanged
- [ ] Any eval expectations or harness docs are updated to reflect isolated planning-eval execution
close_reason: Fixed by isolated functional eval workspaces and hooks: planning evals now create beads state only in disposable temp workspaces, and end-to-end verification confirmed live repo beads state unchanged before/after running evals 0 and 1.

comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text: Discovered after validation task opencode-coder-am02.5 when user asked about unexpected epic opencode-coder-s0xc.

comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text:
## Evidence files are gitignored and not reproducible by another tasker

**What**: The bug references `ai-resources/skills/opencode-coder-workspace/iteration-1/run-1/summary.md` and `VALIDATION-REPORT.md` as evidence. That entire directory (`ai-resources/skills/opencode-coder-workspace/`) is in `.gitignore` line 57. These files do not exist on disk in the current checkout and have never been committed to the repository. A tasker picking this up cannot see the evidence.

**Why**: Without accessible evidence, a tasker must re-run the full validation to reproduce the problem, which is expensive and nondeterministic (it may not produce the same stray issues). The bug claims to be about eval 0 specifically — but without the output, the tasker has to guess which prompt and which harness path triggered the mutation. This turns a focused fix into an open-ended investigation.

**Suggested action**: Either (1) inline the critical evidence directly into the bug description — specifically: the exact beads commands that the eval output contained, and the harness invocation command used — or (2) commit the relevant evidence files to a non-gitignored path (e.g. `.beads/evidence/`). The stray epic `opencode-coder-s0xc` is still in beads and can serve as partial evidence, but the harness execution path that led to it is the missing piece.

comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text:
## No acceptance criteria defining "fixed"

**What**: The bug describes what happened and why it's bad, but does not define what a successful fix looks like. Is the fix (a) adding dry-run support to the eval harness? (b) Wrapping eval prompts to suppress tool calls? (c) Running evals in an isolated beads database? (d) Post-eval cleanup? (e) Something else entirely?

**Why**: A tasker will read this, understand the problem, and then stall on "what should I build?" The fix space is wide — from eval harness changes to beads isolation to prompt sandboxing — and the bug gives no guidance on which approach is expected or preferred. Different fixes have wildly different scope and complexity.

**Suggested action**: Add acceptance criteria. At minimum: "After the fix, running the full eval set against the live repo produces zero new beads issues in the real tracker. Validation must verify this by running the eval set and checking `bd list` before and after." Optionally, state the preferred approach (e.g., "prefer eval harness isolation over prompt modification").

comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text:
## Cross-cutting: all four validation bugs share the same evidence accessibility problem

**What**: Bugs j6nc, 4zbm, 9io8, and akh0 all reference evidence under `ai-resources/skills/opencode-coder-workspace/` which is gitignored. None of them inline the critical evidence needed to reproduce or fix the issue. This is a systemic pattern, not an isolated omission.

**Why**: The validation workflow produces artifacts in a gitignored directory, then files bugs referencing those artifacts. This means the bugs are only actionable on the machine where the validation ran, in the session where it ran. This is a process gap — the validation workflow should either commit evidence to a non-gitignored path, or the bug-filing step should require inlining evidence into the issue description.

**Suggested action**: As an immediate fix, update all four bug descriptions to inline their critical evidence before assigning any of them for execution. As a longer-term fix, update the validation workflow to either (a) save evidence outside the gitignored workspace, or (b) require that filed bugs include self-contained reproduction information. Consider filing this as a separate process improvement task if it's not addressed inline.

comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text: Additional fake issues now fully closed: opencode-coder-o67c (+ children), opencode-coder-xf6y, and opencode-coder-ue03.

comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text:
## Bug is valid but is a process/tooling gap, not a plugin code defect

**What**: The eval infrastructure runs planning prompts (eval-0: webshop search endpoint, eval-1: checkout crash bug) against the live repo, which means bd commands in the eval output actually execute and create real issues. The stray artifacts (opencode-coder-s0xc and children, opencode-coder-o67c, opencode-coder-xf6y, opencode-coder-ue03) have been closed per the last comment, but the underlying problem remains: there is no isolation between eval runs and the live beads database.

**Why**: This is a real problem for repeatable validation. However, the fix space is constrained by the OpenCode eval infrastructure — the plugin does not control how evals are executed. The realistic fix options are: (a) post-eval cleanup script that removes issues created during the eval window, (b) eval prompts that instruct the LLM to use dry-run or plan-only output instead of actual bd commands, (c) running evals against a disposable beads database (requires a separate workspace). Option (b) is the simplest and most maintainable — modify the eval prompts or add a system-level instruction that says "describe what you would create, do not actually create issues."

**Suggested action**: Reframe this bug as: "Eval prompts for planning workflows must instruct the LLM to describe planned beads output without executing bd commands." Acceptance criteria should be: running the full eval set produces zero new beads issues in the live tracker. The preferred fix approach should be prompt-level, not infrastructure-level, because the plugin does not own the eval harness execution environment.

comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text: Discussion update (2026-03-31): user suggested isolating planning evals from the live project tracker by running them in a disposable example/temp project with its own .beads instance rather than against the repository's project-based tracker. Need to evaluate whether the eval harness can copy a fixture workspace or synthesize a temporary git project, run evals there, and assert plan quality without mutating the real repo. This is now an active candidate fix direction alongside prompt-only suppression.

comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text: Feasibility update 2026-03-31: current eval runner already supports per-run isolated cwd via a temporary sandbox, so the temp-workspace approach is compatible with the framework direction. Gap: the sandbox only injects the skill and does not yet copy a fixture project, initialize git, initialize or seed beads, create prompt-referenced files, or export sandbox beads state before cleanup. Reusable fixture-copy patterns exist in tests/e2e/helpers/harness.ts and scripts/manual-test/index.ts. Likely fix is to extend the runner so each planning eval executes inside a copied fixture project with its own beads state and then records that temporary tracker state as artifacts while also checking the real repo tracker did not change.

comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text: Discussion outcome 2026-03-31: temp-workspace isolation is feasible with moderate harness work, but not supported end-to-end as-is. Current behavior runner already executes each eval in an isolated temporary cwd, yet it lacks project-fixture setup, git/beads initialization, prompt-file seeding, and artifact export of temporary beads state. Proposed approach: add a committed fixture project plus runner setup steps so planning evals execute in a copied disposable project and are graded from exported sandbox tracker artifacts instead of the live repo tracker.

comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text: Scope refinement 2026-03-31: user clarified the fix must be generic across many projects, so a repo-specific committed fixture is not sufficient as the primary design. Preferred direction is now a project-agnostic isolation mechanism in the eval harness: synthesize a disposable git workspace with isolated beads state and optionally hydrate eval-declared files into it. Repo-specific fixtures may still be useful for individual test cases, but the core protection must be harness-level and reusable across hundreds of repositories.

comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text: Discussion refinement 2026-03-31: in a generic temp-workspace harness, eval-declared files are only needed to recreate project context the prompt explicitly depends on. Many evals can run in an empty synthesized repo with fresh git + beads. Files become necessary when the prompt references concrete project artifacts or markers (for example , existing docs under , , , , or stealth/team markers). The harness should therefore support optional file hydration rather than requiring repo-specific fixtures for every eval.

comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text: Implementation note 2026-03-31: current framework does not automatically copy eval  into the temporary sandbox. In the existing Python trigger runner (), the per-run sandbox only contains injected skill content under  plus , and the runner reads only query/trigger fields. The  field exists in the eval schema/docs but is not presently wired into sandbox setup, so file-dependent behavior evals would require new hydration logic that writes those files into the synthesized workspace at their relative paths before execution.

comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text: Current runner insight 2026-03-31: the eval files field is inert in the present trigger runner. The model is not automatically given those files as injected context, and the runner does not copy them into the sandbox. Today the only guaranteed sandbox content is the injected skill plus minimal opencode metadata, so any file-dependent eval behavior would require explicit hydration or attachment logic added by the harness.

comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text: Clarification 2026-03-31: the concrete 'files are ignored' evidence applies to the current Python trigger-eval runner in this repo (skill-creator/scripts/run_eval.py), which operates on trigger-eval query sets and does not materialize eval files. The original Anthropic skill text does define a files field and instructs the orchestrator to pass input files to spawned runs, so the intended contract is that files matter. However, SKILL.md alone does not prove how the original runtime delivered them (copy into workspace, attachments, or explicit path handoff). Actionable takeaway for this bug: our OpenCode-side behavior-eval workflow needs an explicit generic file-hydration/input-files mechanism if we want parity with the original intent.

comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text: Discussion update 2026-03-31: likely no changes needed for trigger-eval pipeline. New candidate design is for functional evals only: add configurable pre-run and post-run hooks in eval metadata so each eval can prepare and inspect a disposable workspace (for example git init, beads init/seed, config markers, artifact export, cleanup/verification) without hardcoding project-specific fixture logic. User is considering hooks as a replacement or complement to the current files field.

comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text: Design direction 2026-03-31: functional eval isolation may be best expressed as workspace lifecycle hooks rather than repo-specific fixtures. Candidate model: eval metadata supports static input files plus  /  executed inside the disposable workspace, with explicit cwd/env/timeout semantics and artifact export. Trigger eval pipeline remains unchanged.

comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text: Design decisions 2026-03-31: for functional evals, hooks should use script paths only (no inline shell). Hook cwd should be the same disposable workspace root used for the eval run / skill execution. after_run should execute even if the model run fails. No separate after_failure phase for v1. Open design questions now center on hook naming/labels, script path resolution, args/env schema, timeout defaults, and artifact capture.

comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text: Hook design decisions 2026-03-31: functional eval hooks should use script paths only, resolved relative to the skill root. Hooks run with cwd set to the disposable workspace root used for the eval itself. Hooks may accept args. No per-hook env overrides in v1; runner should inject only standard eval/workspace variables. Hook entries should require human-readable names for logs/artifacts. after_run executes always, even when setup or model execution fails.

comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text: Hook schema refinement 2026-03-31: hook entries should support a human-readable name field for logs/artifacts, but the field is optional rather than required. When omitted, the runner can fall back to phase/index labels such as before_run-0 or after_run-1.

comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text: Hook naming refinement 2026-03-31: hook name remains optional. When omitted, the runner should derive the display name from the script name rather than using phase/index labels. Example: evals/hooks/init-beads.sh -> init-beads.sh (or the basename equivalent used consistently in logs/artifacts). Phase/index can remain available internally if needed for uniqueness, but the human-facing default label should be the script name.

comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text: Implementation work has been planned under epic opencode-coder-n3rw with child tasks opencode-coder-n3rw.2 (schema/lifecycle docs), opencode-coder-n3rw.3 (functional eval runner), opencode-coder-n3rw.4 (fixtures and regression coverage), plus acceptance review opencode-coder-n3rw.1. Trigger-eval automation remains unchanged; the plan focuses on functional-eval workspace hooks and isolation.

comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text: Added dedicated implementation task opencode-coder-n3rw.5 under epic opencode-coder-n3rw to create a reusable beads workspace setup hook script for functional evals. The bug now depends on acceptance review opencode-coder-n3rw.1 because the planned hook-based workspace isolation is the intended fix path.

comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text:
## Design Review Verdict: Q1 — Does this design fix the bug class?

**What**: Yes — the design is sufficient to fix the live-beads-mutation bug class. The core mechanism (each functional eval gets a disposable workspace with its own git init + beads init) creates a physical boundary that prevents bd create commands from touching the real .beads/ directory. This is the right kind of fix: structural isolation rather than prompt-level suppression.

**Why**: The isolation is enforced by filesystem boundary (different cwd → different .beads/ → different tracker), which is the strongest available guarantee without modifying the bd CLI itself. As long as the runner sets cwd correctly before handing off to the model, there is no path by which an eval-generated bd command can reach the live repo's tracker — bd resolves .beads/ relative to the working directory.

**Suggested action**: No change needed for this question. One guard to add during implementation: the runner should verify that the disposable workspace cwd does not contain a symlink or parent-traversal path that could accidentally resolve back to the live repo root. A simple realpath() check before execution would close that edge case.

comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text:
## Design Review Verdict: Q2 — Is the functional eval framework design sound?

**What**: Mostly — the hook extension model is sound, but there are several gaps that will cause implementation friction or runtime surprises if not addressed before coding starts.

**Why**: The before_run/after_run hook lifecycle, script-path-only execution, relative-to-skill-root resolution, and finally-style after_run semantics are all sensible and well-specified. The design avoids over-engineering (no per-hook env, no after_failure, no inline shell). However, several important behaviors are unspecified, as detailed in separate comments below.

**Suggested action**: Address the specific gaps called out in the follow-up comments. The framework shape is right — the issues are about missing boundary definitions, not wrong architecture.

comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text:
## Design Review Verdict: Q3 — Does the framework stay generic?

**What**: Yes — the design successfully separates generic framework (hooks, disposable workspaces, lifecycle phases) from beads-specific logic (init-beads.sh hook script). The framework knows about scripts, cwd, and artifacts. It does not know about beads. The beads setup is a reusable hook script that happens to be the first consumer, properly located under evals/hooks/ rather than baked into the runner. This is the right layering.

**Why**: Task n3rw.5 (the beads workspace hook) is correctly scoped as a consumer of the framework, not part of it. The runner in n3rw.3 has no beads-specific code in its acceptance criteria. The hook schema in n3rw.2 defines generic script/args/timeout fields with no beads vocabulary. As long as the runner-injected environment variables (n3rw.3 instruction #5) stay generic (workspace path, artifacts dir, eval id, skill root), there is no beads leakage into the framework layer.

**Suggested action**: One preventive measure: the docs task (n3rw.2) should explicitly list the standard runner-injected env vars by name and document that they must remain project-agnostic. If the env var list is left as "for example workspace, artifacts dir, eval id/name, phase, and skill root metadata" without a normative definition, implementers may accidentally add beads-specific vars to the runner itself.

comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text:
## Risk: Existing evals 0 and 1 remain unfixed until the full epic completes

**What**: The bug (j6nc) is currently blocked on the acceptance review of the entire epic (n3rw.1). Evals 0 and 1 in evals/evals.json are planning-style prompts that exercise bd create. Until the functional eval runner and hooks are fully implemented, documented, tested, and acceptance-reviewed, these evals remain dangerous to run — they will still mutate the live tracker.

**Why**: The epic has 4 implementation tasks with dependencies. If any task stalls, the bug stays open and the evals remain hazardous. There is no interim safeguard against someone accidentally running the eval set and polluting the tracker again.

**Suggested action**: Add an immediate, low-cost interim safeguard: either (a) move evals 0 and 1 to a separate file (e.g., functional-evals.json) with a clear comment that they require the functional eval runner, so the trigger runner cannot accidentally pick them up, or (b) add a warning comment at the top of evals.json noting that evals 0-1 must not be run against the live repo. This is a 2-minute change that prevents the bug from recurring while the real fix is in progress.

comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text: Concrete design decisions are now locked into epic opencode-coder-n3rw tasks: functional evals will run from a bare disposable workspace with hook-created git/beads state only, before_run failure skips model execution but still triggers after_run, after_run always runs and can fail the eval, and trigger-vs-functional evals are separated by runner and schema. These decisions directly address live tracker mutation by moving planning-style beads setup into isolated functional eval workspaces.

comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text: Added implementation task opencode-coder-n3rw.6 under epic opencode-coder-n3rw to apply the new functional-eval hook system to the real opencode-coder planning evals. This ensures the bug is fixed in the actual opencode skill by moving beads-creating evals onto isolated workspace-local hooks and fixtures.

title: Duplicate: /simplify command-mode failure matches known headless slash-command limitation
description:
## Description
Manual validation of `/simplify` via `opencode run --command '/simplify ...'` in headless command mode fails, but this is not a new product bug in opencode-coder. It matches the already-triaged behavior from `opencode-coder-5vx`: agent-mediated slash commands are not a valid acceptance path in headless `--command` mode, especially when the workspace is not aimgr-initialized with installed skills.

## Validity Verdict
Invalid as a standalone bug; duplicate of `opencode-coder-5vx`.

## Why
- Same execution mode: headless `opencode run --command`
- Same symptom: slash-command run exits without useful workflow output and falls back to a generic command-route error
- Same constraint: slash-command workflows rely on skill loading and interactive agent/tool behavior that `--command` does not provide

## Expected Handling
Use interactive shell or TUI validation, plus an aimgr-initialized workspace with installed skills, when manually validating slash-command workflows such as `/simplify`.

## Resolution
Close this issue as a duplicate of `opencode-coder-5vx`; do not implement a new product-code change for this report.
close_reason: Duplicate of opencode-coder-5vx; headless --command slash-command validation is a known unsupported or invalid path rather than a new product bug.

comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text:
## Missing the actual error — "UnknownError" is not a diagnosis

**What**: The bug says logs show "UnknownError from /session/.../command route" but does not include the actual error message, stack trace, or log excerpt. The run IDs (run-ql1HcJ, run-bf9dmC) are mentioned but these are ephemeral manual harness outputs — a tasker cannot look them up.

**Why**: "UnknownError" is the generic fallback error. Without the actual error payload, response status, or stack trace, the tasker has no starting point for diagnosis. They would need to reproduce from scratch, which requires knowing the exact invocation command, opencode version, and environment state. The bug says "exits without executing workflow" but doesn't say whether the command was recognized and failed, or was never routed at all.

**Suggested action**: Add to the description: (1) the exact command invoked (e.g., `opencode run --command '/simplify ...'` — what was the `...`?), (2) the relevant log lines around the UnknownError (at least the error payload and 5 lines of context), (3) whether the command appeared in the skill's command registration output during startup (the "service=skill count=10 init" line suggests it was).

comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text:
## Scope unclear: is this a plugin bug, harness bug, or eval infrastructure bug?

**What**: The description says "may indicate command routing regression or harness/permission incompatibility requiring explicit handling." These are three completely different fix locations: (a) plugin command registration code, (b) opencode manual harness `--command` mode, (c) eval/test infrastructure permissions. The bug explicitly hedges between them without narrowing.

**Why**: A tasker needs to know where to start. If this is a harness issue, the fix is in the test infrastructure. If this is a command routing regression, the fix is in the plugin's command handler. If it's permissions, the fix might be in opencode itself (upstream). Assigning all three possibilities to one bug without narrowing guarantees the tasker will spend most of their time on diagnosis, not on fixing.

**Suggested action**: Before assigning for execution, do one of: (1) reproduce the failure and narrow to a single root cause, then update the description, or (2) split into a triage spike task ("determine whether /simplify failure is plugin routing, harness, or upstream") with a follow-up fix task. The current description is a triage task disguised as a bug.

comments.author: Hans Kohlreiter
comments.text:
## Likely duplicate of closed bug 5vx — same root cause, same harness, same behavior

**What**: This bug describes /simplify failing in opencode run --command '/simplify ...' mode in the manual harness, exiting with "UnknownError" and no simplify output. Closed bug opencode-coder-5vx documents the exact same failure pattern for /opencode-coder/docs, /opencode-coder/improve-doc, and /opencode-coder/init — all exiting cleanly with no output in --mode=command (headless). The extensive analysis on 5vx (6 review comments) concluded this is NOT a product bug — it is expected OpenCode platform behavior: opencode run --command is headless one-shot mode, but agent-mediated slash commands require interactive TUI/shell mode to work because they invoke skill(), question(), and multi-step tool chains.

**Why**: If this is the same root cause as 5vx, then 9io8 is not a real bug. It is an invalid test expectation. Keeping it open as a P1 blocker misleads the next person into investigating a plugin routing regression that does not exist. The "UnknownError" is likely OpenCode's fallback when a command template invokes skill() in headless mode with no installed skills in the isolated fixture workspace — the same scenario documented in 5vx.

**Suggested action**: Before investing any triage time on 9io8, verify the overlap by checking: (1) Was the failing run using --mode=command? The description says "command-mode manual run" which matches. (2) Was the fixture an aimgr-initialized workspace with skills installed, or a bare fixture? If both match the 5vx scenario, close 9io8 as a duplicate of 5vx with the same resolution: slash-command manual validation must use --mode=shell or --mode=tui, not --mode=command.

title: Investigate behavior eval automation timeouts in full opencode-coder validation
description:
## Description
Three behavior evals timed out at the current 240s budget during full validation, but the root cause is unknown. This is investigation work, not a fix-ready bug.

## Problem Statement
The timed-out evals are:
- eval-0 — planning-heavy webshop epic/task creation flow
- eval-1 — customer bug capture plus post-mortem flow
- eval-11 — incident-driven improve-doc workflow

13 of 16 behavior evals completed successfully. The goal here is to determine whether these 3 timeouts represent real regressions or simply prompts that exceed the current automation budget.

## Investigation Goals
1. Reproduce each timeout with enough logging and timing data to see where time is spent
2. Determine whether the cause is:
   - timeout too short for inherently expensive prompts
   - prompt/tool retry loop or agent confusion
   - actual workflow latency regression or code defect
3. For each eval, recommend one outcome: increase timeout, simplify prompt, file targeted follow-up bug, or accept as expected limitation

## Likely Affected Areas / Files
- `ai-resources/skills/opencode-coder/evals/evals.json`
- Validation harness/config that sets the 240s timeout for behavior evals
- Workflow docs and prompts exercised by eval-0, eval-1, and eval-11

## Deliverable
